Preferably in real life with an updated mission architecture & without the American flag on the suit…
… or an appearance from Mr John Connolly – my boss at the International Space University’s summer program in Haifa until September, when he returns to NASA to become their new head of Human Mars Mission Planning.
And a trip to any American theme park/exhibition wouldn’t be complete without a trip to the gift shop. I’d end up coming back to the gift shop on my last day to buy a waterproof jacket with the NASA logo embroidered on it, knowing I’d need it for storm chasing two weeks later… but it was nice to dream in the meantime;
Chances of this surviving the trip home intact 0%
Chances of this fitting in my backpack Also 0%
The heat was knocking it out of me, but with a few hours left until the visitor’s complex closed I decided to fully commit to seeing the best KSC had to offer:
Entrance to the KSC visitor complex’s Atlantis exhibition
I’d wanted to save seeing Space Shuttle Atlantis until the next day – I’d been repeatedly told it was the best of all the space shuttle exhibits, so I wanted to experience it when I was fully rested… but the temptation was too great to wait till the next morning;
SO. TOTALLY. WORTH IT.
I’m yet to see Space Shuttle Endeavor at the California Science Center, but of the three shuttles I’ve seen so far KSC’s Atlantis exhibition is without a doubt the most extraordinary shuttle experience yet. From walking under the external tank/boosters and passed Carl Sagan’s “The Sky Calls To Us” quote on the wall, to the ground shaking in the theater during the simulated shuttle launch, to the moment the theater screen suddenly goes transparent and you’re greeted with a view of the very final shuttle to fly – seeing Atlantis in all her glory is breathtaking.
I’ve heard from more that a few who’ve been that they became quite emotional – I just know probably shouldn’t have been cutting onions at a space shuttle exhibit.
The shuttle itself is absolutely stunning, and with Atlantis tilted over with its payload doors open to show the inside the hold you get a true sense of just how BIG it is. There’s also a whole bundle of shuttle artifacts on display, from the original shuttle prototype:
To the van that took astronauts from their suit-up area to every shuttle flight;
Right through to tires flown on Atlantis for STS-135, the very final shuttle flight:
And while I couldn’t get any pictures of it, the “Shuttle Launch Experience” is one hell of an experience. I can guess at how they do it, but numerous astronauts have said that it is easily the most accurate simulation of a real space shuttle launch they’ve experienced outside of actually riding a space shuttle. It was pretty incredible, but I’d recommend using the free lockers to secure your wallets, keys, sunglasses, ect – with all the shaking and tilting there is no way you’re going to want that stuff in your pockets.
Beneath space shuttle Atlantis there was also a special section dedicated to two of the space shuttles that didn’t come home: Challenger & Columbia. Personal artifacts of each of the 14 astronauts who perished in the two disasters are displayed in their memory.
Several of the wall quotes, the gallery, and Ilan Ramon’s display
So the first (half) day at the KSC visitor complex was frankly pretty full-on. I basically collapsed on the bed back at the hotel that night with a hamburger and watched This Week Tonight, until I heard through Twitter around 11pm that the SpaceX barge had returned to Port Canaveral with the landed JCSAT-14 first booster on top of it! Port Canaveral was only 25 minutes away in the car, but at nearly midnight I didn’t like my chances getting there, driving around a port to find it, then driving back – I figured I’d have better luck in the morning.
And luckily, 14 story rockets are pretty easy to spot in the morning daylight;
Port Canaveral is obviously an active port so I didn’t want to snoop around too much, but getting a good photo (without chain-link fence in the way) proved surprisingly difficult. Getting from Port Canaveral back to the KSC visitor complex was pretty straight forward though, so I drove in ready for another full on day – starting with lunch listening to, then meeting, Apollo 15 Command Module Pilot Al Worden!
Apollo 15 CMP Al Worden with yours truly
The remaining Apollo astronauts are an interesting bunch, so it was fascinating hearing Colonel Worden talk about his experiences before, during and after the Apollo years. As the Command Module Pilot he never walked on the Moon, but stayed in orbit around it for 3 days alone – a unique experience as one of the most physically isolated human beings in history. He’s also one of the very few people who have conducted an EVA in the deep space transiting between the Moon back to Earth.
Al Worden during his Apollo 15 EVA
There’s so much more to see at Cape Canaveral than just the visitor center though, so straight after meeting Al I headed out on a tour of the Cape’s launch pads
Space Launch Complex 40, leased to SpaceX
SpaceX’s “Horizontal Integration Facility” where their Falcon 9’s (& soon Falcon Heavy) are put together
Delta IV Heavy (carrying the NROL-37 spy satellite) that I’d planned my trip around seeing launch – it finally launched 5 weeks later
Besides looking at launch facilities from a far, we also got to stand a fairly significant distance from the Vertical Assembly Building;
The star I’m standing on is exactly the same size as each of the 50 stars painted in the flag on the VAB
As you can tell the “up close” part of the tour was pretty oversold, but again these are working launch facilities. On the flip side, we got significantly closer than we probably wanted to the local alligator population;
Don’t pull over & get out is all I’m saying
After the tour I had to make a critical decision: there was just enough time to get out to the Apollo/Saturn V center to have a look before it closed, but it would mean missing out on getting Al Worden’s signature at the same time. I couldn’t do both, so while I enjoyed meeting Al and lunch wouldn’t have minded getting him to sign a photo, I really couldn’t miss the opportunity to see a full-sized Saturn 5.
I can’t even begin to describe how big this thing is
The Apollo center is also home to the original firing room used for the launch of Apollo 8 – the first launch to send humans around the Moon and back;
The firing room was a complete experience just like space shuttle Atlantis, with the full Apollo 8 launch being re-enacted through voice-over and lights showing the control panel operators confirming GO/NO-GO for the launch. I was genuinely blown away by it all. Out in the main hall near the Saturn V was also the Apollo 15 Lunar Module that never was;
The Apollo 15 LEM was completely built and ready, but a redesign to incorporate the lunar rover meant it was cheaper and easier to build a whole new LEM and launch it rather than modify this one – so it survived for display, and the other one is in pieces on the Moon. Ultimately the only things that came back to Earth in one piece from any of the Apollo missions were the Command Modules… and they had one of those on display too;
Apollo 14 Command Module
The Apollo/Saturn V center was closing, but I managed to catch the very last show in the Apollo theater before the final bus back to the visitor center left me there;
The show was a perfect end to what had been an absolutely extraordinary couple of days at KSC. When I flopped back into bed in the hotel that night I was overwhelmed by everything I’d been lucky enough to see – so many things you’ve read about, thought and dreamed about for so long… right there in front of you. Real.
After all the exhibits, tours, lunch with an astronaut, and so much more; I had one more thing left to do at the Kennedy Space Center. I arrived early on the third day and had a breakfast burrito & coffee outside at one of the cafes, making a new friend in the process;
Breakfast at KSC: “Squirrels are cute” jumps up leg, steals food, runs away “Squirrels are assholes”
Then headed into the IMAX theater to watch a movie about the future of human Mars exploration narrated by Patrick Stewart (which subtly mentions Mars One)… but I was really just killing time. Because what I was really back at KSC for was to meet another Mars One candidate: George Hatcher!
GINGERS REPRESENT!
I’d put out a call to Mars One candidates in Florida to meet up while I was there, and both Hampton & George had responded, but logistics made all three of us being in the same place impossible. It was great getting to meet George – like Hampton he worked on the space shuttles when they were flying, but he now works as a planetary scientist at Kennedy Space Center. He’d been flat-out the days I was exploring the visitor complex, but there was enough time for us to meet up, have lunch on my last day in Florida, and get a selfie in front of the Atlantis exhibit building.
After saying goodbye to George I headed back to Orlando, returned my hire car and got an Uber to the train station – ready to start the next leg of my adventure back in Washington D.C. for the Humans 2 Mars conference. Florida has been the best and the worst of the trip so far – overpriced & difficult to get around, and yet there was something really magical about being at the Kennedy Space Center. I was frustrated at having missed the SpaceX launch, and yet incredibly grateful for the 3 days I spent in the Orlando hotel just taking care of overdue responsibilities and myself. Florida knocked a hole in my finances more than it should have, yet the entire trip would have felt incomplete without it.
Climbing back on board the overnight Amtrak back to Washington D.C. I was both genuinely glad I’d come and equally glad to be leaving, and grateful again for the time on those long train trips give to think and write about it what’s going on – there was no way I’d have the opportunity to really process things again until I was well and truly on the West Coast, preparing to leave for my two months in Israel with ISU.
title: Website - Florida

content:
Flying into the US is always an entertaining experience. Travelling with just two carry on bags certainly makes the whole luggage side of things a lot simpler, and customs have never been an issue, but I’ve had mixed results with immigration every time. Things didn’t get off to a great start when the folks in Iceland wouldn’t even let me get on the plane because my electronic visa wasn’t being recognised.
After a bundle of confused phone calls I realised I’d provided them with my old passport number – the one I’d flown on for 10 years till it expired mid last year – because I’d used it enough to memorise the number and didn’t recognise the passport number had changed. The bigger question is how I got out of Australia, through South Africa, the UK, Ireland & Iceland, all without anyone else noticing… but without thinking about that too much, once I got my numbers straight leaving Iceland there was no issue. Not a great start before flying to the US for 2 months though.
US immigration turned out to be a breeze, probably because I freaked out right before the flight from Iceland & gathered together every possible piece of info on my trip that I thought they might ask about at the immigration desk. So without too much trouble I was on a bus and on my way to downtown Boston! The vague US plan has been to travel down both the East & West coasts entirely by train: stopping along the way to meet as many Mars One candidates and see as many space things as possible, while getting to watch the country side go by from a train carriage along the way. And while I know the West coast pretty well & have plenty of friends there, my only experience with the East has been a couple of very brief stop-overs in New York.
Boston was completely new, and a fairly sharp reminder that things are just straight up different in the US. Like adding tax and tipping. What the hell America Showing me a price, THEN adding tax AND a tip is bordering on rude. Tell me what the whole thing is going to cost upfront, and pay your dining staff minimum wage or more. You know, like everyone else on the planet does. And while we’re at it: imperial measurement. WHAT. THE. FUCK. You know that the only countries that haven’t switched over primarily to Metric are the US, Myanmar & Liberia, right It’s like the founding fathers arbitrarily set fire to a bunch of stray cats in a park, then measured how far they ran before they put themselves out or died, and used those measurements to define different distances (eg. one flaming cat furlong) then multiplied that by the number of cats who survived to define larger measurements (eg. the total distance run by the 14 cats who survived the flaming is equal to 1 US flaming cat mile). I can only guess Fahrenheit is how many flaming cats it takes to melt American cheese or something; that weights are measured with how much fur the cats lost through this whole process (1 burnt cat fur pound); and fluids are measured in units of how much milk the cats drank during the partial lunar eclipse in Virgo a month afterwards (1 flaming cat lunar Virgo gallon).
Seriously: you lost a spaceship mixing up imperial & metric, and accepted a 93m tall copper statue & Freedom Fries from the French – why not do everyone a favour and borrow their system of measurement too?
Ahem Rant over, moving on…
Truth be told Boston itself didn’t hold a lot of appeal, it was only a very brief visit to catch my breath after Iceland and see a few folks who live there. After a day in the hostel trying to kill a lingering cold, it was great being able to catch up with Alex: an old friend I hadn’t seen in 10 years, who in one of those quirks of circumstance now does post-doctoral research into cloud-formation on Mars! Alex and I had barely stayed in touch since our physics undergrad days when she was on exchange in Perth, so it was all a little bizarre catching up for a few hours to chat about all the weird and wonderful things we’ve both done over the last 10 years. Even weirder sitting in a cafe at MIT and looking back to see how a fairly even mix of hard work & pure chance have led each of us to where we are respectively now.
We couldn’t spend too long reminiscing though – she had a 1-year-old bub to get back to, and I had a meeting with the folks from Boston’s Museum of Science! Given all the publicity around the #bringhimhome event and Cosmic Nomad, the museum had reached out to see if there was a way for us to collaborate on some sort of public event, and while nothing completely solid has come out of the meeting just yet it was fantastic being able to talk to folks who are passionate about science communication for an hour about the challenges of colonising Mars. They also invited me to roam their gorgeous museum afterwards…
…where I found the small but awesome Gemini/Apollo exhibit full of signed memorabilia and a moon rock…
… and when they kicked me out at closing time I spotted this awesome guy near the adjoining planetarium.
Apparently he ran the Boston marathon…
There wasn’t much time to hang out with Toby the Long-Distance Running T-Rex though, as there were 4 other Mars One candidates converging on a Mexican restaurant just up the road!
(L-R) Sara, myself, Yari, R Daniel & Peter
Sara, Yari, R Daniel, and Peter had all cleared their schedules so the 5 of us could meet up, eat amazing Mexican food, and so I could get them to add their signatures to my Mars One book. It’s always great meeting fellow candidates and hearing their motivations for applying & staying with Mars One – every time I’ve met other candidates it’s been a fantastic reminder that they’re all extraordinary people trying to do something literally out-of-this-world. But the meetup in Boston held a few surprises too: a couple of the candidates started a new trend by writing messages in the book rather than just signing it, which was a brilliant addition to what might have just been a book with a collection of signatures in it otherwise. But the biggest surprise was finding out that Yari has been looking after the one shirt:
** **Former Mars One candidate Randy Bevins had a shirt printed to say “Bas is sending ME to Mars!” a few years back, and since then it’s been mailed around the world to candidates for them to get a photo in it, along with a notebook to track its progress. I’d tried to catch up with the shirt about 18 months ago when it looked like it might be posted to Australia, but it completely dropped off the radar and we’d heard little about it since. So having Yari turn up with it was completely unexpected, and it was an amazing surprise to cross paths with a little piece of Mars One folklore.
After Peter very kindly put me up for the night at his house and dropped me at the station the next morning, it was time to start my epic journey down the coast… with a relatively short 5-hour trip to New York! The trip was long enough to carve a substantial chunk out of the relentless emails, but not long enough to really get on top of it. But if I’m brutally honest I really wasn’t looking forward to New York at all – a month into the oversea leg of the tour I could feel unresolved issues catching up with me, and I started to struggle both emotionally and physically.
Without going into a lot of detail, I had a lot of things end in the final months of 2015: I left the first stable job I’ve had in years, I moved out of the first sharehouse I’d been in since 2008, and a pretty life-changing relationship petered out and died without much resolution. In the months that followed I had a whole raft of fresh starts though: I began working as a TA for the International Space University, the Cosmic Nomad world tour kicked off, and I’ve met a bundle of truly wonderful new people who I’ve formed different relationships with, but all based on strong mutual respect (if not love) as well as clear communication and honest expectations.
But while I had no hesitation leaving my job in Melbourne (I’ve left plenty before) or living with no fixed address to travel the world performing comedy & doing space stuff (actually a dream come true), it’s definitely felt like I’ve been carrying a wound in the relationship department that I’ve been desperately trying to cover up since last year. I’d told myself at the time that I’d learnt a lot from it – and I really did. The issue was that even though in many ways I’d learnt what I needed then tried to move on, there was still an unresolved & lingering hurt associated with all of it. In one of those weird cosmic coincidences, about a month ago I met someone in Cork that had gone through a similar experience at roughly the same time, and was now opening herself up to pursue whatever opportunity felt right to her intuition – exactly the way I’ve been trying to operate. The entire afternoon & most of the evening disappeared as we chatted about life, the universe and everything; and besides realising that I’d hidden away some key parts of my personality, it also dug up a lot of the hurt from 2015 that I’d tried to bury and reminded me that I’d had a lot of the same lessons when another major relationship went belly-up in 2010.
I had a little time in Dublin to think about it, Iceland was 4 days by myself to get away from outside influences and go through a lot of what had resurfaced, and besides the chat with Alex my time in Boston was so rushed I barely stopped to think. But New York became the focal point for all of it: I was in the city that this ex wanted to bring her Mum to see Broadway shows, where we’d talked about touring together – both of us performing standup in some of NYC’s classic comedy clubs.
And as usually happens when you’re dealing with a lot from having the emotional band-aid ripped off, my health went to shit at the same time. I’d been getting a sore throat the day I left Iceland (not related to the ice river swim, before any of you armchair web doctors chime in), but now it seized up to the point where I couldn’t sleep at night because of the pain of swallowing, and was pairing up with a lovely headache every morning. Frankly everything felt pretty bloody average.Unwilling to be a miserable git for too long though, I loaded up on lemsip and forced myself out of the hostel to see Times Square…
Less than amusingly, I had to walk along Broadway to get here
…before heading to the USS Intrepid…
… where I’d get to see my first space shuttle – the Enterprise.
She may never have orbitted, but Space Shuttle Enterprise was key in the aerodynamics tests to validate the entire Space Shuttle program. USS Intrepid also had with a flown Soyuz capsule, that they keep under the tail of the Enterprise in the background for size comparison.
Spurred on by an amazing morning at the Intrepid, I headed uptown to the Rose Center for Earth & Space – where Neil DeGrasse Tyson is Director of the Hayden Planetarium.
I didn’t see Neil, but I did see another moon rock – this one collected by Dave Scott during Apollo 15
I also very nearly bought a life-size Triceratops plush toy because fuck you it’s majestic.
The day out in the cold New York air got to me though, and besides a few ventures to the local Chinese take-away I mostly stayed in the hostel feeling shit, trying to recover, and fighting through a long-overdue email inbox.
It was still worth going to New York. But given everything that had been dredged up in a few weeks before, along with all the baggage attached to being in New York, it was even better knowing that the worst part of this entire global tour was undoubtedly over as I climbed onto the train to Washington DC. With all that baggage staying in New York where it belonged.
I probably could have skipped it and gone straight from Boston to DC, but that would have meant continuing to ignore what’s been eating me for months… as well as missing out on seeing a fucking spaceship. And my new relationship rules are if you can’t talk about something that’s troubling you, or if they’re a barrier seeing a spaceship, then they don’t deserve to have an influence in your life. The other rule is if they don’t at least giggle at Rick & Morty or Airplane! the first time they see it then you’re straight-up wasting your time.
I ended a relationship once mostly because a girl didn’t laugh in the first 15 mins of this movie
New York was the bit on the rollercoaster where it pauses upside-down during a loop-de-loop. And while you’re hanging from your chair feeling sick, all the shit you should have left behind falls out of your pockets for the carnies to collect. Seconds after you tip over the balance point you’re racing through the loops and turns again, and there’s no point thinking about what fell out – you’ve let go of the shit that you thought was so precious before, and will hopefully learn not to bring it with you on the ride next time… or better yet, not carry it at all.
As you’d expect though, this story gets a lot better. Between getting to DC to meet more Mars One candidates, seeing another space shuttle, an SR-71 Blackbird, and the Apollo 11 command module (all before I got to Florida to embrace the space madness on a whole new level there) you’ll probably understand why the last two weeks of this trip have finally started to feel like this is my trip now, without the emotional baggage… and why I fell so far behind with these updates, trying to process it all of that while on the move through a foreign country.
Washington DC and Florida up next 😉
title: Website - Boston Buddies

content:
While there’s been a rough plan on where to go and what to do this trip since July last year, I’ve deliberately held off booking things too far in advance to keep myself open to random opportunities along the way. So a week before I was slated to fly from Dublin to Boston I decided I should actually book the flight, and was in for one hell of a surprise.
Far and away the cheapest option was to go via Reykjevic, and after the Ethiopia episode there was NO way I was going to fly all the way to Iceland to spend the entire time in the airport again. Even if it DID have free wifi. So I booked flights and set 4 days aside to explore the land of fire & ice.
I woke up in Dublin the day before the flight to Reykjavic cheerful, bouncing out of bed ready for the next adventure and put the kettle on for my morning coffee. Waiting for it to boil, my stomach suddenly dropped as I realised: – I don’t speak Icelandic, – I’m travelling so light I don’t even have a jumper, and – I actually have no idea what the hell to do in Iceland for 4 days.
My entire knowledge of Iceland in 4 minutes & 7 seconds
After some furious research I created something vaguely resembling a plan, made a couple of bookings, was given a jumper, and figured if it all went horribly wrong at least my frozen corpse would be cryogenically preserved striking an awesome pose inside some Icelandic glacier.
Hopefully long enough there’s been 3 or 4 alien invasions to really clear the place out before I’m revived
First impression flying into Iceland was that it’s not… really… inviting…
Unless you’re really into lifeless volcanic outcroppings
Also turns out you don’t fly into Reykjavik: you fly into Keflavik, out on the Reykjanik peninsula about 50km away from Reykjavik. Which suited me just fine, as where I’d hired a campervan from was right near the airport and I’d had more than enough of seeing/hearing/smelling/tasting people over the last few months – avoiding the capital fitted well with my plan to escape humans for at least a few days.
Picking up my “Happy Camper”, I decided to test out this whole “driving on the right-hand side of the road business” by driving around the local neighborhood to get the hang of having everything reversed. After driving the back streets (only going around a roundabout the wrong way once) I managed to grab camping food for the next 3 days from the local supermarket (using a combination of mime & animal noises to communicate with the cashier who spoke perfect English) and found an awesome Viking statue.
My bird, beard & axe game are severely lacking here
Emboldened by my Viking brethren, it was time to start the adventure and venture out onto the highway: I was on it 2 minutes before I stalled the camper trying to take an exit, stranding me halfway across a dual-carriageway on a blind corner. The camper refused to start, the car behind me started beeping, I threw on the hazard lights sending the car behind me into a blind honking-rage, before the engine eventually restarted on the 6th go and I pulled clear of an oncoming semi-trailer. Glad to say the driving for the rest of the trip was relatively uneventful…
Rather than racing to all the usual tourist spots I wanted to get out and away from people (especially ones driving other vehicles). Hafnir was relatively close, on the coast, and sounded vaguely like the name of a battlemech in Mechwarrior (because I’m psychologically 7 years old). And as you’d expect from a place I randomly chose based on its tenuous link to a video game I played 15 years ago, there was nothing to see except the set of Biodome 2.
Pauly Shore films don’t get the budgets they used to
But just down the coast was a place where you could walk across a bridge connecting the North American & Eurasian continental plates…
Shout out to my high school geography teacher who said “plate tectonics are just a theory”… just like gravity
And another place called Gunnuhver, where the Icelandic believe a demonic ghost lives and geothermal steam jets out of the ground (these two things are probably connected).
“Please don’t shove your face in the vent of stones producing super-heated steam that we named after a demon”
Working my way around the peninsula, I found myself being followed by a pair of German tourists. This became a common theme during my time in Iceland whenever I was on any of the “ring” roads – the same people stopping to look at the same incredibly stunning scenery you stopped to look at, leaving after about the same amount of time it took you to get bored with it, before driving in the same direction and turning up to ruin your next stop with their peopleness.
The Atlantic Ocean – largely untainted by peopleness
We reached peak peopleness when I stopped at the Blue Lagoon. The Blue Lagoon itself held little to no appeal to me, but everyone raves about it being a “must visit” and it was on my way, so I figured I’d at least call in to see what all the fuss was about. And lo and behold, it’s a pale blue lagoon.
Please hold your gasps of shock & astonishment
It was also terrifyingly touristy. The whole place was setup like a hotel-resort, funneling everyone into a lobby and restaurant, charged access to swim in the lake, and you literally had to exit via gift shop. And every asshole in Iceland was there with their obnoxious screaming kids. I snapped a selfie as evidence I’d been there (above), used their marble toilets and bolted out of there.
How’s the serenity?
The whole point of spending a few days in a camper driving around Iceland was that I didn’t have to interact with people if I didn’t want to (I didn’t), and I could disconnect from the rest of the world to enjoy the natural beauty of Iceland. So I connected my SIM-less phone to the stereo, put the Martian soundtrack on loop, and followed the south coast.
The camper hire guy had said I’d get around Iceland a lot quicker than I might expect, and he was dead right – I’d driven half the south coast before midday, and my only plan had been to drive that before heading to Thingvellir national park to camp overnight ready for my dive at Silfra the next morning. So with about 11 hours of sunlight left (welcome to the land of the midnight sun) I headed inland towards Geysir instead, where the word “geyser” comes from.
The Icelandic are a very literal people
With the icy wind blowing off the mountains, I decided to have my first meal in the camper – cracking the side door just enough not to gas myself on the stove fumes but without freezing either.
It’s a delicate balance being this classy
After another venture into a hyper-touristy hotel/resort at Geysir – to abuse a toilet, drain the dregs of my 2-minute noodle soup out in the car park, then leave again – I decided “national park” sounded like the place likely to have the lowest peopleness. Heading south-west into Thingvellir national park, you can see why they filmed Game of Thrones here. I think. I mean, I’ve never watched it and never plan to, but I know there’s a bunch of medieval families straight up murdering each other at an awesome wedding, and vague claims of dragons. Which all sounds like it should be filmed in the same place Vikings came from. It also probably explains why the show “Vikings” is filmed here. Which I’ve also never seen.
Probably because I’m too busy visiting these places instead of watching shows filmed here
There was still plenty of light when I parked at Silfra – where I’d be diving the next morning – so I decided to have a look around. Walking along a path through a schism in the sheer rock face, I turned around and saw this…
All of the pretty
… about 10 seconds before another tourist walked up to me and said “Excuse me, do you know which side is North America?”. Just like the bridge between two continents, Thingvellir national park is situated right where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are pulling apart. I worked out we were facing North and told him “The mountains on the left”.
All that smart ass geography knowledge didn’t mean a damn when it came to settle in for the night though – the guy who hired me the camper told me that “most campsites are open all year round” but do you think I could find one with an unlocked toilet and shower After driving around the whole park I eventually found one that at least had the disable toilet unlocked, and seems like it was the only one in the region too because I had multiple people knock on my camper door around twilight asking if I’d seen any other sites with unlocked toilets and showers. So much for escaping peopleness.
I’d be in for a little more peopleness the next morning, but it’d all be worth it though: I’d be taking the plunge at one of the top 10 dive sites in the world. While all of Thingvillir national park is formed by the North American & Eurasian tectonic plates pulling apart, Silfra is the spot in Thingvillir where water running off the mountains emerges after 75+ years of limestone filtering to form a freshwater lake. So besides the fact you’re diving between two continents, you’re also diving in the highest visibility water in the world (measured at over 120m/393ft), and it feels a bit like you’re spacewalking instead of diving.
Camping just up the road meant I was there before all the divers driving from Reykjevik, so I chatted to our surface support instructor Tanya while she set the gear up & we waited. I was qualified as a TDI Advanced Trimix diver and instructing for both PADI & SSI prior to moving to the UK to join the Royal Marines, but I really haven’t been diving regularly since then. So while the knowledge & experience are all still there I was definitely rusty, and it was great having the team from DIVE.IS looking after us. The water at Silfra is also about 2°C, which meant wearing some incredibly sexy dry suits…
Dry suit is borrowed but the sexy beanie is all mine.
I was grouped up with Johnathon (an English uni student who’d just done his Open Water course in the Red Sea) and Pien (an Californian lady who was only on her 4th dive ever) to be led by our dive guide Rob who’d just finished a season instructing and leading dives through the WW1 German wrecks at Scarpa Flow (one of my all-time “places to dive before I die/go to Mars”).
Our first dive was really just a check out so we could get used to the dry suits, but it was still extraordinary. Pien struggled with her buoyancy & ears, so Rob spent most of the dive looking after her. I kept a casual eye on Johnno at the same time, but he adapted to the dry suit really quickly so we spent most of the dive soaking up as much of the underwater scenery as we could.It was still bloody cold though, and after the first dive and a hot chocolate on the surface Pien was so cold she decided to skip the 2nd dive. Which is a shame because it’s when Rob, Johnno & I got the best pictures, like hanging onto two continents at once…
North American plate in my left hand, Eurasia in my right
… and diving on something that felt like a blue-tinged moonscape. You can check out the full gallery here, but it’s safe to say the experience was absolutely extraordinary.
After swapping cards and hugging a huge thanks to everyone, it was off on the next adventure into the Icelandic highlands! In July 2015 Mars One’s CEO Bas Lansdorp was scouting locations for a mock Mars habitat, and posted photos & coordinates for two possible sites in Iceland – one near Vik, and the other in the highlands near Suðurland. So I figured if I was in the country and it was so easy to get around I’d check them out myself, starting with the Suðurland site.
Welcome to the Icelandic Highlands
Turns out driving around Iceland is really easy unless you want to drive on an “F-Road”. I can think of a few things the F stands for, but basically you’re not able – physically or legally – to drive on an F-Road unless you’re in something that is half 4WD & half monster truck.
Do your wheels even lift bro?
There’s no way my puny campervan was going to cut it, but sure enough as I pulled up at the sign marking the start of the F-road the camper’s Tom Tom was telling me the Mars One site was another 8km ahead. What the Tom Tom wasn’t telling me though was that I’d be slogging the whole way through about 2 feet of snow drift to get there. There’s no doubt it was cold when I started the hike, but it was less than 20 minutes before I was stripping out of my thermals down to a shirt & jeans. And hour & a half later I was walking around in circles trying to get a GPS lock on the coordinates Bas had shared…
… before finally finding the right spot It’s difficult to describe just how desolate the whole area is. Besides some power lines way off to East that you really have to look for to see, there’s no sign of humanity or life generally. I’d kept my headphones in during the hike there, and was dumbfounded by how still & quiet the place was when turned the music off. As in eerily quiet – no wind, no birds, nothing.
After snapping my photo in a place specifically selected for its barren emptiness, it was time to hike back to the camper. With everything covered in snow and no frame of reference I’d had a nightmare trying to navigate in, but using the power lines and the hill I’d climbed to get to the plateau as a heading the return journey was much quicker… and also lead me straight towards a cliff I’d skirted on the way in. After some improvised tobogganing (eg. holding my bag to my chest and sliding on my ass down 200m of snow drift) I managed to get back to the river just a kilometer from where I’d parked.
The snow on the right is a LOT higher than it looks
So after about 4 hours of hiking and without another soul for at least 10km, I figured a trip to Iceland wouldn’t be complete without a skinny dip in water that was flowing off highland glaciers.
I could say this has been tastefully cropped, but the 2 degree water made overexposure less of an issue
There was fair bit of light when I got back to the camper, so I figured I’d at least try to get to the other Mars One site at Vik too. Heading back down from the highlands and toward the southern coast both fuel and light were getting very low, but I still stopped to grab a photo of this little gem.
The hotel of my people
By the time I nursed the car into the service station at Vik and figured out the bizarre payment system for fuel it was well and truly twilight, and there was no way I’d be able to find the second Mars One site in the dark. I’d driven passed some amazing waterfalls and watched the sunset on Eyjafjallajökull (the volcano that shut down air traffic in Europe for 6 days in 2010) and Katla (Eyjafjallajökull’s much bigger sister), so I headed back towards the camping grounds I’d seen on the way to Vik – trying to find somewhere with very few lights in the vain hope of spotting the aurora. With total cloud cover the aurora was a no-show, but unbeknownst to me I wound up parking for the night with a waterfall directly behind me… … and one of Iceland’s most famous waterfalls a short walk away.
Seljalandsfoss waterfall looking glorious
And as you’d expect from one of Iceland’s most famous waterfalls, the place was packed with tourists. After a few photos of the waterfall (and dunking my head in a stream as a pseudo-shower) I scampered out of there pretty quick. But with the drive/hike in the highlands and a few nights to myself without wifi, I’d had something of a breather from peopleness.
After a gorgeous drive to Selfoss through the southern mountains and skimming the edge of Reykjavik, it was time to drive back to Keflavik and return the camper. I stayed the night in a place about 9km from the airport, watching The Expanse till midnight & waiting for it to get dark enough to finally catch the aurora. But even with clear skies it never really got dark enough before the sun was coming back up again, so I guess I’ll just have to come back when the nights are longer!
And probably stay in one of these bubbles for it
The next day it was time to say goodbye to Iceland, so after a slow start & an awesome breakfast I figured I had plenty of time to skip the taxi and walk to the airport – popping the headphones back in and starting the hour & a half walk. I’d been warned by a friend who’s a huge Kim Kardashian fan (don’t worry, I judge her too) that Kim & Kanye were in Iceland at the same time, and low and behold just as I was walking passed the end of the runway I had their private jet take off right over my head. Personally I’m just really glad Yeezy didn’t decide to flush at the same time.
Please don’t
There’s been so much happening I’m about 3 weeks behind on these posts (currently in Washington D.C ahead of the Humans 2 Mars conference starting Tuesday). But the next step was flying into Boston for a few days before a weird weekend in NYC, and without going into details a lot has changed personally since I got through that. Spending 6 days being a complete space geek in Florida certainly helped too – the trip feels very much like it’s “mine” now. So I’m looking forward to getting those trip entries written & published in the next few days too 😀

I was grouped up with Johnathon (an English uni student who’d just done his Open Water course in the Red Sea) and Pien (an Californian lady who was only on her 4th dive ever) to be led by our dive guide Rob who’d just finished a season instructing and leading dives through the WW1 German wrecks at Scarpa Flow (one of my all-time “places to dive before I die/go to Mars”). Our first dive was really just a check out so we could get used to the dry suits, but it was still extraordinary. Pien struggled with her buoyancy & ears, so Rob spent most of the dive looking after her. I kept a casual eye on Johnno at the same time, but he adapted to the dry suit really quickly so we spent most of the dive soaking up as much of the underwater scenery as we could. It was still bloody cold though, and after the first dive and a hot chocolate on the surface Pien was so cold she decided to skip the 2nd dive. Which is a shame because it’s when Rob, Johnno & I got the best pictures, like hanging onto two continents at once… North American plate in my left hand, Eurasia in my right … and diving on something that felt like a blue-tinged moonscape. You can check out the full gallery here, but it’s safe to say the experience was absolutely extraordinary. After swapping cards and hugging a huge thanks to everyone, it was off on the next adventure into the Icelandic highlands! In July 2015 Mars One’s CEO Bas Lansdorp was scouting locations for a mock Mars habitat, and posted photos & coordinates for two possible sites in Iceland – one near Vik, and the other in the highlands near Suðurland. So I figured if I was in the country and it was so easy to get around I’d check them out myself, starting with the Suðurland site. Welcome to the Icelandic Highlands Turns out driving around Iceland is really easy unless you want to drive on an “F-Road”. I can think of a few things the F stands for, but basically you’re not able – physically or legally – to drive on an F-Road unless you’re in something that is half 4WD & half monster truck. Do your wheels even lift bro? There’s no way my puny campervan was going to cut it, but sure enough as I pulled up at the sign marking the start of the F-road the camper’s Tom Tom was telling me the Mars One site was another 8km ahead. What the Tom Tom wasn’t telling me though was that I’d be slogging the whole way through about 2 feet of snow drift to get there. There’s no doubt it was cold when I started the hike, but it was less than 20 minutes before I was stripping out of my thermals down to a shirt & jeans. And hour & a half later I was walking around in circles trying to get a GPS lock on the coordinates Bas had shared… … before finally finding the right spot It’s difficult to describe just how desolate the whole area is. Besides some power lines way off to East that you really have to look for to see, there’s no sign of humanity or life generally. I’d kept my headphones in during the hike there, and was dumbfounded by how still & quiet the place was when turned the music off. As in eerily quiet – no wind, no birds, nothing. After snapping my photo in a place specifically selected for its barren emptiness, it was time to hike back to the camper. With everything covered in snow and no frame of reference I’d had a nightmare trying to navigate in, but using the power lines and the hill I’d climbed to get to the plateau as a heading the return journey was much quicker… and also lead me straight towards a cliff I’d skirted on the way in. After some improvised tobogganing (eg. holding my bag to my chest and sliding on my ass down 200m of snow drift) I managed to get back to the river just a kilometer from where I’d parked. The snow on the right is a LOT higher than it looks So after about 4 hours of hiking and without another soul for at least 10km, I figured a trip to Iceland wouldn’t be complete without a skinny dip in water that was flowing off highland glaciers. I could say this has been tastefully cropped, but the 2 degree water made overexposure less of an issue There was fair bit of light when I got back to the camper, so I figured I’d at least try to get to the other Mars One site at Vik too. Heading back down from the highlands and toward the southern coast both fuel and light were getting very low, but I still stopped to grab a photo of this little gem. The hotel of my people By the time I nursed the car into the service station at Vik and figured out the bizarre payment system for fuel it was well and truly twilight, and there was no way I’d be able to find the second Mars One site in the dark. I’d driven passed some amazing waterfalls and watched the sunset on Eyjafjallajökull (the volcano that shut down air traffic in Europe for 6 days in 2010) and Katla (Eyjafjallajökull’s much bigger sister), so I headed back towards the camping grounds I’d seen on the way to Vik – trying to find somewhere with very few lights in the vain hope of spotting the aurora. With total cloud cover the aurora was a no-show, but unbeknownst to me I wound up parking for the night with a waterfall directly behind me… … and one of Iceland’s most famous waterfalls a short walk away. Seljalandsfoss waterfall looking glorious And as you’d expect from one of Iceland’s most famous waterfalls, the place was packed with tourists. After a few photos of the waterfall (and dunking my head in a stream as a pseudo-shower) I scampered out of there pretty quick. But with the drive/hike in the highlands and a few nights to myself without wifi, I’d had something of a breather from peopleness. After a gorgeous drive to Selfoss through the southern mountains and skimming the edge of Reykjavik, it was time to drive back to Keflavik and return the camper. I stayed the night in a place about 9km from the airport, watching The Expanse till midnight & waiting for it to get dark enough to finally catch the aurora. But even with clear skies it never really got dark enough before the sun was coming back up again, so I guess I’ll just have to come back when the nights are longer! And probably stay in one of these bubbles for it The next day it was time to say goodbye to Iceland, so after a slow start & an awesome breakfast I figured I had plenty of time to skip the taxi and walk to the airport – popping the headphones back in and starting the hour & a half walk. I’d been warned by a friend who’s a huge Kim Kardashian fan (don’t worry, I judge her too) that Kim & Kanye were in Iceland at the same time, and low and behold just as I was walking passed the end of the runway I had their private jet take off right over my head. Personally I’m just really glad Yeezy didn’t decide to flush at the same time. Please don’t There’s been so much happening I’m about 3 weeks behind on these posts (currently in Washington D.C ahead of the Humans 2 Mars conference starting Tuesday). But the next step was flying into Boston for a few days before a weird weekend in NYC, and without going into details a lot has changed personally since I got through that. Spending 6 days being a complete space geek in Florida certainly helped too – the trip feels very much like it’s “mine” now. So I’m looking forward to getting those trip entries written & published in the next few days too 😀 - Dave Looking good mate - Josh Thanks Dad 🙂 - Mandi Ryan I’m really enjoying your posts Josh. Great to see what you are up to. Hope everything else goes well too! - Josh Cheers Mardi – there’s plenty more to follow! - Shelley Richards Is it weird if your Mum posts comments too? It is, isn’t it? Oh well, here goes: loved reading this one Josh and missing having regular contact with you but great to know that you are (again/still) exploring the big wide world. x - Josh Haha, more than OK Mum 😀 Great speaking to you both this today, and I’ll try to call a little more regularly than I have. ### Recent Posts - News – The best, the worst, & the breather [Florida] - News – Space museum overload & Mars One meetups [Washington D.C.] - News – Boston Buddies, Space Shuttles & Bottoming Out [Boston & NYC] - News – Diving between continents & hiking to desolation [Iceland] - News – Airport Hell, Involuntary Weight Loss, & UK Mars100 Meetup - News – Life in a Box, Festival Madness & Going Global - News – 2016 “Cosmic Nomad” Global Tour - News – The Martian Stunt #bringhimhome - SHSSP16 Week 3 – Fighting Flat Earthers, New Management & Cultured Chaos - SHSSP Week 2 – Goodbye Spaceman, Buzz Day & Payload Tension - SHSSP Week 1 – Droids, Starmen & Grabthar’s Hammer - News – That whole “Moving to the other side of the country” thing - News – Helena National Science Week Tour - Mars One – Parachuting & Media Mayhem - Mars Project – You Are Go To Continue Descent… - News – 2015: The Year Space Kicks It Up a Notch - Random – Fringe World for People Who Aren’t Old & Boring - Random – An Open Letter to Myself in 2020 - News – There and back again… (Part 2: Australia) - News – There and back again… Part 1: Europe

content:
While I was waiting to board my flight from Cape Town to Addis Ababa a few weeks back, a strange thing kept happening on the gate information screen: in clear white letters was “Addis Ababa” with the correct gate and boarding time, but every now and then “Addis Ababa” would change into “Gaborone” and go a dark yellow colour. All the other flight details matched up though, and I boarded the flight with no issues, so I just put it down to being an alternative name for Addis Ababa.
It wasn’t. It’s the capital of Botswana. They flew us to Botswana. Do you know where Botswana is Because I sure as hell didn’t til I landed there.
This looks… inviting?
Turns out we needed to stop and refuel to make the distance to Addis Ababa, but Ethiopian Airlines figured we didn’t really need to know this until we were taxiing to the runway. To be honest stopping for an hour to refuel wasn’t really an issue for most of the passengers, but it was a fairly major issue for me, because I sat on a window just behind the wing & had to watch the plane being refueled by the loosest man alive – hence forth known as “LMA”.
Picture this: The fuel truck drove up, LMA leaps out and places a rickety wooden ladder under the wing. He runs back, grabs a wire off a reel and connects it to the plane’s wing as an earth. Then he wanders back, grabs the fuel line, drags it over to the rickety wooden ladder, connects it to the wing, then wanders back to the tanker and turns the pump on.
All pretty standard stuff, except for the bit where LMA then sits next to the pump pushing hundreds of liters of jet fuel a minute and answers a couple of calls on his handheld radio, makes a couple of calls on his mobile, and then because he’s bored decides to have a smoke…
He’s facing away from us because cool guys don’t watch explosions
LMA managed to refuel the plane without incinerating himself or the ~150 people on-board, and we left to begin a whole new circus in Addis Ababa. The only person I know who’s spent any time in Ethiopia is an old girlfriend I’ve only just started speaking to again (honestly, 5 years almost felt too soon… but we’re okay now), so a few weeks before the flight I asked her if it was worth leaving the airport. She warned me that Bole International Airport was a “hellhole” and kindly organised for one of her old teaching buddies to pick me up and take me out for dinner….
…which would have been amazing if I hadn’t arrived to discover Ethiopian immigration only let people out of the airport if their stopover is more than 8 hours – mine was 7 & a half.
We’d arrived half an hour early (probably because of LMA’s efficient refueling), so after braving one of the toilets I rushed around trying to find wifi to message the ex’s friend and say I couldn’t get out of the airport. Turns out the “Free Wifi” at Bole International is only “free” if you know the wifi password… which you can only get if you pay one of the dodgy shop owners. So after paying $10US to use an internet cafe that wasn’t connected to the internet (“no refund!”), and another $10US to have a shop owner type the wifi password into my phone (“you no look at code!” as she grabbed my phone and turned away from me), I managed to get through the ex’s friend to say I wouldn’t be able to leave the airport, just as she was about to leave her house to pick me up.
I’d had a fairly big night fueled by nachos and margarita-slushies in Cape Town before I left, and there’d been next to nothing to drink on the flight, so with “Escape from Bole” aborted the next challenge was to try to find water. This would have been easy if I could drink what was leaking from the roof, but “Drink Ethiopian airport roof water” isn’t on my “101 Things To Do Before I Die” list.
This is just like the “Free Wifi”, except the buckets are advertised as “Shower Facilities”
I couldn’t even pay to use one of the Ethiopian Airline Lounges (“Are you business or first class Then no”) so after a futile search for water fountains I just curled up in a ball on one of lounges, clutching all my worldly possession to my chest for 6 hours and dreaming of bottled water.
Welcome to WHAT?
After some next-level Orwellian insanity at the boarding gate (3 x-ray luggage scans without leaving the security area of the airport) at 1am local time, I was back on my way to the UK. It’s not that I hated every second at Bole International Airport… it’s just that if I ever go there again in this lifetime it will be too soon.
Accurate photo of me flying out of Addis Ababa
Back on-board things were a little more sane – Ethiopian Airlines isn’t great, but atleast this flight the sound to my entertainment system worked (as opposed to my flight into Addis Ababa where I watched “Edge of Tomorrow” on mute) and there was water: I think I went through half a dozen of those little bottles of water before they cut me off.
I landed at Heathrow around 7:30am, walked straight off the plane to Customs & Immigration (joys of being a registered traveller with no checked luggage) was on the Heathrow Express by 8:00, Paddington station by 8:15, and walked into the Space Innovation Congress (SIC) in St Paul’s at just after 9:00. Because apparently I work on ISU time all the time now.
SIC wasn’t really aimed at me (more for space entrepreneurs trying to start commercial space ventures) but it was fantastic catching up with Dr Alice Gorman over from Adelaide to talk about cultural heritage in space, as well as finally meeting Professor Chris Welch (who run’s ISU’s Masters Program) after emailing & tweeting the last 2 years in since I finished SHSSP14. There were claims of Buzz Aldrin making an appearance that never materialised, and I knew there was an astronaut panel organised after lunch… but it was still a fantastic surprise to see Dr Bob Thirsk again! I’d only met Bob in January at SHSSP16, but that already feels like a lifetime ago.
I’ve been operating my phone without a SIM card since I left Australia (carrier doesn’t allow roaming), so anywhere with wifi has become an oasis in a communications desert. The conference had solid wifi, so I ducked out of the presentations a little early to place a couple of VoIP calls to my boss for SSP16 and some TV folks who want to talk science & comedy when I get to LA in mid-June.
Didn’t have long to chat though, because I needed to get out to Luton airport to meet an ex-girlfriend (Eli) who was flying in from Amsterdam. So I jumped on the nearest tube and bolted out to Luton… to discover you can’t use an Oyster card out to Luton – you have to buy a separate ticket. Just as well there were two inspectors waiting by the gate to issue fines, because it’s almost as if this is something that people do accidentally all the time…
After waiting for Eli at Luton (still no wifi, but atleast the roof wasn’t leaking like Bole International) we headed back into London… when I realised in amongst fighting train ticket inspectors and picking up an ex from the airport, I’d missed one of the most historic moments in the modern space age…
I’m retroactively making this the reason we broke up
With all the chaos going on I’d completely blanked on the fact that SpaceX were launching CRS8. But even if had remembered, there’s no way I could have watched it travelling through the wifi desert of Luton bus/train transfers. Still, mucho disappointo.
After a night in a dingy hostel in London (because I’d somehow forgotten just how generally awful London hostels are) we met up with old comedy friends Robbotron & Jo Jo Bellini for breakfast, then Eli & I headed down to Brighton with Megan – who’s garage I was living in when I found out about Mars One. First stop The best Mexican in the known universe…
Burrito fun times at La Choza with Eli & Meg
By the time we got home I was reaching burn out – the reality is I hadn’t truly stopped in the 3 months since SHSSP16 started, I’ve been carrying the ghost of a throat infection for the last 2 months, and emotionally really just needed to not see or speak to anyone for a solid few days. We struck a compromise by staying in so I could curl up on the couch, I introduced Eli & Meg to Rick & Morty, and Meg went and picked up fish & chips from down the road for dinner. Eli & Meg stayed up drinking wine and chatting, while I passed out on the couch in the lounge.
No no – just leave me here
At about 3am something stirred me, but I just lay there being angry at the world for disturbing my slumber – I found out the next morning someone was killed 50m down the road around that time, when a bar fight spilled out into the road and in front of a truck. But to be honest that was the last thing on my mind, because as I rolled over to go back to sleep my stomach suddenly turned… then turned again… and about 12 seconds later I was diving for a sink as the fish and chips made a surprise return to the world.
Food poisoning is a barrel of laughs if you’ve ever had it – fantastic way to lose weight. After hurling my body weight up, I managed to sleep through till about midday and also managed to pull off “being a pathetic mess” for the rest of the day too. So while Eli & Meg embraced the pancake love, I sipped on a flat coke. We ended up staying in again and I only started to get part of my appetite back nibbling on a pizza and watching the LEGO movie.
After the great purging of April 9th, atleast I woke up the next morning not wanting to die. Eli & I headed back to London, she flew back out to Amsterdam (after a weekend for us to catch up where I’d spent 3/4 of the time being a tragic, miserable asshole) and I headed out to dinner with a friend and to see the UK premiere of “Last Man On the Moon”.
Eugene Cernan – Gemini 9 pilot, Apollo 10 Lunar Module Pilot, and Apollo 17 commander – was literally the last person to stand on the Moon, and “Last Man On The Moon” is a documentary based on Cernan’s autobiography that’s been getting a lot of traction in the US. Cernan had been supposed to conduct a Q&A after the documentary screening, but health issues prevented him making the flight to London for the UK premiere.
The documentary was… I don’t know. It’s hard to be disappointed with a documentary about the last human to have walked on another world. But I really struggled, and the non-space friend who came with me was less than polite about it. There were some truly memorable & emotional parts (the interview with Roger Chaffee’s widow about the Apollo 1 fire comes to mind) and I’d still recommend people see it, but by the time we got to Cernan going to the Moon with Apollo 17 I was… bored. And to be honest it felt like it kind of ruined the otherwise great night I had with an old friend.
The next night in London was definitely an improvement though, because I was getting to meet 3 more of the Mars 100 had come all the way down from Durham, with Ryan MacDonald joining us from Cambridge and Clare Weedon too.
L-R: Ryan, some ginger skinhead, Hannah, Clare
It was incredible meeting Hannah, Clare & Ryan – besides it being a great get-together of folks all dedicated to the human colonisation of Mars, it’s also been fascinating seeing how my preconceived ideas about different candidates (gleaned from watching & reading their interviews) marry up with what they’re actually like in person. I’m sure given how many ridiculous interviews I’ve done over the last few years I’m sure many of the Mars 100 have a fairly skewed image of what I’m like, but on a selfish note it’s been really interesting to have those some of my preconceptions of the others challenged (and some confirmed) by meeting in person. I’m really grateful for the flexibility in this trip to meet as many of them as I can.
London town grows pretty old if you’ve lived their before though, so the next day it was time to head out to Bristol. It’s clearly been awhile since I took a train around the UK, because this one had on-board wifi all fancy like, and apparently it’s standard on a lot of the lines now. Getting into Bristol I had enough time to walk from the station to the hostel, drop my bags at the hostel in town, then walk back to the station and head back to Bath for dinner with some old friends from my time working for Damien Hirst! 100% worth it though – Vicky has always been my pseudo-sister in the UK, her boyfriend Olly is a fantastic guy, and the three of us had a lot to catch up on. The take home line for the night came from Vicky: “Josh, next time you’re planning on changing your whole life for some woman, just call me – I’ll tell you not to”.
I never listen though…
There were a half dozen people I could have caught up with in Bristol, but given I’d been bed-ridden by food poisoning a few days earlier I figured a rest day might be in order (sorry Ollie & Roxie). I managed to catch up with one other friend from Damien Hirst – Hugh, our carpenter who was one of the guys I worked closest with – but otherwise most of the day was spent trying to find a decent place for breakfast, writing, and booking accommodation for the rest of the trip.
As you’ve probably figured by now, there’s a fairly serious mis-match at the moment between my instagram feed (which shows where I am in the world at the same time I’m there) and these posts (this one’s about a week behind). Doing things is great, but catching up with people has certainly taken it out of me the last few months. Atleast the “bat shit crazy” time schedule has eased to “hectic” now though, so I’m starting to catch up.
Next stop was Dublin to catch up with good friend, science-communicator extraordinaire and ISU-buddy Niamh Shaw and her hilarious partner Peter (he ought to be funny, the man’s been a comedian/MC forever). There wasn’t much time to chat to Niamh & Peter though, because the mighty Barry was driving from Derry to pick me up for so we could wreak havoc on Cork for the weekend!
Two of Cleo’s 2016 Most Eligible Bachelors
We had grand intentions for our Saturday night in Cork, but the reality is after the best pizzas in the region at the Franciscan Well Barry and I kind of stumbled around a bit like lost sheep. We ended up befriending a couple of German girls who looked interesting but equally lost, found our way to Crane Lane (which I remembered from my last visit), mingled about, and then just kind of bailed: everywhere was wall-to-wall with people, and against our initial hopes of a big night I don’t think Barry or I were really feeling it.
Cork is also home to ISU’s 2017 Summer Space Program too, so Barry and I went and caused mischief for a morning at Blackrock Castle – which is playing a major role in SSP17 with it’s observatory and space science outreach program.
And spotted Niamh’s “To Space” show poster behind the front desk!
After Blackrock the only things left were to meet up for a coffee with another friend (which I may write about separately some other time), and drive back to Dublin! I waved goodbye to the mighty Barry from Niamh’s place, and spent the next few days trying to get my life in order by booking more flights, catching up on sleep, and getting some much missed running in – if I don’t get to stretch my legs every few days I get… weird.
Before you ask, yes – weirder than usual
Besides having some incredible evening chats with Niamh about her SSP15 experience which will directly affect the way I operate as a Teaching Associate on SSP16 in Haifa; the only thing of serious note from my days in Dublin was meeting Joseph Roche. Joe is a former Mars One candidate who earned a certain notoriety in early 2015 when he was quoted in a series of highly critical articles written by a journalist I know quite well. As an assistant professor in STEM education at Dublin’s Trinity College though, I’d wanted to meet Joe well before “Rochegate” (as it became known), and have always questioned how much was said “by Joe” was actually him, and how much was the journalist twisting what he was saying to suit her very clear agenda against Mars One (and space exploration generally).
I’d read Joe’s article in the Guardian which seemed to carry a much more reasonable message, but again it was important to meet him in person to get the real story. And the reality is he’s an absolute gentleman, a huge proponent of exploring and colonising Mars, but as time went on he decided Mars One didn’t have what it takes to succeed – and that is entirely okay. Where it all went wrong for him was expressing that to a journalist who had zero qualms twisting what he was saying into articles with titles like “Mars One Finalist Explains Exactly How It’s Ripping Off It’s Supporters” (I’m not linking it – look it up yourself if you must).
So really, the only one who “won” out of the entire episode was the journalist, and she’s not worth saying anything about anymore…
…but Joseph Roche is a great guy, and deserved to be treated a lot better by the world’s media than he was.
Overall though, it was great being able to stop for a good few days somewhere safe to rest properly (thank you so much again Niamh & Peter for welcoming me into your home) and time/headspace to plan the rest of my travels… including a last minute detour to Iceland that I’ll write about in the next post 😉
title: Website - Airport Hell

content: I have no idea where to even begin describing the roller-coaster my last 5 months have been, so let’s start with the basics. I Moved to Melbourne Yup, up and left. No real warning – just gone. Leaving Perth had been in the works since the start of 2015, and given I’d been visiting Melbourne at least once a month since November it made sense it’d be where I wound up… but I sure as hell wasn’t expecting it to happen so fast. The plan had been to visit Tasmania for a holiday in late April, return to Perth to close out a few things and say goodbye, then leave on May 31st – the day before the Sunday Times named me in their list “75 People who make WA great”. Instead what happened was: - Mid April I off-handedly applied for a job in Melbourne as a school lab technician, - The school interviewed me via Skype 5 days later, - They gave me the job an hour after the interview, - I flew to Tasmania for 3 days, - Then flew from Hobart to Melbourne and started work at the school the next day The whole thing – from applying to starting work – took less than 2 weeks. With that rush I wasn’t fully prepared for when I got here, so for the first month I was commuting 2 hours a day to get to a job I’d initially thought was a part-time, but was actually full-time – 8 hours a day, 5 days a week. Needless to say it was one hell of an adjustment. As with everything though, once you’re over the initial shock and start to figure things out, you adapt and problem-solve. Learning Melbourne’s public transport system, buying a bike, and moving into an amazing share-house in Carlton solved the commuting issues – 10 minute bike ride to one school campus, and a 10 minutes walk to the other. Convenience, bitches I switched to part-time work My lab tech job was a lifesaver initially – it got me out of Perth, used my degree and chemistry knowledge, and paid far more than I’d been paid by any job since I left the mining industry. But the plan had always been to work part-time – just enough to pay the bills so I could focus my time and energy on writing & speaking about space. That is what I’d wanted to move to Melbourne for. So while my job was pretty easy – I had far too much free time – and ticked a lot of boxes, being full-time wasn’t really letting me do what I’d moved here to do. It also added evidence to the idea I’m a cartoon character… After a visit to the Victorian Space Science Education Centre (VSSEC) and bumping into a friend in science communication, I decided I’d prefer the uncertainty of casual science communication work than keep going in a secure job that stopped me from doing all the cool stuff I really wanted to do. Rather than leaving immediately and leaving the school in a lurch, I told the school I’d stay the 6 weeks till the end of Term 3 – that way they had plenty of time to find a replacement for the start of Term 4 & I had a regular pay-check while I found something more suitable. The school started planning for my departure, and I started looking for a casual science job in between working and organising everything for National Science Week … until a week later when the principal struck on the genius idea of having me go part-time. It’s a great job, but it doesn’t need someone full-time – the reality is I was bored and frustrated that I had to be there 5 days a week. So now I’m on 3.5 days a week I’ve got the part-time job I was after, I’ve reclaimed the time & energy I needed to write (hence why you’re reading this), and the school has an enthusiastic lab technician who’s excited to be there rather than wishing he was doing something else. It also means I can keep riding to work four mornings a week: one hand on the handlebars, the other casually holding a soy latte like a job-less hipster. But of course right when all this job mischief was being discussed, I was also preparing for National Science Week… Helena Payload’s National Science Week Tour In case you missed it here, here, here, or any one of the dozen other places it was covered by the global media, I helped UWA’s Motorsport Team develop a payload for Mars One’s University Competition this time last year. What you might not know (because I never mentioned it until the previous post) is that the fine folks at Inspiring Australia gave us $15,000 to travel around the country during National Science Week to speak about Helena’s development and the experience of working on an aerospace engineering project. So Andre Van Vulpen, Rowan Heinrich, Claire Quy, and I bundled off for a flash tour of the country – taking in Perth, Hobart, Adelaide, Sydney and Melbourne. Speaking about Mars One at Hobart’s Festival of Bright Ideas Slipping away from the festival to visit Mt Wellington The Helena Team together at the University of South Australia In Adelaide, setting up our first presentation In Sydney to speak at OrbitOz Speaking at Uni High in Melbourne Speaking at Simonds Catholic College in Melbourne The Helena Team after our last presentation Speaking about Mars One at Monash University The chaos didn’t stop for me there though – while the rest of the team was flying back to Perth, I was running my “How To Become An Astronaut” workshop at Laneway Learning’s Science Spectacular, and the next evening I was presenting on the International Space University’s Southern Hemisphere Summer Space Program at RMIT’s Aerospace Industry Night. And somewhere in there I turned 30 too. Becoming Adult(ish) and doing Adult(ish) things Apparently 30 is some sort of arbitrary figure where ordinary people grow up emotionally, settle into a safe and secure job, get married, have 2.4 kids, and start the slow descent into death by mediocrity. But because I’m awesome and intend to die on a different planet to the one I was born on, I turned 30 and got a tattoo of a 7-leaf clover; 100 points if you get why this is about Mars … and because I’m wildly irresponsible I had a robot spaceman tattooed on my right ass cheek at the same time; By this point you might suspect I watch a lot of Futurama. You would be correct. Turning my life back into one long punch-line In July Mars One announced that the final astronaut selection phase will take place in September 2016. The candidates knew there were two possible selection periods (March or September 2016), and after being on this roller-coaster for nearly 3 years already a big part of me was hoping they’d go with March. But instead of being frustrated by another 6 months, I’ve realised I’ve got another 6 months to do all the stupid shit I want to do from the 101 Things list and write/tour a new comedy show about it. So now the race is on: since July I’ve attended a film premiere (#44), gotten a tattoo (#75), and I’m still chipping away at the greatest books list (#52). This whole website is due for some serious renovation, and updating the 101 Things list is the first thing to be updated. It’ll continue to be updated too as I do more stupid shit from the list when I return to full-time comedy next year. I’m currently writing my next science-comedy show “Cosmic Nomad”, so I’ll leaving my lab tech job (properly this time) at the end of 2015 to perform the show throughout 2016 – touring all the way around this shiny blue-green ball we call Earth until the final selection phase in September. The details of the tour are are still being worked out, but I’ll share them here as soon as everything is confirmed. In the meantime keep an eye out as I start to publish chapters from “Becoming Martian”; the book I wrote last year on how humans will change in physically, psychologically and culturally by colonising Mars. After sitting on the manuscript for 12 months I’ve decided I’d rather it be available for free online, rather than have it remain unread on my hard drive waiting for a publisher to wave a magic wand over it. And who knows – maybe I’ll collect all the posts together and sell it as a book during the 2016 Cosmic Nomad Tour… ### Recent Posts - News – Boston Buddies, Space Shuttles & Bottoming Out [Boston & NYC] - News – Diving between continents & hiking to desolation [Iceland] - News – Airport Hell, Involuntary Weight Loss, & UK Mars100 Meetup - News – Life in a Box, Festival Madness & Going Global - News – 2016 “Cosmic Nomad” Global Tour - News – The Martian Stunt #bringhimhome - SHSSP16 Week 3 – Fighting Flat Earthers, New Management & Cultured Chaos - SHSSP Week 2 – Goodbye Spaceman, Buzz Day & Payload Tension - SHSSP Week 1 – Droids, Starmen & Grabthar’s Hammer - News – That whole “Moving to the other side of the country” thing - News – Helena National Science Week Tour - Mars One – Parachuting & Media Mayhem - Mars Project – You Are Go To Continue Descent… - News – 2015: The Year Space Kicks It Up a Notch - Random – Fringe World for People Who Aren’t Old & Boring - Random – An Open Letter to Myself in 2020 - News – There and back again… (Part 2: Australia) - News – There and back again… Part 1: Europe - News – NatSciWeek Wrap Up & Roll on Europe - Mars Project – Becoming Martian & Other Science Week Madness
