content:
7 Step Parachute Landing Fall
One of the first things you’re taught when you learn to parachute is how to land without breaking a leg. If you’re learning to free fall like I did, you’re eventually taught to pull down on the control handles and “flare” your parachute at just the right height for a smooth and soft landing. But the first landing you’re taught – and the only one you can use if something goes wrong or you’re using a round parachute – is a “PLF”, or Parachute Landing Fall.
Regardless of what others might say, a PLF still hurts… it just hurts less than trying to stay on your feet when you can’t slow down a landing. I’ve only ever had to do one: the free fall went fine, but when my parachute deployed I realised the wind was suddenly blowing at 20 knots in 180 degrees opposite to what it was when I jumped out of the plane. 180 degrees and 20 knots opposite what the jump was planned for.
I knew my parachute tracked forward at 15 knots in still air, but I was flying backwards. So I now had to choose between:
A) Turning with the wind to weave among trees before hitting the ground at 35 knots (~65km/hr) B) Turning against the wind to PLF into a hill before the trees, but hitting the ground backwards at 5 knots (~9km/hr)
I chose B: performing a PLF but still slamming backwards into a hill just meters short of the trees, and 8km off where I was supposed to land. I came home with a sprained ankle and a story – choosing A could have saved my ankle or killed me.
My point is that no matter how much you prepare and plan ahead for a major event, the unexpected can and often will happen. All you can do is take a deep breath, look at the problem in front of you, and use all you know as you do your damnedest to solve it and get out alive. Once you’re through the initial impact, you bundle up your parachute, say a quick thank you to the sky and the people who trained you, then you start limping home – a little wiser than you were before.
Over the last two years I’ve been slowly building up a network of journalists, educators and science communicators to update on Mars One’s progress. It’s why I left doing stand-up in the UK and moved back to Australia – I knew I could do more as an Australian in Australia than I could as an Australian in the UK. I’ve reached out to anyone I thought would be interested all across the world, and while I’ve had fun playing a role in raising awareness about Mars One the media interest hasn’t been overwhelming.
What I didn’t expect though was the sudden jump in interest that came with being selected into the final 100 astronaut candidates two weeks ago. I sent out a press release at 2pm WAST on Monday February 16th to ~30 people, expecting replies over a few days from the usual 4 or 5. Instead I did 8 radio and TV interviews in less than 2 hours. The next day there was another 16 interviews for radio, TV and newspapers. The same again the day after. As the news broke journalists shared my details amongst each other, and the whole thing started to snowball.
I’m still catching up on messages, and genuinely lost track of how much press I’ve done – at its peak I was doing 2 to 3 phone interviews via speaker phone while driving to a studio for another run of interviews. But here are a few of the highlights:
WA Today – Mars One: red planet a step closer for Perth man into top 100 (Feb 16) Triple J Hack – A Guy From Perth Could Be Going To Mars (Feb 16) SBS’s The Feed – The Mars One Mission: will it ever launch (Feb 16) News.com.au – WA comedian Josh Richards makes shortlist for Dutch space project Mars One (Feb 16) Channel 7’s Sunrise – Interview with Aussies waiting for Mars trip (Feb 17) Channel 9’s Today Perth News – Mission To Mars (Feb 17) RTRFM – Going To Mars (Feb 17) The Australian – Mars One mission: The seven Australians bidding for a one-way ticket (Feb 17) The Guardian UK – Mars One shortlist: the top 10 hopefuls (Feb 17) CNN – Round Two: 100 vie for one-way trip to Mars (Feb 18) That’s not even including the Today Tonight interview (can’t find the link) or the plethora of other radio interviews that happened: most assumed I lived in Melbourne or Sydney instead of Perth, so I was getting phone calls from east coast breakfast radio stations at 3am each morning saying “Sorry to call you at 6am”. It was unexpected, relentless and draining… but certainly nothing in comparison to surviving the sleep deprivation of a 5 day exercise with the Royal Marines, only to then be forced-marched through the night where I was hallucinating fences/training staff/oncoming trucks that weren’t there.
Or any other point in my time at Lympstone Commando. Like I said – you bundle up your kit, say thank you, and keep moving.
It was a welcome relief when the initial media rush slowed down on Wednesday afternoon though. I had a chance to embrace the end of the Perth fringe festival, support some incredible local comedian friends, see other amazing inter-state and international comedian friends, and finally retire Keith the Anger Management Koala with two incredible guest spots for “Mac the Comedy Computer” and “Tomás Ford is the End of the Fringe”.
That’s right: Keith the Anger Management Koala is dead.
Thankfully, thankfully dead
Many of the people interviewing me asked if “being in the Mars 100 has made the mission feel more real?”. The selection really didn’t change anything about the way I see Mars One, but finishing my final performance in a furry grey koala suit did. Everything I’ve done for the last two years (and everything I continue to do) has been shaped towards helping put humans on another planet. Keith was a shield so I could share stories from the military that were still too raw to share as myself – I shared those stories on stage at the Edinburgh Fringe in 2012, and the wounds were healed. I’ve wanted to retire Keith ever since, but it wasn’t until a few months ago I made the decision to let go of the suit completely – the Mars 100 announcement just before the end of the fringe was the perfect catalyst to make that happen.
That felt like I’d finally closed the book on something – letting me move forward without needing to glance back. So if you want more of the koala, the suit will be available to buy in a few months when I start fundraising for my flight to Mars One’s final selection phase. I’m not ever putting it on again, but I might dry clean it if you want it.
To seal in the decision, I slipped away to Margaret River for 3 days last week. Besides seeing some incredible sunsets,
and exploring some gorgeous caves…
…I had a chance to think about my past, present and future, and discuss it honestly with someone I love and trust. The Mars 100 announcement has been important, but in the grand scheme it’s just a fork in the road – if I hadn’t been selected to progress to Round 3 I’d still be trying to inspire people through space exploration, and would be in the process of shifting into building spaceships instead of training to fly them.
That may still happen in the future, but for now I’ll keep flying the flag as an astronaut candidate for Mars One. Especially when it gives me a chance to talk about colonising other planets to a crowd of astronomy fans gathered to break the Guinness World Record for “Largest Astronomy Lesson” in Kalamunda on Saturday night.
The previous record was ~830 people, we had over 1100.
And yes – the lights were turned off for the actual lesson…
I have no idea what comes next. But I’ve packed up my parachute, I’m eternally grateful for the incredible and continued support through this, and we’re already moving toward the final round of selection in the second half of this year – let’s see what the rest of 2015 brings.
title: Website - Parachuting & Media Mayhem

content:
The last two and a half years have been pretty odd.
In September 2012 I started researching how to send people one-way to Mars for a comedy show, and found an organisation aiming to do it for real. In 2013 I was one of 202,586 people who applied to be on the first crew to go, and one of 1058 short-listed for it. In 2014 I was one of 705 that passed the medical selection, and one of 660 offered an interview.
Today, I’m one of 100 people worldwide progressing to Mars One’s third round of astronaut selection.
Today I can tell you I had my selection interview in early December, and that I’ve waited to tell you about it for the last two and a half months because of a non-disclosure agreement with Mars One. And today I can finally tell you the knot that’s been sitting in my stomach for the last two weeks started to unwrap on Friday when I found out I’d made it through, that it’s unwrapping a little further sharing this with you now… but that it won’t fully clear until this all really sinks in Wednesday morning.
This afternoon I’ll be speaking to:
2UE in Sydney minutes after this is published (14:07 in Perth, 17:07 in Sydney), 6PR in Perth at 14:35 Perth Time Michael Smyth on Drive with ABC 891 Adelaide at 15:05 Perth time (17:35 in Adelaide), Barry Nicholls on Drive with ABC Regional (WA) 20 minutes later (15:15), Going national with Triple J’s Hack at 17:45. Tuesday morning I’ll be Channel 7’s Sunrise, and RTRFM’s Breakfast with Caitlin shortly after that. With the embargo lifted expect to hear a lot more of Mars One in the media this week. All 100 remaining candidates are expected to undergo group testing (likely in the US or Europe) before Mars One selects 24 to 40 of us to start full-time training in June/July. But right now I don’t know much about what the next few months will involve.
I’m grateful to have so many incredible people believe in what we’re doing – so many incredible people who believe in me. Some of you I’ve known for years, some I’ve really only just met. But all of you are vital to this journey – thank you so much.
I don’t know what happens next… but I’m really glad you’re here.

content:
Let’s be honest here – a lot of people are really quite dull. They work, they eat, they sleep. Occasionally they watch A Current Affair to feel real emotions about how much they’re spending on dish-washing liquid, or if their 3 bedroom home in Ellenbrooke will be safe from ISIS.
Which is a shame, because life can be pretty amazing if you get off your ass, try new things, and stop being so damn scared of making mistakes. Some of you may already think you’re making a mistake reading this – this is entirely possible. “Hey, the title said something about Fringe World – I wonder if he’s got some show suggesti…”
Shut your face, I’m having a moment here.
There’s been a bunch guides recommending different Fringe World shows this last week, and almost all of them have recommended shows that have already sold out or will do soon. Don’t go to them. I’m not saying they’re bad shows – many of them are very, very good. But they don’t need you to see them – they’ve already got plenty of people who follow safe recommendations going, because “Hey, why would you want to see what might be the next big thing, when you can play it safe and see the current big thing?”.
Fringe festivals are supposed to be a chance for the less conventional, the less well-known, and frankly the flat-out weird performers out there to showcase what they do though. It’s not about loading up on more of the same safe crap you already know: “Oooooh, let’s go see him! I loved his TV special on Channel…”.
Seriously, I’m going to ask you to stop reading this if you keep interrupting with your beige-coloured, vanilla-flavoured opinions.
As I spent four years at the Edinburgh fringe and used to regularly dress up as a ukulele-playing koala that screamed at people for a living, I think I’ve got the authority to tell you what is “fringe” and what isn’t. Almost certainly more authority than anyone from the Sunday Times. If anyone from the Sunday Times would like to question that, please get in touch so I can arrange a meeting for you with my alter-ego Keith The Anger Management Koala, and he can politely inform you as to why you’re wrong.
And also explain why Christmas has been cancelled
The Fringe World UV Rating is reasonably accurate for finding weirdness, but there are some VERY notable exceptions. So I’m also going to give you a list of amazing shows to see to avoid being that boring wanker who turns up on Monday morning to work telling everyone he “saw Will & Woody doing stand-up“. Because while they’re nice guys, YOU CAN LISTEN TO THEM EVERY DAMN WEEKDAY MORNING FROM 6.
I’m seeing a lot of shows, but this is the proper fringe stuff I’m going to and you should too. Feel free to push your comfort zone at…
A Young Man Dressed As A Gorilla Dressed As An Old Man Sits In A Rocking Chair For Fifty-Six Minutes And Then Leaves. (Jan 29 – ONE NIGHT ONLY)
This is exactly what it says on the tin. It is also the ULTIMATE fringe experience. It’s so fringe it’s not even listed in the Fringe World guide, nor is it on their website. I saw “A Young Man…” in Edinburgh 2011, and it remains hands down the absolute best show I have ever seen at any festival anywhere in the world. It’s free, and I’ll be rocking up two hours early to make sure I can get in.
I say this without irony, or as part of any kind of trick: Please. For the love of God. See this show.
Mac The Comedy Computer’s Variety 52-Minute Spectacular! (Jan 24-Feb 21)
Ever watched a MacBook sit inanimate on a stage for nearly an hour, while the pre-recorded electronic voice of a sociopath plays over the sound system It’s hilarious and haunting. Mac is doing his first full fringe show, being joined on stage by Steve the Horribly un-PC PC as well as a variety of the weirdest and most confronting performers at Fringe World. This will probably destroy you.
Dr. Professor Neal Portenza performs his own autopsy live on stage. One night only. (Obviously). (Jan 28-Feb 12)
Whatever lunatic gave this a Fringe World UV Rating of “Medium” clearly didn’t even read the show title, let alone see the show. This show IS also running over multiple nights, because Neal Portenza is a mad man who clearly needs to be stopped.
Roaring Accordion (Feb 11-20)
Mimes cause a rather primal desire for violence to well up inside me, almost as much accordions do. That I’m still keen to see this should be an indication of how highly recommended the show is. I will however remain both skeptical and possibly armed.
Sarah Young’s Magical Murdery Mystery Tour (Feb 11-14)
Sarah Young is a ball of borderline-psychotic energy both on and off stage, who just won the Blue Room’s 2014 Judge’s Award for Best Writing for her play “Giving Up The Ghosts” where two people eat McDonald’s and then kill themselves. She also knows way to much about Big Foot, and will argue he’s real until she has an aneurysm. This show is not about sasquatch – it’s a whimsical show about serial killers. With hand puppets.
Pro-Choyce (Feb 18-21)
This is the full-size poster of Sian Choyce’s first solo show “Pro-Choyce”. Before you go to her show about how much she hates kids (I’ll be in the front row on opening night), you should click the image above and have a really good look her poster. Zoom in and read it. Look that – it’s an excellent poster. It’s also a poster you’re unlikely to see on walls anywhere at the festival, because Fringe World enlarged Sian’s A6 flyer to poster size and distributed THAT all over town instead.
Because it wouldn’t be a true fringe experience unless hard-working and talented performers were overcharged for incompetence.
Jeff Hewitt: V For Vagina (Feb 18-21)
I like Jeff. He’s a fun guy, and undoubtedly one of the best stand-up comedians in Perth. But he was also the kind of comedian that I’d never take a girlfriend to see unless I was trying to break up with her. Until now. From the trial material I’ve seen and the article Jeff recently wrote on why he’s doing a show about women called “V For Vagina”, I’m willing to take the risk.
But Jeff I swear to God, if I bring a date to this and afterwards she never wants to have sex for the rest of her life, you’re coming off the Christmas card list.
BRUCE (Feb 13 & Feb 14)
Bruce is a puppet made from a hacked apart block of foam, and needs two guys to make him talk. Those two guys however happen to be two of the most talented puppeteers in the world, and Bruce is one of the weirdest/funniest things you’ll ever see. Sammy J and Randy are great, but with my artist pass this is one of the only shows I’ll be paying to make sure I can see.
BLUES AND BURLESQUE:HOTTER THAN HELL (Jan 29-Feb 15)
I genuinely don’t get burlesque. Someone took me to see Dita Von Teese and her burlesque showcase in Seattle, and while it was great… I still didn’t get it. The women who do burlesque are unfailingly incredible, but the sexiness is usually all a little too serious for me. So unless it’s something hilariously warped – like a woman awkwardly trying to get out of a bee keeper’s outfit on stage – I’ll usually try to miss it. Maybe I’m just wired wrong.
There’s no sexy, angry bees in Vicious and Scarlett’s show, but they do have a hysterically warped sense of humour however, and Pete Saunders is absolutely exceptional providing the bluesy accompaniment.
If you enjoy regular burlesque shows, then Things That Go Bump…and Grind in the Night is definitely the place to be – all of the most entertaining burlesque dancers I know will be on, if they’re not actually behind the scenes running it.
Tomás Ford Is The End Of The Fringe (Feb 14 & Feb 21)
Everyone’s favourite, creepy cabaret fringe uncle/urban legend is back – bigger, badder, bulgier than ever. Besides coordinating all of the Noodle Palace shows and running the Late Night Gala, Tomás is also playing a valentine’s day mega show as well as ENDING THE ENTIRE FRINGE FESTIVAL with Tomás Ford Is The End Of The Fringe.
Keith the Anger Management Koala will be playing both the Valentines Day and the End of Fringe shows for Tomás, as well as a raft of other gigs throughout the whole fringe that I’ll put on the “Upcoming” page shortly. In the meantime go out, step beyond your comfort zone, and support some incredible talent by witnessing their abject on-stage madness.

content: AUTHOR’S NOTE: I’ve broken this up into two posts because the original was just waaaay too big. “Part 2: Australia” will be published once my fingers recover. Looking back, the last Mighty Ginge update was August 29th: to say a lot has happened since seeing Chris Hadfield in Canberra is a gross understatement. You probably could have followed some of it via the fairly consistent Instagram, Facebook & Twitter updates, but here’s my vague attempt to sum up the two months of utter chaos that was the European & Australian tour of Becoming Martian. **Germany (August 29th-September 1st) ** Meet “Identity Crisis Bear” Berlin was supposed to be a breather. But coming off the flight from Doha what it really devolved into was a mad dash to try to find three things: 1. WiFi to write & submit a proposal for a payload on a Mars lander 2. A printer to print my train ticket onward to Cologne 3. Food/Sleep In that order of priority. The initial submission deadline for Mars One’s University Competition was August 31st, so I had 24 hours to write an outline for the Helena payload – a scientific payload proposal to generate oxygen from the water in the Martian soil, that also includes a digital art library to Mars. In the process of trying to find wifi to access the payload reference documents I got to wander around Berlin a little, but since I’d visited before in late 2006 I was primarily just trying to find a cafe that I didn’t need a translator to ask for the wifi password… Even with the help of some friendly German cafes, the proposal still wasn’t written by the time I needed to board the train to Cologne. So I ended up writing and submitting a payload proposal for a Mars lander minutes before the deadline using the wifi on the train as it raced through the German countryside at over 230km/hr… Welcome to the future In Cologne I was back in more familiar territory, having stayed there for a few days last November while visiting Europe for the 2013 Living On Mars Convention. Not that I had time to enjoy the familiar sights – I crashed as soon as I checked in, and was up early the next day to visit the European Astronaut Centre! Do you know the way to astronaut street? One of my fellow Mars One candidates Andrea Boyd is EUROCOM – the European Space Agency’s communicator to the International Space Station. So she invited me to see where the European Space Agency’s astronauts train for expeditions to the space station, and where I could muck around in a Soyuz simulator… Not pictured: Hypoxia-induced hallucinations of George Clooney Netherlands (September 2nd – 8th) There was actually a day or two during the week in the Netherlands where I didn’t have to rush anywhere… but it sure as hell wasn’t the day I arrived. There was barely enough time to drop off my bag in Rotterdam before it was back on a train to The Hague – just making it in time for an event on solar weather hosted by the Netherlands Space Society, featuring ESA Astronaut Andre Kuipers and World Space Week ‘s Executive Director Remco Timmermans. Aurora expeditions with Remco Friday brought more space madness, meeting up with ESA’s Communications Director Juan De Dalmau for a tour of the European Space Research and Technology Centre (ESTEC) with fellow International Space University alumni. Me being a “Price Is Right” showgirl for ESA’s next spaceship The ESTEC visit had to be cut short though, because the same night the all important Redhead Days festival kicked off. I’d been in the Netherlands a month too late in 2013, so this year was a great chance to catch up with some old faces and see just how much the festival has grown since I last attended in 2012. Redhead Days Launch To be fair I was pretty burnt out by the time I got there, but something with Redhead Days also seemed to have shifted. The atmosphere of having so many redheads in one place from all across the world is still absolutely amazing, but it wasn’t quite the life altering event my first visit was. I’m certainly not the same person I was when I arrived lost at Breda train station two years ago, so maybe it shouldn’t have come as a surprise that there wasn’t the same impact coming back. The pub crawl continued to be the best event of the weekend’s official program, and this year there was the added bonus of trying to meetup for an interview with a French TV crew during it – they eventually found me (slightly more sober) the next day. But the real highlight was ticking off #22 on the 101 Things To Do Before You Die list by going up in a hot-air balloon the Monday the festival finished. Our balloon was obviously the one with the giant smiley face It was brilliant being back for the Redhead Days festival, but more importantly this visit closed out a lot of unfinished business in the Netherlands from the last 2 years. Maybe one day I’ll go back again for a bit of a laugh, but it very much feels like the festival did what it needed to do – starting my transition from a successful but half-hearted comedian, into a fully fledged space advocate. Ireland (September 9th – 14th) If the Netherlands was about closing out unfinished business, Ireland was very much about starting afresh. I’ve been providing support (viaSkype ) to Niamh Shaw as she developed her Dublin Fringe show, so when I found out the premiere of “To Space” was the night after the Redhead Days festival finished I knew it was the perfect chance to finally visit Ireland! Niamh’s premiere was amazing, and it was great to meet so many fantastic people from Ireland’s burgeoning space industry at the drinks afterwards. When Space Gingers Attack One of the completely unexpected parts of the evening was Niamh drawing names out of a hat to win a piece of original space art from Clare Henderson, and suddenly finding I had to tick off another entry from the 101 Things To Do Before You Die list: #92 Own an Original Work of Art Now safely mounted on my office wall The 48 hours in Dublin was awesome, but with only another 4 days to see as much of Ireland as possible it was into the hire car and off to Cork! Fellow Redhead festival-goer Irene had come over to Ireland too, so we shot down to Cork and met up with Joleen Cronin – organiser of the Irish Redhead Festival. Welcome to the Red-olution We also discovered that Cork is infact a magical and never-ending series of multi-story carparks, after inadvertently driving into 4 of them… Endless, ENDLESS, carparks Depending on how everything pans out with Mars One in the next 6 months, there’s a good chance I’ll be heading back to Cork for the 2015 Irish Redhead Festival to lead their “Ginger Ukulele Orchestra”. Whether I’ll be too busy with training to colonise another planet – or if this planet is ready for hundreds of gingers to start playing ukulele together – remains to be seen… Next stop on the flying Irish tour was the Ring of Kerry, where we witnessed panoramas like this: So… pretty… As well as some blatant racism towards my proud gold-loving cousins: As if we need a special crossing point – we’ve got enough gold to OWN the road Driving on to Dingle Bay, the leprechaun abuse stopped but the overwhelming pretty didn’t: View from the hostel’s balcony The western coast of Ireland – please collect your jaw before you leave Most of the time in Kerry & Dingle Bay was spent just trying not to have an aneurysm over the scenery, and we barely saw 1/100th of what the Wild Atlantic Way had to offer. But there was one really important historical stop we managed to squeeze in. Tom Crean was an Irish explorer that partook in some of the greatest Antarctic expeditions of all time: leading a team on Scott’s 1902 Discovery expedition, surviving Scott’s fatal follow-up Terra Nova expedition in 1910, as well as Shackleton’s ill-fated Endurance expedition. But once Crean had earned his 3rd polar medal & served a further 4 years with the Royal Navy, he retired to Annascaul… where he opened a pub. This is a real place that serves “Crean’s Lager”. We had Coke Four days in Ireland isn’t even remotely enough to even explore Dublin properly, let alone Cork, Kerry & Dingle Bay. But Irene had to head back to the US for work and I was off to Northern Ireland for the CultureTECH Festival. We stayed back in Dublin with Niamh Shaw on our last night in Ireland though, and ended the Ireland leg of the trip with Niamh giving me what is easily the best LEGO set ever: XCOR’s Lynx Mark II CultureTECH in Derry, Northern Ireland (September 15th – 19th) The CultureTECH festival in Derry was always going to be the trip’s pressure pot – 3 days as one of the featured speakers for a technology festival with hundreds of events & activities. I wound up staying for 5 days: speaking about Mars One at half a dozen schools that ranged from high-end boarding schools, to running technology workshops, playing Bowie’s “Space Oddity” on ukulele during interviews with BBC radio, performing “Becoming Martian” as a charity event for Children In Crossfire, and talking about having the courage to fail over and over and over again at the Create2014 student-run event. Create2014 – Inspirin’ da yoof with failure It was 5 days of abject chaos… but without a doubt one of the best parts of the entire trip. Because while I was running around like a headless chook trying to keep track of when and where I was, every step of the way there were incredible people to steer me in the right direction. The team from CultureTECH were simply amazing: lining up as many school visits as I could squeeze in, organising interviews with the BBC, and having taxis ready to get me wherever I needed to be. Not only that, they put me up in 5-star accommodation the whole time I was there so I could tick off a third entry from the 101 Things list: #30 “Stay in the Best Suite in a Five Star Hotel”. It wasn’t just the CultureTECH organisers who were awesome either. My old Irish friend Barry had moved back to Derry a few months before, so it was fantastic to finally catch up with him – I’d barely seen Barry since late 2010, when we were sharing a mouldy flat in London and I moved out because my taste in girlfriends had suddenly improved. Without going into specifics Barry has had a particularly rough year, so I think it was good for both of us to catch up and remember that even with the dips he’s had over the last 12 months, life is still way better than it was 4 years ago. Circa December 2010, aka “Evidence Exhibit A” But while we were reminiscing, Barry & I were also causing chaos at the festival and making mountains of friends doing it. CultureTECH had brought in so many inspiring folks from all across the world it was hard to keep track of them all: Heather from Uproar Comics, Alastair from Startacus, the dozen scholarship winners from Honeycomb, and the hysterical team from Ministry of Science … whose children’s shows undoubtedly contain less innuendo than I like to pretend they do. Emma wants to end on a big bang, but Mike isn’t sure they should, in front of all the kids… CulutreTECH was genuinely out of control, and I loved every moment of it – from ridiculous dinner parties that ended with us getting kicked out of the dodgiest pub in Derry, right through to performing “Becoming Martian” while sounding like a koala with emphysema because my voice had gone that morning. It was ridiculous, fun-filled chaos all the way through, and I genuinely hope I get a chance to go back again and do it all again. London, Benenden & Brighton (Sept 20-26) Leaving Northern Ireland was a stark wake up call to the realities of life though… And let us never speak of this again After the nightmare that was my flight out of Belfast to Bristol though, I managed to knock over a bunch of little jobs that I’d been carrying with me since National Science Week. Restitching my bag, sewing patches on my ukulele case, copying all my random scraps of paper covered in ideas into something more permanent… general travel admin. Once you’ve been living out of a bag for a few weeks there’s often a moment where you realise things are going to start falling apart on you if you don’t take a little time to fix them – landing in Bristol was that moment, so on the bus to Bath I sorted everything. Things would start falling apart again before I got back to Perth, but that’s another story. The return to Gloucestershire was very short though. I managed to catch up with Vicky & Olly – two great friends from my days working for Damien Hirst – for a few hours in Bath. But the next morning the infamous Martin picked me up for breakfast in my old town of Stroud, I managed to catch up with Mark Chatterley from InEarEntertainment for a few hours, then it was on the move again down to London that afternoon… For tourists, this is a delightful photo op. For anyone who’s spent 6 hours waiting for a 5am train, this sign causes a rash London was another rushed, overnight visit – caught up briefly with John & Jo to see what wonderful things they’d been doing post Edinburgh Fringe, but the very next morning it was off to speak to the students at the exclusive Benenden boarding school in country Kent. The kids and staff were brilliant, really enthusiastic about World Space Week, and I even managed to find a fellow ukulele-er among the staff! The compulsion to play “Duelling Banjos” was significant But Benenden was really just a fun detour for where I really wanted to be, was here… Into the Temple of (burrito) Sacrifice … with it’s amazing interior decorations… Mexican eating establishment protected by The Space Jesus Last stop of the Europe leg was back to that other old stomping ground of mine: Brighton, with the best burritos on the planet at La Choza. The world’s best housemate, Megan – whose garage I was living in when I decided to sign up for Mars One at the end of September 2012 – put me up for a few nights while I prepared for the return to Australia, partaking in all the awesome food and coffee Brighton has to offer at the same time. And in amongst it all I even managed to get up to London again to catch up with Lizzy from Ginger Parrot at an open mic cabaret night in an underground toilet. With all of that going on, you’d think it would be time to go home and have a bit of a nap. And if you call all of Australia home, then yeah I did go home – “home” to run a space conference in Adelaide, present at a different space conference, speak & perform at a Newcastle writer’s festival, dress up like an aluminium-foil covered robot with plastic cups for boobs, bolt up to Brisbane to speak at schools & universities, as well as meeting dozens more amazing people along the way. But I guess that will all have to wait until the epic conclusion of Josh’s Europe/Oz Odyssey… This Odyssey involves considerably less scurvy… - Paul Ahhh EasyJet. content:
The only commandments you’ll ever really need
I’ve just finished George Carlin’s “sorta-autobiography” Last Words, and it’s pretty rough reading at times. My first exposure to Carlin was
Bill & Ted’s Excellent Adventure, and quickly became hooked on his pitch black stand-up and surreal wit. Carlin was my first proper exposure to social commentary through comedy, and I loved hearing him brutally cut through much of the crap we humans like to tell ourselves.
“It’ll all be okay if you work hard and respect your elders.”
“Get a good job, meet a girl, get married, start a family and a mortgage.”
“Support your country and pay your taxes.”
The George Carlin I knew unceremoniously ripped away at all of it. But he certainly wasn’t always like that. His early career was chock full of bland mainstream material, he appeared on stage in a suit, and regularly guest-hosted the Johnny Carson Show. He had his fair share of trouble growing up, got himself kicked out of the Air Force, and started doing some edgier material in the late 60’s… but then fell right back into mainstream naval-gazing in the 70’s.
As I said, Last Words is an emotional roller-coaster in parts: it’s tough reading someone so talented and successful describe their life falling apart through booze and coke, the bottoming out, and the intense shame that went hand-in-hand with the recovery. Reading “Bill Hicks: Agent of Evolution” (by Hicks’ life-long friend & collaborator Kevin Booth) is the only book that’s ever given me that same sick feeling of despair. Maybe it’s from having been in a relationship with someone with incredible talent who’d fallen into the same spiral, and my experience of trying (and effectively failing) to help them come to terms with that same recovery shame. But there’s something that hits me particularly hard when someone I resonate with describes their experience with the alcohol-cocaine addiction cycle.
Carlin turned the corner with “A Place For My Stuff” in 1981 and his return to Carnegie Hall in 1982. He’d started to clean up a little (it was a long journey to sobriety) and his material was for the first time developing the overt anti-establishment edge he’d become so famous for. Carling started to recognise and release a lot of the physical & emotional “stuff” he had, and start to focus on what he really cared about.
I’ve collected a lot of pointless crap over the years. As a kid I collected hundreds of stamps (dozens of exactly the same ones), model aircraft, Star Wars cards out of promotional chip packets, everything. And all of it just sat on my shelf as decoration – I never played or really looked at any of them, it was just stuff that I had. Like every 9-year-old boy I was obsessed with dinosaurs, so my parents subscribed me to a monthly dinosaur magazine. After awhile I stopped reading the magazine, but we didn’t cancel the subscription – I would just get them and store them in the special binder I had. Same went for my subscription to New Scientist during uni: I just kept collecting them and piling them up in the Physics common room.
Things got really weird in Year 7 when I started chopping up erasers into little cubes and storing them in a tissue box under my bed. I have no idea how this started, but for some reason I’d always had this plan to melt down all the bits into one oversized mega eraser. But looking back all I really did was steal hundreds of erasers and chop them up into useless crap for about 12 months, which I’m sure is the sort of thing you’d find on those check-lists used to profile serial killers. “Broke all of his toys Nope. Played okay with the other kids Yup. Chopped up erasers into tiny pieces with a plan to melt them all down into one impractically huge eraser?… BINGO!”
In the end, all the police needed to do was follow the trail of eraser shavings…
I know it’s really easy to blame your parents for things – George Carlin certainly did – but I’m pretty sure my tendency to collect stuff in my younger years came from my Dad’s penchant for collecting shit. The current inventory is our rather large house, two shipping containers, an 8 x 20m single story shed, a 16 x 20m double story shed. My folks even built a house next door so my Aunty could move in, and now we’re storing her crap too – feel free to come around and steal it. Every time I’ve come back to Perth it’s like that reality TV show where some middle-aged housewife turns up at an embarrassed dude’s house with a camera crew, and starts digging through his pile of broken pool toys screaming “WHY DO YOU HAVE THESE?”. Except in our version no one gets famous or manages to reduce the piles of useless crap.
POOL NOODLES WHY?! YOU LIVE ON A FARM!
For the last few years Dad and I have quietly clashed over the stuff: his desire to keep things just incase, and my desire to sell/burn/give away anything that sat in one place long enough to collect a particle of dust. In Dad’s defence the place is much better than it was, but I’m not sure if that’s because he got wind of a stand-up set I started doing in early 2012 called “Shit From My Dad’s Shed”, where I played an increasingly rage-filled game show host giving away actual items from my Dad’s shed to random people in the crowd. Either that or I just got rid of a lot more stuff than I realised… but there’s certainly a lot less shit in the shed.
Burn ALL of the things
I can’t speak for Dad, but I know a lot of my desire to collect stuff was to feel a little more complete – you’d finally find that last Star Wars card, or you’d finally have a painted 200-point Warhammer 40k army, or you’d finally filled the tissue box with chopped up erasers… because you’re a 12-year-old psychopath. You have a complete something, and feel a little more complete inside for it. Even now after two years of putting it off,
I’m finally trying to write-up my completed 101 entries with these articles. To complete the set.
The biggest thing leaving Australia to join the British Royal Marines taught me was to let go of all my stuff – I landed at Heathrow with just a hiking pack to start a whole new life. And then the marines taught me to carry anything else I’d ever need on my back too. When I discharged I’d managed to collect more stuff though, so I gave a mountain of military kit away before I came back to Perth. And on my return here I walked into my old room to find it full of old stuff I hadn’t missed for a year. So I gave all of that away too – if I hadn’t needed it in 12 months, then I certainly didn’t need it and maybe someone else you use it.
As I’ve travelled since, I’ve found it progressively easier to travel with less and less. When Paul and I travelled through the US in 2005 I left Perth with 3 t-shirts, 2 pairs of shorts and a pair of jeans, but came back with an 80 litre pack FULL of books. When I went to the Netherlands for 6 weeks late last year, I brought a regular backpack and carried a library on my Kindle instead. For years I planned to buy the entire Futurama series on DVD when it finally finished – now I’ll just stream any episode I want on my tablet, and do it from anywhere in the world.
Because even Bender can appreciate the cloud
There’s certain things you keep for the memories they carry too – I keep framed copies of my solo show posters on my wall, and they’re a reminder of the memories I have of writing & performing them. But at the same time they’re just posters. They’re only a stand-in for those memories. And memories are stuff too: unless you learn something from them, or you can use them to pass on lessons to others, why are you still carrying them around?
I’ve still got a lot to clear, but there’s progress every day. It’s not just giving away the very limited amount of physical stuff I have left after all the years of purging – it’s also cleaning out some of the ugly old memories that go with it. I’ve still got a black box of old memorabilia from my time with the military, and it’s a fear I’ll lose those memories that’s stopping me from getting rid of it. But if those memories don’t serve me any more, who are they serving And what am I holding myself back from by hanging onto this old stuff I’d be lucky to be allowed to take a shoebox of memorabilia with me to Mars, so why am I carrying around a black tub filled purely with memories from a previous life?
The arrow is rather apt in retrospect
Ultimately, I can’t take any of this crap with me when I die, and hanging onto it now is living in the past. I’m digitizing all my favourite literature I can onto a portable hard drive: books, music, movies, ect. And you’ve probably guessed it by now, but writing these recent 101 Thing articles is a great deal more than just completing a list of articles – much of it is digitizing those memories too, so I don’t have to carry them around in my head any more. Maybe others can read and learn something from them, but it’s mainly about giving so many of these untold stories an airing, then letting them go.
I don’t have any pointless collections any more – even at “home” I live out of a backpack, I collect stories and small items I can learn from, study them for a while, then pass it on to someone else. Then I ask if there’s anything else I can give away. There’s not much else to it – I just try to let it all go.

content:
[
In theory, starting a fire without matches or a lighter is fairly simple – all you need is the right fuel and a spark. Some will swear by a fire plough, others a fire bow. Use can use anything from a magnifying glass to potassium perchlorate to Swedish Firesteel. You can even hook your car battery up to a piece of steel wool, and use it to ignite cotton wool.
Or you could not make your life harder than it needs to be, and use a match.
In all of the different arms of the military I worked with, I never ONCE had to start a fire without matches. Even when the Royal Marines stripped us down to our uniform and boots for survival training, you still had 5 waterproof matches in your pocket. Lighters become pretty difficult to use when your fingers are frozen, but you always had matches: every daily ration pack (both Aussie & UK) came with a little green waterproof tube with 6-8 standard safety matches, 1 storm match, and a striker on the side of the tube. You’d use 2-3 matches a day at an absolute maximum, so you’d wind up with dozens of matches and these little green tubes left over after an exercise.
Before heading out into the field I’d empty all the tubes, collect the storm matches together into one tube and bin the rest. More often than not you couldn’t have a fire at all, because if you were doing sneaky squirrel business it would give away where you were. But if you DID get to light a fire to heat up the amorphous slob in the meal packs, then you wanted a storm match that would light the first time and stay lit – regardless of the weather.
10 storm matches in one tube What is this SORCERY!?
I can and have started a fire without matches while camping though. But just like several of my former relationships, it was a hell of a lot harder than it needed to be.
In August 2010 I flew back to the UK for two reasons. First, to help behind the scenes while
John Robertson ran his début solo show at the Edinburgh Fringe. The second was to keep a promise to spend the week of my birthday camping & hiking in the Lake District with my girlfriend at the time –
the primary teacher I’ve mentioned before, who for this article we’ll refer to as… that primary teacher.
Those initial 10 days in Edinburgh were great – helping out on a fringe show and learning from John was exactly the kind of comedy apprenticeship I needed after the disillusionment that followed leaving the Royal Marines. It also helped that John’s girlfriend (now his wife) Jo and I get along like a house on fire – I’d be one of her bridesmaids at their wedding 3 years later. Mix in a mountain of laughs from the masterful wit of Cameron Davis, and meeting that ginger sign-post I’d eventually name my ukulele after – it felt like this was closer to what I should be doing, and Edinburgh closer to where I should be doing it.
Although anyone who remembers this gig will know that some nights were better than others…
I was anxious about going out to the Lakes though, and not just because of my mortal fears of catching the bus. Things had been less than great with the primary teacher when I’d left the marines – it was a fight between us the night before I was supposed to go out on a 5 day exercise that led me realise I wasn’t supposed to be in the military. But my visa was tied to my service, so by discharging I had to go back to Australia and organise a new visa. And no matter how much I said I would, she was convinced I wasn’t coming back.
But here I was. The bus ride had been thankfully uneventful, the sun was shining and the Lake district was stunning. She was waiting for met me at the stop in Keswick, and kissed me as soon as I stepped off the bus. Then we got on another bus, then walked to our camp site about 4 kilometres from the last stop (I’ve just tried to look up on where we were on Google Maps, and I have absolutely no idea where we were). But I didn’t care – we were back together, and I thought the whole world had exploded in rainbows & unicorns.
And then predictably, it all turned to shit.
It’d been sunny the afternoon we arrived, but then it poured down with rain for the next 6 days. The tent she’d brought didn’t have all it’s parts, so it flooded every night – soaked sleeping bags for everyone. The only showers were in a sheep barn (“What do you need a shower for We’re camping!”) and you had to trudge through a muddy field to get to them. The list went on, but what it really boiled down to was:
I’d just left 12 months of walking up & down hills while being screamed at in the Royal Marine Commandos – all I wanted to do was sit & admire the scenery. 2. She’d just finished 12 months of in classrooms being screamed at by kids during her teaching practical – all she wanted to do was yell at someone else while climbing the scenery. I’d nearly died from Lyme disease 6 months earlier, and fractured both ankles just 2 months before – the last thing I wanted to do was trudge up and down hills. But I did it, because I loved her. We were doing something together, just like that couple at a camp site who seem to hate each other and everyone else asks why they’re still together.
Literally seconds before pushing her over the edge of Niagara Falls
Because my aversion to bread was clashing with her intention to survive on sandwiches the entire week, we’d gone on a day trip into Keswick to pick up some meat and a disposable BBQ as a treat for my birthday. We’d been soaked getting off the bus, but getting back to camp the rain slowed to a drizzle. Back at camp she’d popped on her rubber boots and rushed through the mud to have a lukewarm shower, so I decided to get the BBQ started. I dig out my tube of matches, then spot the magnesium-flint block I’ve carried for years but never used. And in one of those Rain Man moments I used to have, I decide to delay something that will help break me out of my miserable mood (eg. eating real food) to start a fire without matches and tick off a “101 Things” entry.
Sometimes I like to pretend the entire week was a Rain Man parody – I’m always Dustin Hoffman
I dug out my multi-tool and shaved some magnesium onto a pile of grass I’d found, but the knife wouldn’t shave properly in the wet. The grass was soaked too, so I tried to tear off some of the cardboard from the top of the disposable BBQ – it’s soaked after the walk back to camp as well. I’d shave off some magnesium, throw sparks at it by running a steel file over the flint and see a few little flashes, but nothing would actually catch fire – the grass and the cardboard were just miserably wet.
They say the definition of insanity is doing the same thing over & over again, and expecting the same result – after 15 minutes of scraping, sparking and despairing I was well and truly mad. The frustrating part was seeing the magnesium dust/shavings catch for a split-second, then disappear without igniting anything else. Over and over again. The matches were right next to me, but now it had become a matter of pride – I wasn’t going to let some stupid wet cardboard beat me. I was pissed off, hungry, and fighting with a piece of soggy cardboard – great combination.
I decided to try one last time with the mother of all magnesium shaving piles, and ground off half the block onto the cardboard & grass pile. I’d make this thing light, and I would create a flame without matches. The moment of truth came just as she started walking back from the shower: I hovered over the shaving pile, ready to strike the flint… and FLASH! The shaving pile scorched white-hot for a second, and suddenly there was a flame from the cardboard! It flicked over the edge where the pile had been, and glowed red underneath.
And a second later it was gone.
The one redeeming part of that week in the Lakes was that tiny flicker of flame. A flicker of flame I created, without matches, on my 25th birthday. Even if it burnt out in less than 2 seconds, I realised I could do it – the blackened edge of the cardboard proved it. That I was worthwhile. I’d made my life considerably harder than it needed to be (entirely out of misplaced pride) but I’d done it. I took out the matches, and after several goes got the rest of the cardboard from the BBQ burning. The coals were wet though, so the fish & sausages didn’t cook all the way through. But I didn’t care – I’d proven I had plenty of spark and commitment, I just wasn’t going to ignite properly if I wasn’t working without the right fuel.
A friend of mine pointed out a few years later that life keeps throwing lessons at us until we learn and avoid the same mistakes. Like a spiral, the cycle of shitty situations that “always happen to me” keep happening (with slight variations to the theme) unless you learn to recognise the larger pattern. It’d be another 6 months before I fully recognised the spiral I was in, but that little flicker of flame was the start of a dawning realisation that I needed to seriously reassess who I’d become, who I wanted to be, and who I wanted to surround myself with.
And when that realisation finally came – and I started to act on it – the results were pretty spectacular.
But that’s another story.

content:
Michelle Smith – Australia’s only jazz harpist
Some people are born musicians. The first time they picked up a recorder in primary school, a majestic cacophony of melody poured out that stunned their teachers & peers. When they sit down at a piano or pick up a guitar, every note is loaded with harmony, every strum filled with emotion and meaning. Michelle Smith (pictured above) is one of these people. They shift effortlessly between different notes, chords and keys, as if they’re simply switching in time to the ebb and flow of different resonate frequencies in the universe.
I’m not one of those people.
The first time I had to learn a musical instrument in school I was 10 – two years behind every other kid in the Western Australian education system. My family and I had just returned from living in Jordan for two years, and learning to play an instrument wasn’t part of the distance education curriculum at the time. So I returned to regular schooling to discover that not only did I have a sociopath for a year 6 teacher, but I was expected to already be a reasonably accomplished recorder player having never seen one of those horrid tubes of despair before in my life.
So I sucked at it. And I naturally hated class music lessons.
My school didn’t give up though. At the start of Year 7 we were all given a musical aptitude test – I failed it. But somehow they decided that I’d scored just high enough to learn the double bass. In reality I think my school just thought it would be comical to watch a kid who was barely 4 foot tall carry home a 7 foot bass each day, and they were probably right.
But as you’d expect, I sucked at it.
This didn’t stop me from falling in love with listening to music though. While I’d been a slow starter, my first high school crush introduced me to Merrick & Rosso on Triple J, and my life was altered forever. Next thing I’m tuning in every morning & evening, expounding the virtues of non-commercial radio to people in the street, and trying to impress girls that I knew whatever the latest underground indie rock band was too, like some sort of awkward pubescent wannabe-hipster. Actually looking back now I’m not sure if I was in love with the music, the crush who introduced me to it all, or Merrick & Rosso’s roving reporter at the time – the very lovely Myf Warhurst.
Lets be honest – it was mostly Myf
All I knew for sure was that I couldn’t get enough of the radio, and was soon amassing a hefty collection of alternative rock albums. So I knew I loved music, but I sucked at playing it myself. I tried bass guitar for a while, then somehow wound up playing in a Christian rock band through Year 11 & 12. Which was pretty awkward since I was also a vocal and hard-line atheist at the time… I hit university, sold my bass guitar & bought more albums, dive bombing even further into appreciating music and completely forgot about playing music for over 8 years.
Less bass, more bass girls…
Fast forward to Christmas 2010 and I’m breaking off a year-long relationship with a primary school music teacher, who in horrifying retrospect bares a striking resemblance both physically & emotionally to my old Year 6 teacher. I’ve packed my bags and left for the icy streets of London three days before Christmas, preferring to chance it and not know where I’ll sleep each night rather than deal with any more of the crazy. And a week later she sends me a message asking to “patch things up and give (me) a Christmas present”. We talk, resolve to try to remain friends, and she gives me a £20 ukulele. I didn’t even touch it.
Because I probably would have done this to it. (Image Credit: Oddsock)
After 4 months of bouncing in & out of bed bug-ridden hostels through London (during which I wrote my first solo show “Apocalypse Meow” rather aptly about having your world implode) I finally managed to land a job as a technician & science advisor to Damien Hirst way out in Gloucestershire. The teacher and I were still trying to be friends at this stage, but my tolerance for her bat-shit-crazy episodes was starting to drop at the same time – you only put up with people who treat you slightly better than you treat yourself, and I was discovering life was a hell of a lot happier out of the military and away from her.
It wasn’t until she came out to visit me in Stroud – where she threw a hissy fit and I abandoned her in a field to be eaten by wolves – that I decided to actually learn to play the ukulele she’d given me instead of glaring at it in the corner like the ghost of relationships-past. And the very first thing I learnt was the opening riff to Duelling Banjos, then sent a video of me playing it to some people in Perth …
It wasn’t until I realised the comedy potential of electronically heckling people from high school for getting married to each others sisters – by playing a guitar made for hobbits – that I started to really love playing music and not just listen to it.
Suddenly it was easy to play along to your favourite songs, and then laugh at how ridiculous (or awesome) they sound on ukulele. I went from someone who came out in a rash at the idea of learning to play music to buying new strings to improve the tone, within a week. Within a month I was writing my own songs, and just 2 months after that I spent the day walking all over Bristol with John Robertson to find a new semi-acoustic tenor ukulele – the ukulele I would use in my début solo show at the Edinburgh Fringe festival: Apocalypse Meow.
It’s also where Gerald the Baboon would threaten to rub baby oil into bald men’s scalps at every show…
Now the first thing you need to do when you buy an amazing instrument, is name it. It took me a month before finding a name that even remotely fit. After I huge day at work I sat out on the back patio for a few hours, looking out over Stroud and writing songs on my new ukulele ahead of the festival. I realised was shattered but was only a few verses off finishing a song, so I left the ukulele on the patio couch and wandered inside to make a coffee. Walking back outside I glanced up and just about dropped my cup – for half a second the cushions & ukulele had combined to look like one of the girls from work was sleeping on my the couch.
Cherry had been over a few weeks before and we’d sat on the same couch for dinner, which seemed to be enough inspiration for a ukulele name & a full blown visual hallucination. “Cherry” didn’t really seem to suit this uke, although “Sheree” fit a little better. But after Edinburgh 2011 the name “Sheree” stopped seeming to fit too – a lot of weird things had gone down at the festival, Cherry and I had stopped hanging out, and I felt like a different person. And the tone of the ukulele seemed to reflect the confusion: she developed a buzz, and all the strings started to sound muted & flat.
A friend from the 2010 fringe got back in touch just as the festival finished though: one of those sign-post gingers I’ve mentioned, Amanda. And weirdly enough when I tried calling my ukulele “Amanda” in the December, the buzzing stopped and the life in that beautiful varnished wooden box seemed to spring right back. So while things went pear-shaped with Amanda the girl way back, the ukulele has always kept the name – “Amanda” just seems to fit her really well.
And when I met Amanda Palmer & Neil Gaiman at the 2012 Edinburgh Fringe, there was only one thing to do…
I was supposed to know who Neil Gaiman was when Amanda signed this – I didn’t.
I don’t play her now as much as I used to – for a while there I was playing for an hour every day, but now it’s probably a few times a week. When the feeling grabs me. Like a lot of things I often think I should practice more, or I should write more songs. But to be honest I’m pretty happy just having her with me – either on her stand in my room or wrapped up in her carry bag when I’m travelling. She’s always with me and ready to play when I feel like it, rather than being compelled to follow some sort of rehearsal schedule.
And I guess that’s what playing music is really about – having a relationship with it, rather than it doing it because you have to.

content:
If you read through many of my completed 101 things, you’ll notice I usually put my own slant whatever I’m doing. Something like the all-time greatest films list was as simple as sitting down and watching 132 films. But by then writing 2 line reviews, mixing up a couple of Monty Python’s films & calling Jules et Jim “film noir ”, I managed to do something special by creating a post that causes instant nervous breakdowns in film geeks all over the world. I didn’t need to go to a gun range specifically to complete #43 – I just listed some of the more interesting experiences I’ve had shooting & blowing things up instead.
Now #4 on the 101 Things is “Catch a Fish With Your Bare Hands”, and it’s supposed to be a very calm, zen-like experience. Stand peacefully in some shallow stream, carefully and silently move your hands around the fish without splashing, then gracefully snatch the fish up. Which is pretty much the exact opposite of how I did it.
You’re supposed to be shirtless too, apparently
Likewise, my 2009 trip to Gnarloo Fishing Station with my Dad was supposed to be a photography trip. While Dad and his mates love fishing and I get the whole peaceful zen aspect to it, you’ve probably already guessed that the idea of sitting in a boat somewhere hanging onto a rod & waiting to hook some unsuspecting fish doesn’t hold a lot of appeal to me. But a trip to Gnarloo is a perfect opportunity to practice my underwater photography while capturing images of stunning sea creatures you simply don’t find anywhere else in the world.
A Nudibranch – it’s only about 2cm long
It’s also a great place to get eaten by a shark if you try hard enough. And by “hard enough” I mean “if you’re in the water”. Spear fishing at Gnarloo had gone the way of the Dodo bird a few years previously – partly because the catch-limits are restrictive, but mainly because every time you speared a fish and got blood in the water big-bitey-shark-things would start turning up. One of the few times I did use the speargun up there, the fish I speared was ripped off the spear by a 4 foot reef shark about 30 seconds before his 15 foot Tiger shark mate turned up and chased me out of the water…
As a general rule, we leave them alone and they leave us alone. Sharks are a constant presence in a place like Gnarloo (or further south at the aptly named “Shark Bay”), and rightly so – it’s their environment. But I’ve only ever been forced out of the water by sharks for one of two reasons:
I was covered in fish blood from spear fishing, or 2. The sharks had started eating other sharks AND I was covered in fish blood from spear fishing. Meet Bruce – he’s a Libra, likes long swims in the ocean and the taste of neoprene-clad free-divers
But generally no fish blood = no problem. You’re still careful though – the black neoprene wetsuits that many free divers are so fond of are easy for a big shark to confuse with a delicious seal. So you try to avoid making too much commotion on the surface, keep an eye out for big-bitey things swimming up underneath you, and you always dive with a buddy so there’s someone to stab and leave as easy pickings while you swim like hell for the boat.
Now on this particular Gnarloo outing, Dad and his mates were keen to remain safe and secure just hanging fishing lines off the back of the boat, while everyone’s favourite ADHD kid wanted to do some free diving to get poorly-lit photos of turtles & stingrays. So I jumped into some of Western Australia’s most hostile waters alone.
Armed only with an oversized camera and a snorkel. Because I am an idiot.
The boat was about 100m away from the nearest reef, with a mix of sandy bottom and seagrass – prime turtle country. Sure enough, paddling toward the reef I managed to get some of the best photos I’ve ever taken of Green Sea turtles, and saw a Loggerhead turtle for the first (and so far only) time.
Taken minutes before it all got WAY too real
Reaching the reef, I noticed all the smaller fish were hiding under rocks and staying out of sight right before I noticed the 4 foot white-tip reef shark hanging around. But it’s not usually that quiet just for a reef shark – something else bigger and more bitey was hanging around in the shadows too. But ADHD kid didn’t think about that very much, noooooo. Because there was gigantic painted crayfish sitting in the first hole I looked into.
Actual size
Now when I say “gigantic”, you need a sense of scale here. Most adult crayfish have bodies about 30cm long, can wrap their legs around something the size of your arm, and you catch them by looping a wire snare around their tail and pulling them gently out of the reef. This monster was over 60cm long with legs over 30cm long. I clipped my camera off to my weight belt, duck-dived down to the crayfish, reached in to pull it out of the hole… and it pulled me in with it.
Planting my feet on the reef either side of monster cray’s home I started fighting it: I would pull it out a few centimetres, it would pull me back a few centimetres. I had the advantage of overall strength, but it had the advantage of being able to breath underwater. I came to the surface gasping a few times, all the while the crayfish dug itself into the hole further. But eventually I wore it out, and wrestled out of its home. Grabbing my bulky camera in one hand, and holding the crayfish held to my chest with the other, and I flicked over onto my back to swim back to the boat.
Which is exactly the time the crayfish started to crawl across my chest to try to latch onto my face and push me underwater.
Just like this, only underwater and made of WAY bigger nightmares (Image Credit – Chapdeus)
So now I’m about 80m away from the boat in open water: $1500 camera that’s heavy enough to pull me underwater on its own in one hand, thrashing around on the surface in a black wetsuit looking like a panicked seal, knowing full well there’s atleast one shark big enough to eat me hanging around, all while using my other hand to fight a monster crayfish that can’t decide if it wants to drown me or eat my face…
The crayfish goes for a third option, deciding my chest can replace the reef as its new home after all, wrapping its gargantuan legs around my back and starting to dig in. I managed to grab its carapace and hold it’s head down against my chest – away from my face – while trying to peddle across the surface and get out of the water before big-bitey-things come to see what all the noise is about.
Once the crayfish was under control and had securely wrapped itself around me, I checked that my camera was still clipped off to… my weight belt WHY AM I STILL WEARING MY WEIGHT BELT WHEN I’M BEING DROWNED BY THE KRAKEN? I glanced down into the water to see that not only was is it now too deep to retrieve my weight belt if I drop it, but as an added bonus an 8-9 foot size bronze whaler (see: “big-bitey-shark-thing”) has decided to follow along as a spectator to my war against crustaceans & drowning.
Suddenly a huge shadow loomed up behind me just as something else brushed the back of my leg. I squealed, then realised I’d swum into the shadow of the boat and kicked the anchor line… I spat out my snorkel, yelled at Dad to take the camera, threw my fins & mask/snorkel into the boat, and scrambled up the ladder with mega-crayfish still latched onto my chest. Then we spent the next 5 minutes trying to get it to detach from my chest, because mega-crayfish had dug into the neoprene of my wetsuit with its legs.
Just before cooking the corpse of my defeated foe
And the worst part I don’t even eat crayfish.

content:
Just a bit of background – this was written way back in April, but it somehow slipped through the scheduling process. As such the “most recent employer” comment toward the end actually refers to another previous employer.
——————————————————————————————————————————-
This week’s 101 Things entry is all about some of the stupid shit I did during my education. It is far from a comprehensive list of my school stupidity as I’m sure “ Abducting your Year 9 English teacher’s teletubby and blowing it up on camera ” isn’t on the 101 list. But these are the stupid things I did (mostly) at school that relate directly to the list…
10 – Leave Your Mark in Graffiti I’ve never had any interest in graffiti at all. But I did go through a stage in year 8 where I inexplicably started calling my myself “Isbu” and running around with saying (in a mock Indian accent) “I AM ISBU!” for months, driving my parents to despair. Which is weird and seemingly unrelated – until I wrote “ISBU WAZ ERE” on a wall at a holiday camp with a marker pen. And my Dad saw it about 15 minutes later. And I was made to clean it off with a scourer while I cried tears of guilt. And let us never speak of this dark and bizarre period of my life ever again…
21 – Be a Human Guinea Pig For most, university is about experimenting and experiencing new things. For me in the Curtin Physics department, it was about trying new things while messing with people and unsuccessfully chasing girls. And I do mean unsuccessfully – one afternoon in first year three of us went exploring the other common rooms on campus, eventually meeting three girls in the Chemistry common room (we didn’t venture far). And over the next 6 months we all seemed to pair off – one pair went on to date for about a year, the other for over 2. Not me though: I got turned down by my Chemistry girl pairing because the fourth season premiere of The Amazing Race was on…
So it’s probably no surprise that when Keel’s – the only remotely attractive, under 30 and female member of the Physics faculty – mentioned that her equally attractive younger sister (making her our age) was running a research study in the Public Health building, about 6 of us immediately run across campus to take part…
…to find out it was a double-blind study tasting cheese and the only person we actually dealt with was mid-50’s tutor who looked at us in disapproval when we walked in the door. Although in fairness, we were probably looking at him with considerably more disappointment than he was sending at us.
83 – Skinny Dip at Midnight Ahhh, the wonders of year 9… or not. I have no idea how I wind up in these situations, but the facts are these:
It was I was at a chick friend’s place with another guy and girl - It was about 11:30pm - I had nil interest being there, and was frankly bored - The other guy was trying to convince the two girls to nude up, so I did it myself – partly to spite him, partly because at least it made the night remotely memorable. Actually, I do know how I wind up in these situations – a combination of boredom and ADHD. This whole post is turning into a collection of “Josh’s Greatest Fails”…
But wait, there’s still…
95 – Get Revenge Before people start jumping to conclusions here, I’d like to make something very, very clear – I don’t believe in revenge. I do however believe in assisting the universe at fucking over shitty people when the opportunity presents. And besides one fairly nasty ex-girlfriend – who’s cosmic punishment is to wake every single day being her – I’ve really only been forced to deal with two people who’ve seriously pushed my limits. People who, just by being there, turned an otherwise fun and healthy learning/work environment into something I dreaded going to each day. One of them was my most recent Line Manager, the other was my Year 6 teacher. The Year 6 teacher is an easy one – she hated me because I’d just come back from living overseas and she’d been teaching in the same classroom for 15 years. And her way of dealing with the stress of teaching was to be sweet as pie to everyone except the one kid she singled out each year to direct her frustrations at – foolishly she picked me.
She told my parents I might be mentally handicapped (she actually used the word “retarded”), and that I was an attention-seeking troublemaker (at least that wasn’t a lie). Only unlike the kids from previous years she’d picked on, I fought back – told her she was a bully, and that I wanted to discuss all the abuse she’d been directing at me with the Principal. So she had a nervous breakdown. And I do mean a nervous breakdown – when she left the principal’s office she’d been balling her eyes out for an hour and immediately went on 3 months psych leave.
So we got a substitute teacher for the last term of Year 6. But to top it all off, the following year I won an award for being the highest scoring student in Western Australia in a national science competition. To recognise my achievement, the principal presented the award from UNSW to me in front of the entire school at our weekly school assembly. And once he handed it to me and shook my hand, I turned to the crowd, held my award in front of the whole school, then stared straight at her and grinned until the other teachers made me sit down.
“Retarded” you say?
Dad You are a nutta – what did the Royal Marines do to my son???
