Details Identification Feature type: Cave Source: WikiCave.org Cave and exploration data Exploration potential: Medium Tourism potential: High Goes to water: Yes Additional Notes The dry cave area of the Bue Marino system was opened to the public as a tourist attraction . In high summer, some boat operators travel here on a daily basis, to show the tourists the magnificent Stalactite formations. Right next to entrance, where the transport boats are moored, the dive starts. We descent to shallow water (1.50m), once inside we ascent to the surface in a large room. In this large hall you can still use the old stairs once used by tourists and explore the dry area of the cave safely. Our journey takes us underwater below a small bridge to the actual cave entrance of Bue Marino. Equipment check, safety drill, air planning and we are of into the cave system.
The entrance area is a bit milky, maximum depth here is 15m. Fresh water flows through the cave entrance in the open which off course enhances the effect of the Halocline strongly (fresh and salt water mixing). Many sumps present themselves in this cave system and it is always worth it to accent and view the unbelievable beauty of the formations. The cave seems to be endless. Massive rooms or chambers showing beautiful formations.
A part of this system goes up and down. There are many other tunnels in different connecting with the main tunnel. Some ending fairly soon in a dead end sump, others continue for several kilometres. There is a possibility to continue with a dry walk to the next sump and dive further. The dry passages on themselves are worth the dive. There is much to discover in this system!
Equipment configuration: Back mount and Sidemount for the Sumps.
Protec Sardinia - Cave: https://protecsardinia.com/bue-marino/?lang=en The dry area of the cave is open to the public as a tourist attraction. In midsummer there are several daily expeditions to show the fantastic formations.
The dive starts in a nice big entrance. You dip under an over hanging arch and surface in a large subterranean lake. Old catwalks from seasons past decorate the chamber. Our path leads 15m underneath to a milky entrance. Fresh water pushes out of the cave, which of course creates haloclines.
The formations in this cave are breathtaking. Several side passages cleave through the halls. Some end in sumps and others extend for several kilometers.
EQUIPMENT CONFIGURATION: Backmount and Sidemount for the Sumps
GASES: Compressed Air
EXPLORATION: We discovered many new passages and laid over 2km of line, but the cave continues.
Vimeo: https://vimeo.com/6791782 Slawek Packo (2009)
“We did two dives in this cave. Both to the first dry part. It was around 90 min swim in - so long because of making video, then 3 hours trip around dry part and then 60 min swim back. This cave is truly amazing both under and above the water.”
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/groups/715466411806907/permalink/7989137561106386/ References Cave Atlas: http://caveatlas.com/systems/system.asp?ID=581&co=IT
title: Grotta del Bue Marino

Details Identification Feature type: Cave Source: WikiCave.org Cave and exploration data Cave rating: Cave Exploration potential: High Tourism potential: Medium Goes to water: Yes Additional Notes The entry is spectacular. Dive into this system as if it were the entrance to an Indonesian temple. The ground is covered with snow-white sand. The sidewalls run together like a pyramid. After a short swim you emerge into a huge dry cave. Like all good temples the secret passage between cavern and cave is hidden and unmarked.
This dive is especially worthwhile if you join in the tour of the dry cave.
MAX. DEPTH: 15 Meters
MAX. PENETRATION: 60 Meters
MAX. MEMBERS: 4 Divers
CAVERN LINE? None present
Protec Sardinia - Cave: https://protecsardinia.com/del-fico/?lang=en This system is challenging. Depths change quickly and often. Good buoyancy is required and knowledge of personal weighting is paramount to handle regular variants in water density. Sidemount systems are preferred in order to pass restrictions and easily walk from sump to sump.
EQUIPMENT CONFIGURATION: Backmount and Sidemount
GASES: Compressed Air and Nitrox
EXPLORATION: Routes were discovered during an expedition in collaboration with a speleologist group from Brunei.
InDepth - GUE: https://gue.com/blog/charting-sardinias-grotta-del-fico/
SKEP: https://protecsardinia.com/project-grotta-del-fico/?lang=en
The mountain massif called “Supramonte” is located on the east coast of Sardinia. With a summit height of 1463 m and an extension of approx. 50 square km the largest limestone area in Sardinia. Due to the strong karstification of this region, all surface water disappears in rugged mountain gorges to finally collect in the numerous underground cave systems and exit again in karst springs or flow into the sea. The cave “Grotta del Fico” is part of this subterranean system and it can be assumed that it plays an important role in the water balance of the Supramonte due to its enormous size.
Since the entrance to the cave is under water directly in front of the cliffs in the Mediterranean Sea, the entire logistics can only be carried out by water or by boat. By exploring the cave “Grotta del Fico”, this exploration can provide an important building block in the exploration of the mighty Supramonte karst system and contribute significantly to the understanding of the underwater household and the history of the formation of the “Supramonte” mountains.
References Protec Sardinia - Cavern: https://protecsardinia.com/grotta-del-fico/?lang=en Images
title: Grotta Del Fico

content: Details Identification Feature type: Cave Cave and exploration data Cave rating: Advanced Highest cave rating: Advanced Goes to water: Yes Diving data Water type: Fresh Tidal: No References Portions of the following information were taken from www.protecsardinia.com This entrance is spectacular. One dives into this system as if you were entering a Indonesian Temple. The bottom is covered with snow white sand and the inner walls get together in pyramid like shape. After a short time one ascents to the surface and finds him self in a massive dry cave. Depending on the water level, take off the fins and get to the actual entry. The entry is hard to find as the water is right on top of it and the cave narrows to a restriction. A very appealing cave with rapidly changes depths, it is recommended to dive with a Nitrox blend. After a short while one approaches the main line, further through a narrow tunnel where the cave shows a side tunnel short after which leads to the right in to the deep. Further on the mainline to a opening in the bottom where the line suddenly falls down from 8 meters deep to 23 meters deep. One has to be careful not to disturb the sediment as the walls are covered with the finest cave dust. Without perfect neutral buoyancy there is a risk to the disturb the fine sediment resulting in a complete silt out. This cave system is complex in its shape. Shafts leading from 25 meters deep into sumps make this system very interesting, but only for the experienced cave diver. Equipment configuration: Back mount and Sidemount.

content: Details Identification Feature type: Cave Cave and exploration data Cave rating: Advanced Highest cave rating: Advanced Vertical access: Yes Exploration potential: VeryHigh Goes to water: Yes Surveyed length: 2000 m Amenities hasShowers: No hasToilets: No References Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/100001986734462/videos/408447545033427/ Google Maps: https://maps.app.goo.gl/8YQY6Ki81Smt8gsY7 latracciaescursioniemontagna.com: https://latracciaescursioniemontagna.com/2022/03/12/676-grotta-dellacqua-nera/ “The origin of the name is unknown, certainly the cave that opens up between the light rocks is black, but the water is completely normal. It is thought to derive from the color of the bottom, covered in dark moss, on which the underground stream flows out before flowing into the Senaiga. Unlike today, it was once always well fed even in periods of drought, raising questions about its origin. In the thirties it was proven, with the introduction of dyes, that the cave is in communication with the Castel Tesino Caves, located at 1000 meters above sea level and a few kilometers away as the crow flies. The fine sand rich in granite crystals sedimented inside the cave indicates a supply of water much further away, coming from the Cima d’Asta Group. This suggests that there is a vast and intricate system of communicating caves inside the mountains.” “…exploration began only in the 70s by a Speleo diving group from Padua and continued in recent years by a Speleological Group from Valstagna (VI), 1600 meters have been explored overcoming three challenging siphons and many difficult passages.”
title: Grotta dell'acqua Nera

About The cave was discovered by chance in October 1886 by the owner of the land while he was excavating for the construction of a wall. The cavity was explored by the owner of the land who found the bone remains of Ursus spelaeus. Hence the name given to the cave. The first systematic exploration was by Capello in 1952, the GSP passed the first siphon upstream in the sixties reaching the next tunnel. In 1991 the CSARI group from Brussels passed a series of siphons reaching a fourth impassable siphon.
The cavity opens approximately 500 m east of the hamlet of Ponte di Nava, in the upper Tanaro Valley, in correspondence with an isolated house, approximately 15 m from the road; the entrance, which leads directly into the initial room, is in correspondence with a dry stone wall and closed by an old wooden door.
The cave consists of a series of sub-horizontal galleries that branch off from the entrance hall. On the left, a large sub-circular gallery quickly leads to the active and large lake-siphon. A few meters of lake and the speleo-underwater part begins, at a first siphon crossed by a good flow of the main stream (S1, L = 60 m, depth 8 m, ) follows on the right a concretioned aerial gallery that extends for about 200 m stopping at an impassable narrow passage, while on the left are S2 (L = 15 m, depth -2 m) and S3 (L = 90 m, depth -18 m). The exit of the third siphon can also be reached from the previous concretioned gallery, from here starts S4 (L = 40 m, depth -9 m) which is narrow, difficult and with poor visibility. Returning to the initial room, a second central gallery leads after about a hundred meters, progressively narrowing, to narrow spaces closed by small landslides. Still from the initial room, on the right, a series of fairly complex, close and interconnected spaces allow you to reach a small lake and a small gallery closed by concretions. From a hydrogeological point of view, the cavity is crossed by an important stream in which it is not difficult to find small trout. The temperature of the water changes greatly during the year, in winter it is around 4° C, while in summer it can reach 10° C. From all these indications it seems very probable that the watercourse is linked to sub-channel losses of the Tanaro river. The resurfacing of the waters is near a series of pools, a few hundred meters downstream, near the river itself. (taken from: Atlas of the Piedmontese karst areas - Volume 2 (2010)

digilander.libero.it: https://digilander.libero.it/enrlana/e_nava1.htm Discovered in 1886, this cave is situated few hundred of metres from the village of Ponte di Nava; it has been so called because of the skeleton of Ursus Spelaeus found in one of its halls. It is formed by the intersection of several tunnels in which the waters of the Tanaro river worked in different periods. Into this cave still flows a remakable river that has two siphons both towards valley and huphill.
https://www.deepdivingacademy.it/: https://www.deepdivingacademy.it/wordpress/2023/09/02/la-grotta-orso-del-ponte-di-nava/ [Translated from Italian] The cave “Orso di Ponte di Nava” (Ormea, CN) is a gym for all of Attilio’s students, including me. Inside the cave, a short distance from the entrance, there is a lake of clear water, from which a siphon begins, short but just over a meter high and with a sandy bottom. Attilio takes the neophyte cave divers into this siphon; after a few meters he stirs the sand on the bottom. When you can no longer see anything, the diver’s tranquility is put to the test in conditions of poor visibility, an essential prerequisite for cave diving.

Details Identification Feature type: Cave Source: Google Cave and exploration data Vertical access: No Exploration potential: Medium Tourism potential: Medium Goes to water: Yes Additional Notes fix872 (2009)
prometeoricerche.eu: http://www.prometeoricerche.eu/GIGI/Report/rio_torretta_2010.htm (Translated from Italian) RIO TURRET 2010
09-03-10 I am with the Pied Piper and G i Bi at the house where we will be staying, that is, in a hamlet of Pedemonte. Fanni, the local muse, organized everything: a different house than last year but, like that one, uninhabited in the winter, even if in perfect working order, apart from the internal temperature which is certainly not the warmest. This is a detail of little importance because in the afternoon I will receive, procured by Simone, a new sleeping bag which I hope will do the job for him. We reach the cave, after having unloaded the car and reloaded the necessary equipment, at noon or almost. We carry all the Pied Piper and I, while G i B i he dedicates himself to outdoor shots. Around 13.30 Simone arrives, while we are still arranging the regulators on the cylinders; while chatting, we mount my hybrid (Copis-Meg) then, given the time of 2.30 pm and hunger, we go to eat something. For today the work is finished and tomorrow morning we will dive.
10-03-10 Morning wake up after a freezing night with 5cm of fresh snow that makes the landscape white. The snow brings happiness but the problems will come from the Pied Piper who will take three times longer than necessary to get up here. Boaria and Giuseppe arrive punctually, at the only bar in the area where we wait in the warmth, to get everyone together. Finally full, we reach the cave at 11.00. When all the equipment, including Copis, is ready, shortly after 12.00, we start transporting the cylinders in the siphon. Since the level is very low, it will be more difficult than usual to carry everything up to the third siphon, but the visibility is good and the desire to continue is excellent. The first to leave are Boaria and I: the others will follow closely behind us. Once passed the first siphon, we stack the cylinders on a stone that seems made for it and we reach the second siphon with the diving equipment on our shoulders; I stay there and wait while the brave companions, once they have unloaded the bibo, make a couple of trips each to finish the transport. Once the equipment has been put back on, we leave for the third siphon. It is here that we realize how low the level is because, to get over the neck of debris, we have to go up it for a couple of meters in dry conditions. Four of us, the handrail is fast but, when we go down the other side, we realize we have to continue for a few more meters before finding water; the only positive thing is that with the level so low, the room between the second and third siphon is not under pressure and therefore there will be no Co2 stagnation problems. Again Boaria and I at the start, the Pied Piper and Franco will leave after about ten minutes so as not to block the passage through the bottlenecks. My Copis is normal and I’m convinced I can pass easily even without the changes I made last time. Boaria goes down first while from above I pass the reel, the three 12lt cylinders. and one of 10lt; once the bottleneck has been released, with a 12lt cylinder. I slip in with decision and in a moment I come out on the other side. I load myself with three 12lt cylinders. and I proceed while Boaria, with the reel, a 12lt cylinder. and a 10lt. follows me closely. In the siphon there are arrows indicating the exit direction of the super-ego of the person who placed them who, not being able to explore, gratified himself by filling the walls of the siphons with his name. At -21m I find the skein of thread which, broken about fifteen meters further on and carried back by the current, has accumulated treacherous in a corner like a trap. I proceed by pulling it to extend it again, and when it stops, from behind Boaria who has noticed, solves the problem. I continue to the end of the garment and then tie it with the following garment. I tell Boaria to go ahead, because he is in an open circuit and these stops only contribute to consuming gas. We are at -28m, thirds on his 12lt bibo. they are finished so Boaria leaves me the cylinders and begins the return. I remain alone as I like, free from tying myself or tying my partner: I reach the bottleneck which at these levels is at -32m, I leave the 10lt tank and go through the hole with my 12lt load. The path is easy, almost too easy and incredible if I think of last year’s work, but the news we had was dramatic. After the bottleneck, I think there might be something on the left, but the thread continues to the right and so I follow it. At -40m I deposit two cylinders and the exploration reel and after about twenty meters down to -44m, I leave the cylinder which will remain there as an emergency, while the other two I will carry further on until the next passage. I go back calmly, arranging the thread as best I can in some places where it is damaged and too loose. I returned to my companions after exactly one hour and all together we quickly returned to the second siphon. Having recovered from that too, we leave part of the equipment and we just have to overcome the last obstacle. Outside at 16.00, we find 10cm of beautiful fresh snow which requires us to be very careful in traveling along the hyper-slippery river bed. It’s already late for me because I have to hold a screening at the Lthe ons of Bassano. Considering the abundant snowfall that is coming down and knowing that the forecasts announce good weather only starting from Thursday afternoon we decide to skip the dive the next day. I run to get ready, going to take a hot shower in a freezing bathroom.
12-03-10 We leave from the cave entrance at 10.00, we are Boa, Franco, Moses, Giuseppe and I determined to carry out a perfect team work to achieve a good exploratory result.
Perfect collaboration to transport the equipment up to the third siphon, few cylinders but between lights and camera, the weight should not be underestimated. Moses and I enter the third siphon, the only ones with the rebreather. I swim slowly to allow Moses to shoot, with the shallow depth playing in my favor and even if my concentration for exploration suffers, I stop at various points to allow Moses to reach shooting areas in front of me. We reach the -32m bottleneck together, then we separate. I greet, as I enter the little hole with the 12lt relays and starting to walk the already paved tunnel, I recover my concentration for exploration. After the deep part, I start the decompressive stages, until I reach the limit of the last exploration. I attach the thread and, as I progress, what I see does not seem like the right continuation: after only 30m I reach a surface, and while the tunnel is filled with mud, I am more and more convinced that it cannot be the right route. Anyway I’m here and I decide to remove the rebreather to go and see the dry gallery. After another 20m of dry trail, I stop on impassable bottlenecks. I go back to the water covered in mud, I dress for the dive and I go back into the water which, in an instant, becomes completely cloudy so that I have to hold the line in my hand up to a depth of -3/4m then, as I descend into the room, I reflect that there must be a continuation and it must be here. At -10m the visibility has definitely improved so I start looking. Maybe we’re here: a tunnel seems to open up on my right; I’m at -15m, I plug in my reel and start unwinding the line. I go up to -10m then I go down almost immediately to -20m, the tunnel is 5m wide by 3m high, there are no mud deposits, the rocks are white: this is not just the continuation but something more. I progress through amusing ups and downs until I stop for having reached the limit allowed by the emergency open circuit at -30m and after having pulled a further 240m of line. Not bad I tell myself, I kicked for over a kilometer and now I still have to go back through the gallery in reverse and, what’s more, recovering all the tanks. I leave the bottles at the -32m bottleneck, thinking about the filming we will do tomorrow and return, making the few necessary decompression stops before resurfacing. I exchange my impressions with friends who have patiently waited for me: curiosity is obviously great and my revelations make us dream of incredible explorations even on this side of the Asiago plateau massif. We go back together and, between the third siphon and the exit, I think that if I had a piglet, I could try to continue on Sunday. Dreams, only dreams, the piglet is in Lecco and I don’t have time to go get it.
13-03-10 The night was spent mulling over how to solve the problem of exploration crippled by the lack of the piggy. With everything prepared as we did, I don’t like the idea of ​​precluding a good advance, so in the morning, while having breakfast, the Pied Piper suggests that a piglet could lend him G i B i . As soon as G i B i joins us, we immediately ask for their availability. Boa, Franco are also there on Sunday and the Thing can then be done. For today, Moses dedicates himself to the video camera filming me while I’m going to reposition the cylinders in the siphon, one more task but which I carry out with great happiness; Boa, Franco, Nadia and the Pied Piper help in the air transport after which they will go to see something on their own. This time Moses waits for me at the -7m bottleneck to film even a little bit of the return and, passing it on my way back, I find visibility reduced to just over a metre. When we re-emerge, we find the others waiting for us, all happy to inform us that they have explored a 95m lateral gallery at a depth of about -3m, which continues. This spring is a real surprise.
14-03-10 At the “breakfast bar”, Francesco, Laura and Nadia arrive with a tray of fresh pastries and Boa is no less with the brioches. Although this binge is welcome, the most awaited by me is the G i B i piglet which turns out to be a pig due to its size and weight. With the arrival of Giuseppe and the Pied Piper, the team restarts the work. The last to appear is the Proteus who will join us beyond the siphons later to help. Between one siphon and another I try not to sweat but that doesn’t seem possible, even if I only have to carry the rebreather on my back; the others, Boa, Giuseppe, Nadia and the Pied Piper will carry the maialone up to the third siphon. Boa accompanies me up to the narrow passage at -7m to help me pass the thruster because given the dimensions I have some doubts about the possibility of succeeding. The beast is perfectly balanced in the water but once challenged, its speed disappoints me a lot; used to my little ones this is slow, so much so that even Boa manages to follow me finning, without even too much effort. Anyway, with the big beast I won’t bear the effort of finning. The bottleneck is easily overcome and I can be towed to the exploration point. I pass the deep part -55m, I go up observing the few minutes of decompression which force me to forced stops then, finally I can spin in the tunnel explored the day before yesterday: I recognize the point where I cut the line, I stop, attach the new reel and I begin to pull a new thread making me pull from the piggy. The meters of new wire flow, the altitude varies with some ups and downs until it reaches -40m after about 150m of progression, the tunnel continues to descend and this is a limit for me again due to the open emergency circuit. At -50m, when I decided to stop, I laid out 235m of new line, and I’m happy even if I would have liked to go a little further, but that’s it for this time. The return time passes quickly between a few deco stops and the recovery of the relay cylinders. I pass the bottleneck at -32m with four 12lt and one 10lt cylinders in addition to the maialone; but the funniest part is overcoming the bottleneck at -7m, the most selective, with two other cylinders , one 7lt and one 10lt .The decompression is so short that I don’t even realize I’m doing it and I resurface carrying everything with me. Now the heavy part of the work remains, that is the transport of the material in the dry stretches that will be done by the other members of the group. I re-emerge greeted by the lights and the laughter of the members of the group: I can’t get out of the water if I don’t speak first. Sounds like a full-blown interrogation. The first piece of information I give is that it is not necessary to go to the bottleneck to recover the cylinders because, feeling fit, I recovered them all by myself, the second, the most awaited, is a quick description of the exploration and the possibility of continuing. Few words that nevertheless give an important charge of energy for the work still to be done. I go alone with my Copis-Meg on my shoulder and the emergency tank while Boa, Giuseppe, Nadia and the Pied Piper take care of the transport between the third and second siphon, Proteus takes a tank and goes towards the exit . I re-emerge in the open air first after 220’, while the efficient quartet re-emerges carrying practically all the material, after just over four hours. We get one last big help carrying the material from the cave to the car from Iste, Laura and Enniosan. Rio Torretta remained a question mark for many years, now it is becoming one of the longest explorations in northern Italy, with over 1500m of planimetric development.

About Max Depth 35m
Details Identification Feature type: Cave System name: Monte Lungos Source: WikiCave.org Cave and exploration data Vertical access: No Goes to water: Yes Access and warnings Cave with confirmed coordinates. Big enough for backmounted doubles.
Additional Notes Very close to one of the most beautiful beaches in the Golfo di Orosei an entrance to a cave system is located. Hardly visible from the boat one easily dives and pass the entrance without ever knowing what a fantastic cave system lays behind. The dive leads into a small passage through solid rock. Onto the walls hundreds of mussels have attached. After a short period of time we reach the main cave line and continue deeper inside the mountain. The visibility is surprisingly good changing rapidly after 8 minutes. The water starts to get milky again and you will approach a halocline.
The shape of the main tunnel is quite constant, the passage becomes larger and higher and the wideness of the cave enlarges. The average passage depth is 14 meters. Many large formations and stalactites are there to admire. Several side tunnels appear and after some 40 minutes the main line ends but just before the end of the line the tunnel makes a jump into the deep and leads you to a depth of over 35m where the cave continues its path.
Equipment configuration: Back mount and Sidemount for the Sumps.
Vimeo: https://vimeo.com/15629612 Slawek Packo (2010) “Clip from our dive in Cala Luna cave to UB40 passage.”
SKEP: https://protecsardinia.com/project-cala-luna/ The mountain massif called “Supramonte” is located on the east coast of Sardinia. With a summit height of 1463 m and an extension of approx. 50 square km the largest limestone area in Sardinia. Due to the strong karstification of this region, all surface water disappears in rugged mountain gorges to finally collect in the numerous underground cave systems and exit again in karst springs or flow into the sea. The cave “Cala Luna” is a part of this underground system and it can be assumed that the cave connects with the largest cave system “Monte Lungos” (proven by staining tests).
Since the entrance to the cave is under water directly in front of the cliffs in the Mediterranean Sea, the entire logistics can only be carried out by water or by boat. By exploring the cave “Grotta Cala Luna”, this exploration can provide an important building block in the exploration of the mighty Supramonte karst system and contribute significantly to the understanding of the underwater household and the history of the formation of the “Supramonte” mountains.
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/watch?v=1329890718521917 References Cave Atlas: http://www.caveatlas.com/systems/system.asp?ID=582&co=IT Images

About About “The House Cave” for Kadena Glamping Muna
From Anita: “In the backyard of where we stayed lies Goa La Pahia, the hidden cave, with an unassuming small rock entrance surrounded by vegetation. As you descend, it slowly unveils its secrets. Calcite crystal formations decorate the ceiling. which tum into whole sections covered in crystal straws. As you swim further along the cave it reveals more and more of its unique formations. Small but impressive, it has a special place in my heart. The first underwater crystal cave that I have ever seen was a dream come true. The sheer beauty, uniqueness and the masses of speleothems took a while to sink in. I was on such a high, but at the same time I was so calm and close to a meditative state as I took in the surroundings with awe and wonder. This was my introduction to cave diving in Muna Island. What a phenomenal start that made me curious for what lay in store for the coming days.” References https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pw2oqsmQ9Ew

content:
About New Guinea II is a limestone cave and rockshelter on the Snowy River at the end of New Guinea Track, near Buchan, Victoria. The cave was within the country of the Krowathunkooloong clan of the Gunaikurnai nation. The deep cave system has an overhanging cliff that creates a rock shelter at the entrance facing the river. Excavations in the 1980s carried out by archaeologist Paul Ossa and a team from La Trobe University found stone artefacts, and other signs of occupation that were dated to almost 20,000 BP.
New Guinea II is one of three major cave systems that have so far been investigated in the middle Snowy River area, along with New Guinea Cave (NG-1), and Nuigini Namba Fav Cave (NG-5, NG-6. New Guinea II is largely joint-controlled, although the entrance area is formed along bedding planes and has a large chamber and passage with a perennial stream and several entrances. Finger or tool marks made in the dried mud on the cave wall are thought to be of prehistoric Aboriginal origin and are similar to those of Koonalda Cave on the Nullarbor Plain. New Guinea II is the first place where such markings have been recorded in Victoria. Animal origin has been proposed for the wall markings, although many appear to be in regular patterns, including circles and diagonal crosses. They are also generally on smoother parts of the walls and some are in now-dark and inaccessible parts of the cave.
The cave is used by bent-winged bats, which congregate in the large chamber, deep inside the cave.
The cave has been occupied intermittently for more than 20,000 years (21,900 +900/-800 BP and 4,660 +/- 110 BP) with a small, but constant amount of lithic material and bone artefacts, as well as evidence of a hearth on a dry floor near the stream within the cave. Vertebrate fauna remains are abundant but mostly of non-cultural origin, representing animals that used the cave at times it was vacated by humans.
The artefact assemblage is similar to that at the nearby Cloggs Cave in Buchan, and in conjunction with Birrigai in the ACT they represent a general signature of human occupation and resource exploitation of the southeastern uplands during the Pleistocene. This reveals a non-intensive use of caves and shelters and consumption of local fauna. In comparison, southwestern Tasmanian Pleistocene sites appear to have a different signature of cave occupation and the primacy of a single vertebrate resource.

Details Identification Feature type: Cave Cave and exploration data Cave rating: Advanced Highest cave rating: Advanced Goes to water: Yes Diving data Water type: Fresh Tidal: No References Portions of the following information were taken from Florida Geological Survey Bulletin 66.
Diving is open at Hart Springs but there are different conditions for each entrance. No
guide is needed for Little Hart but a guide IS required to enter the cave via Black
Lagoon. Click here for information on
contacting guides for this site. In addition, the guides are all volunteers, guides
are not allowed to charge for services and don’t expect anyone to tip them. However, I
wouldn’t feel bad at least making sure they had a good meal or deco beverage after the
dive.
Hart Springs is located within a county recreation area 6.5 miles northwest of Fanning
Springs. After crossing over the Suwannee River on US 98/27A heading east, turn north
(left) on SR 26 and drive approximately 1.4 miles to the town of Wilcox. In Wilcox, SR
26 makes a 90 degree bend to the east (right). At this bend continue north (straight)
onto CR 232. Drive 4.1 miles and turn west (left) on CR 344. Travel 1.6 miles, then turn
north (right) into the recreation area.
Description – The head of Hart Springs Run has three merging spring runs. In April
2002, the only significantly flowing spring in this system was at the head of the middle
channel and was the one sampled for water quality. The middle spring pool measures 51 ft
north to south and 45 ft east to west. The depth of the pool measured over the vent was
19.9 ft. The water was clear and greenish. In the center of the spring pool, a prominent
boil is produced on the surface by spring discharge. The vent is a vertical limestone
fissure with 15 ft high walls. The spring pool has a nearly rectangular shape and is
enclosed by a 4 ft high metal retaining wall. The metal wall extends several hundred feet
southward and forms the perimeter of the entire southernmost spring and its run. The
bottom is sand in the swimming area where the three spring channels merge. The northern
run was not flowing, but the southernmost spring had slight flow with no boil on its
surface. Exotic aquatic vegetation is abundant in the spring pool. Algae are abundant in
the pool and the run. Other aquatic plants occur on the edges of the pool. From the
swimming area at the confluence of the spring runs, Hart Springs Run flows northwest
approximately 850 ft into the Suwannee River from the east. The springs are situated
within the forested river floodplain. A 0.3 mile long wooden boardwalk follows along the
north side of the spring run and the east side of the river, and footbridges cross over
both the northernmost and main spring runs. An underwater cave system occurs at Hart
Springs.
Utilization - The spring is within a county recreation area that provides full facilities.
title: Hart Springs - Black Lagoon

Details Identification Feature type: Sinkhole Reference: L0040 Source: Forestry SA Location Coordinates: -37.95224754705794, 140.8566677570343 Altitude: 44 m Address: Sea Coast Hill Rd, The District Council of Grant, South Australia, AUS, 5291 Checked: true Cave and exploration data Cave rating: Basic Highest cave rating: Basic Vertical access: Yes Tourism potential: High Disabled access potential: Medium Goes to water: Yes Diving data Maximum depth: 26 m Water type: Fresh Tidal: No Access and warnings ForestrySA
References LSECR: Page 92 Hells Hole is one of the most aptly-named, visually-impressive karst features in the entire South East. Hidden in a small patch of protected native scrub in a recently-replanted pine forest in hilly dune limestone country, this spectacular “cenote”-style sinkhole is 45 metres or so in diameter, and its 30-metre drop to the water often causes unsuspecting visitors to gasp in surprise when they approach its sheer edge! The top portion of the rim is undercut and very sandy, and it overlies much harder, whiter limestone in which numerous small scallop-like erosion cavities have formed. One area is particularly useful for divers requiring access, as they can walk down to a sheltered alcove and step onto a ladder belayed from above if such is desired. Although it is not too apparent from the top of the feature, the walls gradually “bell out”, continuing to do so more obviously once the water has been reached. The talus mound lies at a depth of just 5 metres immediately below the entrance area, where numerous trees and branches lie tangled together (often under thick masses of duckweed which can cover the lake). There was also a dumped 1963 EJ Holden in this area until around early 1983, when five members of the South East Scuba Divers club arranged for its removal (“The Border Watch”, 17 Feb 1983). The feature deepens both to the north and south to a maximum depth of around 26 metres, but no signif icant passages have been reported in recent years. The sinkhole has long been known in the area, and local legend has it that it was discovered by two people who chanced upon it in the dark with a horse and trap. Bob Sexton placed it in CEGSA’s Records in June 1961, when the “discovery” story was mentioned as well as the fact that Hells Hole had incorrectly been called Caroline Sinkhole (and vice versa). Although no fish or other large forms of life were observed by the author in 1980, a single specimen of the crustaceans which were to be later identified as rare syn- carids (Koonunga crenarum) was sighted near the entrance. Forestry SA: L0040, Thin Roof: N, Fence: R. Dimensions: 45m x 30m deep. Features: Rare crustaceans, gating to stop vehicle access (dumping) www.cavediving.net.au: https://www.cavediving.net.au/images/articles/maps/5L-40.gif https://www.trimixdivers.com/trimix5/?p=4927: This sinkhole is located in thick bush to the East & South of Mt Gambier. It has a path leading to its edge, but no vehicular access. Vehicles are parked on the bush track some 70m from the sinkhole?s edge. The sinkhole entrance is about 40m in diameter and a 30m vertical pitch needs to be negotiated before diving commences. Apparently no more than 26m in depth, this is a typical Mt Gambier sinkhole except the water is further down into the sinkhole than most of the rest ! Hells Hole is roughly what the Little Blue Lake near Mount Schank would look like if the water level was to drop around 20 metres or so – perhaps next Ice Age!

A disused slate quarry situated in the Tilberthwaite Valley, near Coniston, Hodge Close is one of many such slate workings in the Tilberthwaite area. The mine was worked from the 19th century to the early 1960s and is now a site much favoured by divers. The quarry, once worked as a open pit, is now now flooded by 150ft, with a chamber coming off the bottom. The green slate quarry walls rise straight up from the water 50m to the trees. The water has a maximum depth of approximately 28 metres. Inside the quarry there are a number of tunnels and caverns. Signposted off Ambleside to Coniston road (map reference - Ordnance Survey map ‘English Lakes SW area’ 318017). The quarry owners will not grant permission for diving - but will not stop divers using the site at their own risk. Access to the lower car park and tunnel can be obtained by paying £4.00 per car at the house with the A-Flag in the garden. Access to and from the water is challenging! It is through a semi flooded tunnel and then down a scaffolding ladder. Height above sea level - 155 metres. Closest Air refills are Kendal High St (about 1 hour away) or from Capernwray dive site (about 50 minutes away).

From the intersection of SR 71 and CR 164 north of Marianna, travel east on CR 164 approximately 1.7

Description - Hole-in-the-Rock Spring consists of a spring depression at the base of a
limestone cliff. Merritt’s Mill Pond waters inundate the spring depression. A 10 ft wide spring
vent is situated on the southeast side of the depression. The vent consists of a cavern leading
into a cave system. Clear spring water discharges from this limestone opening at barely detectable
rates. The oval spring depression measures 30 ft east to west and 20 ft north to south with a depth
of 13.6 ft near the center. A limestone ledge juts out over the vent about 15 ft from the cliff
face. The spring is bordered by the clear water mill pond to the north, west, and east. To the south
rise steep, vegetation covered banks, reaching 25 to 50 ft above the spring. Hole-in-the-Rock Spring
is a swimming and cave diving hotspot. A small wooden platform for swimming and diving access is on
the northwest side of the pool. In June 2003, very little flow from the spring was detected

Holmes Blue Spring is located on the west bank of the Choctawhatchee River 1.4 miles
northeast of the community of Cerrogordo. Exit I-10 at SR 279 and turn north toward
Caryville. Go 1 mile to the intersection of SR 279 and US 90. Turn west (left) and
drive 2.5 miles to the intersection of US 90 and SR 179A/181. Turn north (right) and
follow 179A for 5 miles to Cerrogrodo. In Cerrogordo, turn east (right) toward the
river and follow signs to boat ramp about 0.5 miles. From the public boat ramp in
Cerrogordo, travel 1.5 miles upstream on the Choctawhatchee River to the mouth of the
spring. The narrow spring run flows in from the northwest (left) bank.
Description - Holmes Blue Spring has a circular spring pool that measures 30 ft in
diameter. The vent is a deep, vertical, steep-walled opening in limestone over which
the depth measures 29.2 ft. The spring sits in a conical, circular depression with 8 ft
high clay banks. Limestone is exposed near the circular vent in the center of the
depression. Its waters are bluish and crystal clear. A copious boil emerges over the
vent, and water flows approximately 3 in. higher that the surrounding spring surface.
There are a few sticks and logs on the sand, clay, and limestone bottom. There is no
aquatic vegetation in the spring or its run. The short spring run averages 3 ft deep
and flows 150 ft southeast into the murky brown Choctawhatchee River. Spring-water
levels are closely tied to fluctuations of the nearby river. The spring run is under a
forest canopy within the heavily wooded river floodplain.
Utilization - Holmes Blue Spring is undeveloped and exists in a natural condition.
title: Holmes Blue

The Holton Creek Rise is 11 miles northwest of Live Oak on SRWMD land. From the intersection of US 90
and CR 249 in Live Oak, drive northwest on CR 249 (Noble’s Ferry Road) approximately 12 miles to the
bridge over the Suwannee River. From the bridge travel approximately 0.3 mile to the second right
graded road. Follow SRWMD signs to Holton Creek. The spring is at the head of the creek.
Description - The spring pool measures 225 ft northwest to southeast and 177 ft northeast to
southwest. Along the north shore, a vertical limestone ledge drops quickly off to a depth of 100 ft;
however, the bottom is highly irregular in the rest of the depression. The water is dark and tannic
(water was reported as clear in Rosenau et al., 1977). There is very little aquatic and emergent
vegetation in the spring pool. No boil was observed during October 2001. The spring has steep sandy
banks that rise to approximately 25 ft above water level, and the high ground is forested with pines
and oaks. Holton Creek Rise discharges through Holton Creek, a run that meanders generally southeast
approximately 1 mile to the Suwannee River.
Utilization - Land around the spring is pristine and owned by the SRWMD. The Florida National
Scenic Trail winds along the north side of Holton Creek.
title: Holton Creek Rise

The springs are located within the Homosassa Springs Wildlife State Park and form the
headwaters of the Homosassa River. Coming from the north on US 19/98 into Homosassa
Springs, turn west (right) on CR 490A and travel 0.5 mile. Turn south (left) on access
road to Homosassa Springs Wildlife State Park and travel 0.3 mile to park entrance. The
spring pool, into which all three vents issue, is just below the underwater viewing
platform in the manatee rehabilitation area.
Description - Homosassa Springs Group forms the head of the Homosassa River, which
flows west approximately 6 miles to the Gulf of Mexico. Downstream from the head springs
about a mile, the spring-fed Halls River flows in from the north. The entire river
system is tidally influenced.
HOMOSASSA SPRINGS NOS. 1, 2, and 3 - All three vents issue into the same spring
pool. The pool measures 189 ft north to south and 285 ft east to west. The depth for each of
the vents is 67, 65, and 62 ft for spring nos. 1, 2, and 3, respectively. The springs issue
from a conical depression with limestone exposed along the sides and bottom of the spring pool.
The pool is teeming with salt water and freshwater fishes. Water is clear and light blue. There
is a large boil in center of pool. Surrounding land is Gulf Coastal Lowlands with thick
hardwood-palm forest cover. Approximately 1,000 ft downstream, a fence spans across the river
to keep boats out of the spring pool. There also is a barrier immediately outside the spring
area which keeps the captive manatees in the spring pool. Manatees frequent the spring pool
and river year round, but are especially common in winter. The springs are tidally influenced
year round, especially in winter.
Utilization - The main spring pool and adjacent lands are within Homosassa Springs Wildlife
State Park. The area is developed into an interpretive center for manatee and Florida wildlife
education. There is a floating observation deck in the spring pool with a submerged aquatic
observation room. Injured and rehabilitating manatees are captive in the spring pool for year
round observation. Swimming is not allowed.
title: Homosassa Springs

It doesn’t roar. It doesn’t warn. It just walks up to apex predators and throws hands like life owes it a debt.
You can be bigger. You can be stronger.
But fear? That’s a software this animal never downloaded.
It’s small.
Doesn’t look like much.
No claws like a grizzly. No roar like a lion.
Built like a meme.
Low to the ground, fuzzy, walking like it’s late to a fight it already won.
But then someone gets too close.
And that’s when the wild remembers.
Because this thing?
It’s violence wrapped in fur.
Rage that doesn’t retreat.
It doesn’t just hunt for food.
It hunts because something looked at it wrong.
It eats cobras for breakfast.
Walks off bee stings like mosquito bites.
Takes venom to the face — blacks out — then wakes up and keeps chewing like death was just an inconvenience.
You can corner it.
You can wound it.
But you cannot scare it.
Because fear never made it into the blueprint.
It’ll chase a leopard twice its size.
Bite a lion straight in the crown jewels.
Go 1v3 with a hyena crew just to remind the savanna who really has nothing to lose.
This isn’t a predator.
It’s a statement.
A biological middle finger with teeth.
It’s not interested in dominance.
It’s not playing for status.
It doesn’t give a f*ck who’s sitting at the top of the food chain.
Because in nature’s war for survival,
there’s only one creature that walks through the fire
with no pack, no fear, and no plan to die quietly.
The honey badger: Not here to rule. Not here to flex.
Just here to remind apex predators they’re not untouchable
title: Honey Badger - Nature’s Most Fearless Animal Alive

About Honeycomb Cave is a river cave, which shows boisterous waterfalls and wet drippy formations. Beneath formations and erosional passages there is a wealth of cave life to explore, although it is tiny and often hard to detect. There are large Tasmanian cave spiders, but they are timid with humans and difficult to find. The glowworms are pretty easy to detect becuase of their light. And they even become brighter every spring, when food is more abundant. This small larvae of flies use the light to attract prey, often their own adult parents. They are endemic to New Zealand and rarely found in Australia. Large blind cave shrimps (Anaspides) can also be seen, but only in the right time of the year. Late November is a good time, if there is not too much rain.
Honeycomb Cave is the most visited wild cave in Mole Creek Karst National Park. The tours are guided by Deb Hunter from Wild Cave Tours. It is both an easy beginners cave and close to the meeting point at James General Store, Main Street, Mole Creek. The half day tours start at 8:30 and end approximately 12:30. There are tours on all days of the week, but in general only three to four tours per week. To find the dates check the online booking or call Deb Hunter. All caving equipment, overalls and lights as well as morning tea or lunch (as applicable) are provided. The tours are restricted to people with a certain amount of physical fitness.
There are numerous other caves in the area, which are open on a limited access basis. You need a permit from the National Park, which is regularly given to caving clubs. However, Deb will care for the permit, and so you may visit Baldocks Cave, My Cave, Cyclops Cave, Westmorland Cave, Wet Cave or Sassafras Cave. The tour to Honeycomb is offered regularly and is also the beginners tour. The other tours are made after appointment, and some only as second trip tours, which allows the guide to estimate your fitness and ability. While photography is generally allowed, there are special tours for cave photography, including a workshop for cave photography which is only available after appointment.

Hornsby Spring is located in Camp Kulaqua 1.5 miles north of High Springs. From the
US 441/41 and CR 236 (Main Street) intersection in High Springs, drive north on US 441/41
approximately 1.5 miles to Camp Kulaqua which will be on the east (right) side of the
road. Turn east (right) at Camp Kulaqua sign and follow road approximately 1 mile to
campground entrance. The spring is located inside the campground about 300 ft northwest
of the camp entrance.
Description - Hornsby Spring has a circular spring pool measuring 155 ft north to
south and 147 ft east to west. Its depth at the vent is 34.5 ft. The water is clear and
slightly greenish blue. The spring has an underwater limestone ledge on the north side
under a floating walkway. Algae patches are growing on limestone substrate. The spring
run is approximately 0.9 miles long, 15 ft wide and up to 5 ft deep. It flows generally
westward into the Santa Fe River. During the first FGS visit, the spring was not flowing.
The FGS sampled the spring during a subsequent visit when a small spring boil was visible
near the wooden walkway. This spring is situated on the edge of the lowland floodplain of
the Santa Fe River. The floodplain is forested with cypress, gum, and maple. High ground
on the east side of the spring rises steeply to 6 ft above water level, then gently rises
to approximately 15 ft and is a rolling sand hills terrain. The uplands are open and
grassy. An underwater cave system has been mapped at Hornsby Spring.
Utilization - Hornsby Spring is the central feature of the privately-owned Camp
Kulaqua. The spring is developed into a swimming and recreation area. There are numerous
boardwalks over and around the spring. A slide leads into the spring pool on the north
side. Full facilities are located nearby.
title: Hornsby Spring

References LSECR: Page 256 Horse and Cart Sinkhole is an almost perfectly-circular sinkhole some 40 metres in diameter with extremely undercut walls, and it drops about 8m to a flat, cutting-grass covered floor with a deep, clear lake on its north-western side. Originally, access could only be made via rope ladders and the like, but nowadays visitors can comfortably walk down a small, steep artificial tunnel/ramp (dug using a back-hoe and muscle-power by Messrs. Don and Neville Telford around 1986) which leads to an attractive wooden landing inside the feature. The open lake has a flat, silt bottom with a maximum depth of about 8m, just a couple of metres under the wall. The bottom does not meet the wall in a clear-cut zone; small horizontal solution passages meander on, but they cannot be entered safely by divers. Like nearby Tea-Tree Sinkhole, this feature contained some native species of fish (including native trout and almost-tame eels) and crustacea (crayfish, yabbies and shrimps) until the mid- 1980s, but the ecosystem has reportedly been dramatically altered as a result of the introduction of alien species of fish (including brown trout and redfin perch) and the associated recreational fishing activities. Compared with the other major sinkholes and the spring system of Piccaninnie Ponds just a few kilometres away, it has relatively little to offer recreational cave divers. It is believed that Horse and Cart Sinkhole gained its name as a result of an incident involving a horse which was standing near the hole and was startled, backing its attached cart over the edge and dragging the hapless creature to an untimely end. Perhaps a diver with a keen eye might be able to verify this one day! The feature was first placed in CEGSA’s Records in the form of an August 1971 Trip Report by Ian Lewis, after a visit in November 1970.

Horseshoe Spring is located on private property approximately 2.8 miles southwest of the town of
Aripeka on central Florida’s Gulf Coast. It is approximately 0.8 miles due east (inland) from Horse
Island.
Description - Horseshoe Spring is so named because of its distinct horseshoe-shaped spring pool
and upper spring run section. The spring emerges from an elongated, curved fissure in the limestone
that measures 16.6 ft deep and is 100 ft long. The spring bottom is limestone with a thin layer of
dark silt. The water was tannic and slightly turbid in March 2003. The spring run begins flowing eastward,
then it curves around and flows northwest, creating a narrow peninsula of land between the upper spring
run section and the spring pool. There are numerous karst features along the bottom of the uppermost portion
of the spring run. The spring run meanders northwest through marsh 0.8 miles into Fillman Bayou. Land east
of the spring is heavily forested, and land to the west is open marsh.
title: Horseshoe Spring

Details Identification Feature type: Cave Cave and exploration data Cave rating: OpenWater Highest cave rating: Basic Goes to water: Yes Diving data Water type: Fresh Tidal: No References Hospital Hole is a submarine sink located in the Weeki Wachee River. It is in a
sharp bend (third bend) 1,000 feet upstream from State Hwy 595 bridge. The name
comes from local legend where it is told that injured fish come to this site to
be healed before returning to the sea. Access is restricted from land, but the
site can be easily accessed via boat or canoe from Roger’s Park. The park is open
year round and has a boat dock with a launch ramp. The park collects a $2 fee
(per vehicle) during daylight hours in the summer.
The opening of the sink is about 30 ft across is easily seen through the river
water. Visibility is usually excellent down to the hydrogen sulfide layer at
about 70’. Since this is an artifical ceiling (blocks daylight) you should dive
this as though it were a cave dive. However, finding a tie off for your primary
may prove difficult as the walls of the sink are very smooth.
The maximum width of the sink is about 150 ft and maximum depth is around 140 feet.
There is quite a bit of graffiti on the walls and makes for a laugh. The shape of
the sink itself is like a small boot with no passage or major overhangs. The ceiling
gently slopes upward towards the opening.
title: Hospital Hole

The Grotto walls are hour glass shaped loaded with solution tubes and other objects to look at. The bottom is dome shaped, and the edges average around 100’-110’ feet with the deepest spot being about 155’. This spot is a small opening against the north wall. There are four platforms, three of them just under the end edge of the dock, and one in the middle of the sink. The three platforms are layered like steps, the first one is at 20’, the second at 45’ and the third at 60’. Tied to the white barrel there is a line that runs down to a 100’ platform which is used for Advance Open Water classes. The platform sits next to two boats and lines run to an old VW van, and other interesting objects sitting on the bottom. There are several thermoclines, the mid-water temperature can get pretty cold between 40’ and 80’. However the bottom temperature usually stays in the low 70’s. The water is tannic all year and visibility fluctuates with the algae bloom. Cost is usually around $10-$20 per diver depending on visibility.
title: Hudson Grotto

Sub-regions Caves About Go June to September? (Summer) Calmest Weather & Longest Days:
Iceland experiences milder weather, longer daylight hours (up to 24 hours near the solstice), and calmer surface conditions during summer. This makes logistics easier and safer, particularly when accessing remote dive sites. Better Accessibility:
Many of Iceland’s cave dive sites are in remote highland regions or near lava fields — during winter and spring, snow and ice can make these areas impassable. Roads are generally fully open by mid-June and remain accessible until early autumn. Consistent Water Temperatures:
Iceland’s groundwater-fed cave systems (like those at Silfra and Davíðsgjá) maintain constant temperatures year-round (~2–4°C), so water temps aren’t your limiting factor — surface conditions and access are. Silfra Fissure (Þingvellir National Park) While not a cave in the traditional sense, Silfra offers crystal-clear visibility (~100m) in a tectonic fissure between the North American and Eurasian plates. Accessible year-round, but summer offers the best overall experience due to comfort during gear changes and travel ease. Davíðsgjá A darker, slightly deeper alternative to Silfra with limited overhead sections. Best dived in summer for similar reasons — ease of access and surface comfort. Litlaá Lava Tube Cave Systems (near Lake Mývatn) Actual underwater lava tube systems, rare and remote. These are less developed for tourism and require expedition-level planning. Only realistically accessible between July and early September. Avoid October to May

About Iddlebiddy Cave is a 250m single passage-way, which runs from the entrance chamber and ends in a small, silty room containing an array of largely-formed clay deposits.
Divers must take care when venturing into this cave, as the soft walls and delicate features located in the long passage make the water susceptible to clouding. Divers are encouraged to take their time passing through the passage, to enjoy the many cave features and avoid causing finning or physical damage.
This cave is only available on Saturdays and Sundays. A maximum of four divers per day, multiple dives per day.
A locked hatch has been placed at this site, with the key available for collection from the Mount Gambier Visitor Centre. At least two members of the dive party must be present to show their issued dive permits and collect the key in person.
Entrance The entrance is via a locked hatch that opens to reveal a solution tube about 8m deep and 1.5m wide. You will need either a wire rope ladder or a-frame and ropes to enter the cave. Someone should descend first and then all tanks and equipment lowered down before the other divers descend. Once down the tube there is a metal platform where you can don your tanks and some stairs leading into the water

LSECR: Page 488 At the time of its discovery by a small party of unqualified local divers in late 1983 or early 1984, Iddlebiddy Cave (a satirisation of the mighty “Cocklebiddy Cave” in the Nullarbor, because of its smaller but similar underwater appearance) was one of the most significant cave diving finds of the decade. The cave’s discoverers kept the feature’s location a closely-guarded secret for many years, and the first truly-representative map of the cave was only compiled after members of the Cave Divers Association of Australia undertook an officially-sanctioned assessment and research dive on November 26th, 1988. A more detailed survey was later initiated by the CDAA, and it was this work, from the efforts of Tony Hambling, Frank Homewood and John McCormick, that the map on the opposite page was produced. Like many cave features in this area, the entrance to 51.250 is a relatively insignificant chimney- like vertical solution-tube about 0.7 metres in diameter which drops for about 6 metres into a small, humid cavity containing a very deep pool of blue-green water. The pool is actually “roof-hole” to a very large submerged room, where a silt mound below the entrance attests to the many animals – and a young human - which tragically ended their days in this cave.
The flooded chamber has a short, narrow passage leading off to the north-west, but the main run is in the form of a single, large passage which heads south-east. This passage is generally about 12 metres wide and 5 metres high, and it contains many interesting sedimentary and morphological features which are seen in no other south-eastern caves The floor of the cave is almost totally covered in large, thick blocks of multilayered clay, giving it an “alligator-skin” of tessellated appearance in many areas. The known cave ends in a low, extremely silty chamber where clay seems to be “flowing” out of the walls Iddlebiddy Cave is indeed a valuable cave diving site worthy of considerable protection

Indian Spring is located on private property 13 miles south of Tallahassee near the Bethel Community. The YMCA of Tallahassee, who owns Indian Spring, constructed a summer camp around the pool. Description - Indian Spring has a circular spring pool 185 ft in diameter and 30 ft deep. A large, semicircular limestone cave is located on the north side of the sand bottom pool. Depths in the cave are reported to reach 60 ft (Rosenau et al., 1977). The spring water is clear with a greenish tint. Green algae float in clumps around the spring pool and run. The spring run is 50 ft wide, 2 ft deep, and flows 0.7 miles southeast into Sally Ward Spring at the headwaters of the Wakulla River. The spring has been developed as a recreation area associated with YMCA’s Camp Indian Springs. Platforms, observation decks, water slides, and canoes surround the spring pool. The camp is in a densely forested area.

and forms the headwaters of Jenkins Creek. The spring pool is elliptical in shape; approximately
200 feet in length and 60 feet wide. and water depth at the vent is greater than 100 ft. Discharge

(Rosenau et al. 1977). The spring has two runs, one flowing south and the other northwest to form Jenkins
Creek. Jenkins Creek flows northwest approximately 0.5 miles where it joins with the Mud River and flows
to the Gulf of Mexico.

The Jewish Hole is a submarine spring located in the Gulf of Mexico about 1 mi W. of Hammock point, 3 mi
WSW. of Aripeka, and about 600 ft S. of the “Aripeka Channel,” Pasco County. Wetterhall (1965 p. 29) wrote
that the rim of the spring is approximately circular in shape and about 40 ft in diameter at about 4 ft
below mean tide. The bottom slopes toward the spring opening to a depth of about 10 ft below approximate
mean tide. The spring hole is an irregular, vertical pipe about 15 ft in diameter and 148 ft deep below
the general bottom, which is about 4 ft below approximate mean tide. A vigorous boil at low tide becomes a
“slick” at high tide. The flow has not been measured.

Details Identification Feature type: Cave Additional Notes Jingemia Cave is a distinctive natural feature in a band of low rocky hills that extend between the towns of Carnamah and Moora. The hills are an outcropping of chert and other very old rock types that formed between 2.5 billion and 542 million years ago (mid Proterozoic era). Known as Noondine Chert, this geological formation is significant in the region for having unique plants that grow only in association with chert. The formation also influences an aquifer that supplies groundwater to local towns, and is a source of mineral silica, a vital component in many things used in our everyday lives.

The Ichetucknee Springs Group is located within the Ichetucknee Springs State Park which
is approximately 10 miles northeast of Branford. From the bridge over the Suwannee River
in Branford, drive east on US 27/129 for 7 miles. Turn north (left) onto CR 137 and
continue for 1.3 miles. Turn east (right) and go 4.2 miles through the north park
entrance to the parking area.
Description - This spring is located in the spring run channel of Cedar Head Spring, which is north of
Blue Hole. The spring pool and outflow greatly widens the incoming spring run, and the
combined run flows south a short distance to the Ichetucknee River. The spring pool
measures 87 ft east to west and 117 ft north to south. The depth measured over the vent
is 37 ft. The water is clear and light blue, and a boil is visible on the pool surface.
Water issues from a cavern in limestone. The pool has a sand and limestone bottom with
abundant aquatic grass and some algae. The land around the spring is heavily forested
with mixed hardwoods and palm. The spring run is fenced off approximately 100 ft south
of vent. This is a swimming spot with a wooden boardwalk for spring access. A foot path
leads to the spring from the north.
Utilization - The springs, river, and surrounding forested land are part of
Ichetucknee Springs State Park from the US 27 bridge northward. The park is a high
quality natural area that is partly developed and whose heavy public use is highly
regulated in order to minimize damage to the environment. Camping, hiking, swimming,
tubing, and canoeing are some of the activities that are offered in the state park.
title: Jug Spring

About Kartchner Caverns is a limestone cave system in southeastern Arizona, near Benson in the Whetstone Mountains. Groundwater dissolution formed its chambers and passages.
University of Arizona researchers have studied diverse communities of bacteria and archaea on its formations. Their 2013 research described microbes surviving on scarce nutrients carried by drip water and obtained from rock and soil chemistry.

About Need to dive at night because diver activity silts out the swimming area on the surface
Details Identification Feature type: Cave Cave and exploration data Cave rating: Advanced Vertical access: No Exploration potential: Medium Tourism potential: High Goes to water: Yes Diving data Maximum depth: 10 m Temperature: 32–32 °C References Trimix Divers - https://www.trimixdivers.com/trimix5/?p=4889: This popular tourist site has 34C water flowing out of the small resurgence at a high rate. The water is crystal clear and its source is the same area of limestone as what supplies Bitter Springs and Mataranka Hot Springs further to the South. The water is geologically heated, but is warmed only by the rock in which it collects – layers of limestone which assume the average annual surface temperature. From the small entrance pool, the 3m2 cave passage descends very quickly down to 8m where it levels to horizontal and reduces in size to about 1m high by 2m wide. The effect of this reduction in passage cross sectional area is to dramatically intensify the water flow rate. The floor looks pebbly, but the rubble is cemented into fine silt and any attempt to pull on a rock simply dislodges it. The walls and ceiling are a loose, shaly type of construction and movement in this passage, against the flow is exhausting. After 20m of straight, horizontal passage, the end of the first ever penetration is found, tied off to a rock in the floor. A chromed metal clip connects the second length of guide line onto the first and the passage then slopes up to the left (SE) where a low flat restriction is encountered. Squeezing up through this restriction against very high water flow was very difficult and the second line is tied off in a wider area and small junction above the restriction. Noting that the water was flowing from the right as well as the left hand passages, the low flow path to the right was followed and this descended through a tunnel in what seems to be denser, darker limestone. Popping through a small ‘window’ where the flow is again felt, the cave does a sharp left hand turn. 20m beyond this point, a low flat tunnel to the left was noticed that probably connects back to the junction. 10m further on and to the right, the water flows out of a low flat restriction which has not yet been penetrated. Some excavation here may be necessary. A very streamlined side mount rig with 7ltr (55cuft) tanks is recommended.
YouTube: https://youtu.be/ZKF8r5L2S4c Images

3-Day Trip from Nelson (ChatGPT) Why Nelson works
Legitimate, commonly used longer-term parking (town, campground, hire operators) You can paddle upriver into the gorge country, camp progressively, then return No tidal commitment unless you deliberately enter the estuary No shuttle, no mid-trip road access required Your car is waiting where food, fuel, and reception exist The alternative (parking at Dartmoor) is workable, but Nelson gives you better scenery density per kilometre and more flexibility if weather turns.
This plan lets you:
Camp away from the car Experience the best limestone gorge sections Spend 2–3 hours near McLennan’s Punt on Day 2 without rushing Paddle fresh against current first, then enjoy an easier return Day 1 – Nelson → Patterson Canoe Camp Distance: ~20–22 km upstream Time: ~5–6 hours at a steady solo pace Overnight: Patterson Canoe Camp Why this works
You clear the wider lower river early Enter the more enclosed gorge sections by afternoon Patterson is a logical psychological and physical breakpoint Sets you up perfectly for McLennan’s Punt on Day 2 Expect calm water, slow current, and progressively tightening bends with good limestone walls.
Day 2 – Patterson → McLennan’s Punt (cave stop) → upstream camp Distance: ~12–16 km total (depending how far you continue) Key feature: 2–3 hour stop near McLennan’s Punt Overnight: Skipworth Springs Canoe Camp or nearby upstream site Structure
Paddle upstream from Patterson in the morning Arrive at the McLennan’s Punt area late morning Secure kayak well above waterline Spend your 2–3 hours on the cave investigation Continue a few km further upstream to camp This keeps the cave stop unhurried and avoids camping right on the Punt (which you’ve already ruled out).
Day 3 – Return paddle: upstream camp → Nelson Distance: ~28–32 km downstream Time: ~6–7 hours including breaks Finish: Back at Nelson, car waiting This is a long but friendly day:
Downstream assistance Familiar water Motivation of a clean finish and easy pack-down If wind builds in the afternoon, you’ll already be moving with the river rather than fighting it.
Distances at a glance (approx.) Day 1: 20–22 km Day 2: 12–16 km Day 3: 28–32 km
Total: ~60–65 km of river experienced That’s a lot of Glenelg in three days without ever touching a shuttle.
Why this is the best fit for your constraints Single parking location ✔ No daily returns to car ✔ Proper multi-night canoe-camping ✔ Mid-river cave time without stress ✔ Conservative solo-friendly risk profile ✔ Two important practical notes 1. Wind & timing Paddle upstream early in the day Aim to be back into Nelson before late afternoon Avoid committing into the estuary unless conditions are glassy 2. Campsite bookings Glenelg canoe camps must be booked You can only stay one night per site Build in a backup upstream camp in case your cave stop runs long This also reminds me of…
References This 50km Paddle Along Victoria’s Glenelg River Canoe Trail Makes for a Dreamy Solo Adventure

Sub-regions Caves About Kenya features both limestone karst landscapes and opportunities for cave diving, particularly along its coastal regions.
🪨 Limestone Karst in Kenya Kenya’s coastal areas, notably around Vipingo in Kilifi County, are characterized by coralline limestone formations that have undergone karstification. These processes have led to the development of features such as caves, sinkholes, and underground voids. For instance, studies at the Vipingo Coral Limestone Quarry have documented various karst features and associated geohazards, including cavities and fissures in the rock mass. (ej-geo.org)
Additionally, the Shimoni Caves in Kwale County are natural limestone formations with historical significance, having been used during the slave trade era. These caves are accessible to visitors and offer insights into both geological and cultural aspects of the region. (en.wikipedia.org)

About Kilsby Sinkhole is a naturally occurring karst sinkhole located on private property 10 kilometres south-west of Mount Gambier in South Australia. The sinkhole is renowned worldwide for its crystal clear water and extensive open caverns, making it a popular destination for recreational diving. The site is accessible only via prior bookings, which can be made online or by phone.
Kilsby Sinkhole is the only site of its kind in Australia that welcomes snorkellers and Open Water certified divers, through to those with Cave or Technical dive training. Snorkellers, Freedivers and Open Water divers must be guided by an approved Dive Instructor. With a depth of almost 30 metres directly from the pontoon, the site is a perfect location for freediving and training camps are regularly held onsite.
The sinkhole has an interesting history due to its use as a top-secret space for weapons research in the 1970s, resulting in a range of infrastructure being developed at the site, some of which is still present. An onsite museum space is currently in development which tells the story of this unique site.
Details Identification Feature type: Sinkhole Reference: L0046 Source: Forestry SA Location Coordinates: -37.892382999999995, 140.676105 Altitude: 18 m Address: 525, Unnamed Road, The District Council of Grant, South Australia, AUS, 5291 Checked: true Checked by: CDAA Rated Cave and exploration data Cave rating: Basic Highest cave rating: Advanced Vertical access: No Exploration potential: Low Tourism potential: High Disabled access potential: Low Goes to water: Yes Diving data Minimum depth: 20 m Maximum depth: 50 m Water type: Fresh Tidal: No Difficulty: Hard Entry difficulty: Intermediate Entry type: Shore Access and warnings Graham Kilsby
Amenities hasShowers: Yes hasToilets: Yes hasPhone: Yes parking: Outstanding References LSECR: Page 102 This spectacular waterfilled “cenote”-style sinkhole was a very popular cave diving site in the early 1960s. It was reportedly named after the property owner, Mr. Dene F.A. Kilsby, by mem- bers of the Underwater Research Group of South Australia (including Peter Girdler, a prominent present-day cave diver and his regular diving companion, Barry Fowler) sometime prior to April 1962, when Bob Sexton first mentioned the feature in a CEGSA trip report. Prior to 1990, when a small sloping ramp was cut down to the lake by Mr. Ross Kilsby from the north-western side of the sinkhole under a smaller roof window, it had 10 metre high overhanging walls all around, making access difficult. The entrance is a triangular-shaped hole about 16 metres along each side, and it cuts right back under on the north-eastern side in a sheltered section of lake some 20 metres further out of daylight. The underwater aspects of the cave trend in a north-east to south-west direction (which is about 90 degrees out from most of the other known cave features in this area), and the boulder-strewn floor which is at a depth of 27 metres directly beneath the main collapse on the south-western side drops away deeper in the dark zone. The sinkhole is basically a single huge cavern approximately 50 metres long by 20 metres high in most areas, and ‘despite numerous tales and rumours of awesome depths far in excess of 100 metres, several very reliable sources have reported that the deepest known area in the sinkhole is in fact about 63 metres, in a silty and restrictive cavity behind a large boulder collapse-mound (this is still very deep and more than 20 metres beyond the recommended maximum sport-diving depth of 40 metres, but it is hardly “awesome” by modern cave diving standards). Kilsbys Hole was the first large waterfilled sinkhole to be thoroughly mapped in this country, and members of the newly-formed Research Group of the Cave Divers Association of Australia (CDAARG) felt that the cave’s strange 90-degree corners and clean angular boulders indicated that it appeared to be a relatively recent collapse. It was certainly very different from the more rounded, “dirtier”-looking features which were common to most other sinkholes in the area, and since it had been closed to the public since 1969 (when the Weapons Research Establishment took out a lease for testing purposes), only a handful of divers had disturbed the environment in any way. Some important palaeontological material (including Thylacoleo sp.) was also recovered from an underwater ledge in one area during the mapping study in 1983. At the time of this writing, the lease had just moved across to the South Australian Police Depart- ment, and with the support of the Department and the landowner, the CDAA was finalizing negotiations to allow qualified sinkhole divers to visit the feature on a more regular basis. https://www.cavediving.net.au/index.php/siteinfo/?site=33: Kilsby Sinkhole is located on a private farming property in the South East of South Australia. Since the 1950’s, the unique site has been diving’s worst kept secret, attracting interest from fresh water diving enthusiasts worldwide. The site is known for its stunning water clarity, allowing a unique diving experience which is also perfect for photography and training.
