content:
Mini Essay - April 19 (2026)
I want to preface this by saying I wasn’t expecting to write it, and I’ve been working for the last few days on an entirely different and unrelated post about how I’m preparing for Mars One selection later this year. I’ll still publish that post in the next few days, but I’m not sure if I’ll publish this outside of Patreon. Maybe next year. Truth be told I may not publish this at all – all I know is I just realised what the date is, it stopped me in my tracks, and I need to write this right down while I’m feeling what I’m feeling.
Trigger warning**:** Please be aware that I describe planning a suicide attempt in this post
*deep breath*
Occasionally in an interview it will come up that I worked in the mining industry for about a year, followed quickly by a remark from me that I hated every minute of it. The reality is I worked for a drill and blast company for exactly 1 year, and I didn’t just hate it – I will never work in the mining industry again because it pushed me right to the edge of suicide.
I was (am) very good at handling, designing and using explosives; I soak up details on explosives ordnance like a sponge; and I work very well at problem solving in high risk environments. With all of that in mind, in 2006 during the last year of my physics degree I had my heart set on becoming a rather bland-sounding “ Ammunition Technical Officer “. They’re also knows as “EOD Tech’s” but you probably know them as Military Bomb Technicians.
I’d worked so hard for years to be an exceptional soldier, to always try to give more to the Army, and always sought ways to be better. But my unit wasn’t interested in developing what I had to offer. I’d applied multiple times to become a full-time officer, only to have my unit bin the paperwork as being “too hard to deal with”.
Getting to the final months of my degree I was running out of options, and with some gentle nudging from my Dad I thought maybe I could apply my explosives experience to the oil and gas industry as a “ Perforation specialist ” – lowering frameworks of tiny shaped-charges down an oil well and firing them to punch holes through the steel well casing to let the oil & gas flow into the well. After going through the interview and being offered a job with Schlumberger as an Oilfield Specialist, I was there 3 days before I was told “There’s no way you’ll be working in perforation for atleast 5 to 8 years, if ever”.
A week later I’d quit and – because it was the height of the mining boom – immediately stepped into a job as a blaster in the mines. From there it was a downward slide.
I’ll avoid details of what working in blasting was like, not because it “hurts” or anything like that, but because most of it is just unspeakably boring. Wake at 5am. Shower & dress. Have breakfast. Pre-start meeting at 5:45am. Put explosives down holes in the ground for the next 12 hours. Head back to your room, shower, go to the gym, dinner at 8pm, read/listen to music/watch a movie, sleep. Repeat for two weeks.
Fly back to Perth, spend a week trying to see friends & fix things. Fly back to site. Repeat for another two weeks.
I’m fine doing boring work, and will inevitably make some sort of game out of it. But I also need to see the overall sense in why it’s being done – it needs to have purpose. *I* need to have a purpose. When I first started in the mines that “purpose” was gaining hands-on experience so I could further develop a piece of software I’d written in the final year of my physics degree that predicted the areas in a mine site most at risk of being hit by flying rock from a blast.
That sense of purpose initially got me through the relentless bullying that happened on-site, got me through the pervasive boredom with my job, and helped me overlook the overwhelming incompetence I saw in people supposedly responsible for securing and handling explosives. “It’s fine – I’m doing my job properly, and that’s what’s important” I’d lie to myself.
That sense of purpose slowly wore away in the first 6 months though. It became increasingly clear that the company wasn’t going to ever develop the software I’d brought them, and were simply using me as a blaster. Just like the folks I was barely tolerating at work. That might be OK for some, but I wasn’t happy pursuing a career spending 12 hours a day working with people I didn’t respect to blow chunks out of a planet I care deeply about.
But what the hell else was I was supposed to do? I was 22 and knew I didn’t fit in academia, had been ignored when trying to do something meaningful with the Army, told I’d probably never work with the specialised explosives in the oil and gas industry, and the only thing the mining industry thought I was useful for was blowing things up so others could rip precious metals from the ground. And if you know my Dad, you’ll also recognise I’ve also just listed failing to find purpose in the 3 areas he’s worked in: the military, mining, and oil & gas.
There was still SCUBA diving though, that other past-time I shared with Dad. In Februrary 2008 a family friend – who’d trained Dad to dive 20 years before – said if I sorted out my instructor certification I could work in his Melbourne diveshop at the end of 2008. I’d go to Melbourne, learn everything I needed to from him, and would have enough saved up from working in the mines to buy a diveshop in New Zealand – I just had to stick with blasting for another 6 months.
In early April 2008 I headed back for what would be my final 2 week swing on a mine site. The first week was tedious but tolerable. All through the 2nd week though I had stomach issues – something I’ve now learnt to recognise as a clear sign I’m emotionally distressed, and the worse the symptoms the worse the internal distress.
On the Thursday I’d had to head back to camp mid-afternoon because the cramps were getting too much. The on-site medic couldn’t give me anything more than panadol, and I collapsed for the rest of the afternoon. The next morning I woke as usual feeling fine, but from the pre-start meeting onward I started feeling sicker and sicker, and by mid-morning I was being taken back to the medic’s room to get more panadol and try to sleep it off.
I woke in the evening still feeling weak when the medic knocked on my door, checking on me and bringing me some dinner but I couldn’t eat it. I slept restless through the night, woke again at 5am on the Saturday when when one of the other blasters knocked on my door to see if I was coming to work and I said I was still too sick in the guts. I wasn’t “sick” though – I just felt completely empty inside. Hollowed out, like there wasn’t anything left to feel.
The medic visited again that afternoon to check on me, but otherwise I was just left alone in my little room with nothing but my thoughts. Plenty of time to sit with that empty feeling. To ruminate on my shitty home-life. Ruminate on my complete lack of purpose. To listen to music and try to feel something.
I went to dinner that night and saw the other blasters… and was inevitably informed of how “piss-weak” I was for being sick, and how they “hadn’t even noticed” I wasn’t there because I was useless anyway. So I ate a little but had completely lost my appetite over the last few days, and headed back to my room to listen to music and sleep.
In the last years of high school and throughout uni I’d absolutely fallen in love with Everclear, and had treasured every album… but had somehow missed their 2006 album “Welcome to the Drama Club” until just before my last two-week swing. I’d listened to it quite a bit during the two-week swing, but never all the way through in a single sitting. I put on another album, sat in the shower crying til it finished, crawled out to the stereo and started playing “Drama Club” then crawled back under the shower to keep crying.
Everclear’s “Welcome to the Drama Club” is 54 minutes and 44 seconds long. Somewhere in the middle of that I decided there wasn’t any point living anymore: I was useless, wouldn’t ever help anybody or myself, and no one wanted what I used to think I could offer. I’d stopped crying, but instead sat in the shower trying to find answers to two questions:
How long would it take for someone to find my body? Is there anything in this room sharp enough to slit my wrists? The medic had been checking in the afternoons, and while one of the other blasters would probably knock on my door at 5am the next morning they also wouldn’t think twice if my door was locked and I didn’t answer. So chances were the medic would find me the following afternoon after getting the site manager or housekeeping to unlock my room.
There really wasn’t anything sharp in the room though. I remember methodically turning the room upside down trying to find anything – nothing. I slumped back in the shower defeated again as the final track of the album started: “Your Arizona Room”, about someone dealing with a relentless sense of being broken and wondering if the love they feel for someone else is enough to fix it what’s wrong with them.
But I didn’t have that. There was no sense I’d be able to fix whatever was deeply wrong with me at all, and there was no one around to say otherwise.
Most Everclear songs run between 3 to 5 minutes long. “Your Arizona Room” is listed as over 9 minutes, but it fades out around the 5 minute mark, and it was as it was faded I realised I could break the glass in the bathroom mirror and use that to slit my wrists. I’d been sitting under a hot shower for hours and my blood pressure was up – break the glass, do it in the shower with the curtain pulled across and it’ll be easy for whoever finds you to clean up.
The whole room was silent except for the shower, and I remember my legs feeling so weak from sitting in the shower I was weirdly worried I’d slip over and hurt myself. Or worse I’d slip, knock myself out in the fall, and not be able to follow through with what I’d now planned.
I stood leaning on the basin and looked at the mirror without looking at myself. I could break it just with my fist, but maybe use the steel cap in one of my boots instead?
That’s when the stereo in the next room suddenly exploded into life. I spun away from the basin and looked into the other room.
“What the fuck?“
It wasn’t a track I’d heard before, and I was certain it’d been completely silent seconds before? I moved from the basin to the bathroom door looking dumbfounded at the stereo
“Is that a kid wheezing and talk-singing over some weird drum beat and a harmonica? What the fuck is this?
And that’s when I remembered Everclear put a secret track on their earlier album “So Much For The Afterglow” – one you’d only find it if you left the album playing after the final track faded out then waited through a minute of silence. And I realised they’d done the same again on this album.
Sure enough the weird kid/drum beat/harmonica combo faded out after 30 seconds, and the hidden track “Beautiful Dream” started with the lyrics:
—–
I had a dream I was living by the ocean
I had a dream I was living in the sun
I wake up sad because I’m living in darkness
I know I’m not alone
I know I’m not the only one
I had a dream that I had no depression
I had a dream I had a smile on my face
I wake up hungry so I feed my obsession
I know I gotta leave
I know I gotta run away
Far away
Where the faces all look happy and I know it’s a dream
A beautiful dream
I want to loose myself in the sunshine where I can be free
Yeah I just wanna be free
Free in a beautiful dream
Yeah but it’s a beautiful dream
—–
I immediately burst into tears again and slumped in the doorframe… but as I did I instantly knew two things: I wasn’t going to break that mirror, and I wasn’t going to stay any longer in a place where I had no purpose doing something I didn’t care about with people I didn’t like.
I picked myself up, turned off the still running shower, grabbed a towel to dry myself, cleaned up the things I’d flipped over earlier looking for something sharp, went to bed, and decided as I lay in bed that I would never compromise what I care about so much to ever be that low again.
That’s how I survived the night of April 19th, 2008.
There have been some shitty times over the last 9 years. Really really turbo shitty times. But no matter what happened – friends dying, me nearly dying multiple times, relationships ending viciously, being literally homeless – I know I have never been and will never again be as low as I was that night. And I know that because I created that situation by doing what OTHERS thought was best for me, instead of figuring out what is important to me.
This isn’t blaming myself – this is me taking responsibility for the fact that I chose to stay in that job, stay in a toxic relationship, and continued to accept the things around me that eventually created a situation where I was suicidal. I still fuck things up, still struggle with overwhelmingly turbulent relationships, still wind up doing things I don’t want to be doing.
But you know what? I’m also not 22 any more, and since April 19th 2008 I’ve been continuously getting better at spotting those shit jobs and avoiding them. I spot the warning signs in potential partners early, so even though I can still wind up in turbulent and toxic relationships I’m not as surprised when the crazy comes out, I get out of them sooner, I have ZERO issues walking away when I do, and I’m getting better at dodging them altogether. And as I do more and more of the things I know are important, I have less time to fuck around doing things I don’t want to do because someone expects me to.
Fuck your expectations – I will do things that I know make other people’s lives better, not what others expect of me. Because I could be dead right now. I don’t have enough fingers to count the number of times I’ve gone close, but there’s only been once when I thought I didn’t make the world better by being in it, and that was because I’d stopped listening to what was important to me – helping improve the lives of people everywhere.
April 19th is my annual reminder that the world is a better place because I’m still part of it.

Mini Essay - April 19 (2023)
Having just re-read Mini Essay - April 19 (2023) I realise that I don’t really know how to describe the way I feel about it anymore. That post still hits hard, and it’s a testament to how raw it was. I’m also shocked that it was published just three years ago, although I’m certain it was written years earlier. Reflecting back on things, I realise now that it’s just a date, but it’s a date that is important to me because it’s an anniversary of my choice to live.
Things could easily have been different, and I could not have experienced all the things that I’ve experienced since 2008-04-19. Becoming a diving instructor and guiding people through the Melbourne aquarium, diving the HMAS Junee, joining the Navy, joining the Royal Marines, leaving both, getting into comedy, doing the Edinburgh fringe a bundle of times, going to the Redhead festival, discovering Mars One, writing science comedy shows about going to space, writing books about going to Mars, speaking to literally hundreds of thousands of kids about space exploration. Learning to cave dive, discovering new caves and sharing them with the world, speaking at international conferences about using underwater photogrammetry in overseas caves in order to produce centimetre accurate maps on the fly, meeting Simone and feeling like I’m closer than ever to living the way I have always wanted to live.
There are so many extraordinary things that you’ve seen and done over the last 17 years, and it’s so unbelievably easy to get bogged down in the every day to lose sight of that. You are always pushing yourself, always trying to be a better version of yourself, and the reality is you’re perfect however you want to be. So many of the different things you’ve tried since 2008-04-19 have failed, and yet every step has made your life more interesting, enriched the lives of others, and weaved a tapestry of different experience together into a remarkable human being.
The greatest thing to come out of April 19 is your capacity of adventure and storytelling. You don’t want to be defined by any single thing, but you know that you have often felt your most alive when you’re on adventures and storytelling. You’re a travelling bard at the end of the day, even if you have been so many others things too. Right now I’m not entirely sure what it is I want to do with myself, or how to figure it out, but I do know that I want to be Writing every day to tell my stories, plan my next adventure, and help figure out who I want to be today.
Reflecting on what is important on days like April 19 is important, but it really is just a date - I’m not even writing this on April 19 itself, but the day before. No matter what happens though, it’s vital that I keep looking forward, keep cutting out the things that drag me down into the mud, and keep telling stories in whatever form they decide to take. You don’t need to be in the spotlight, but you do need to be creating, reviewing, editing, and polishing the stories that you tell. April 19 is just one point in your annual cycle of storytelling and adventure - the lowest point, but the point that you build up and create a new life from.

content:
With just three months away, it’s suddenly becoming a big and urgent question of what you want to do before you’re 40, and more importantly what kind of life you want to live in your 40’s. You never really thought you’d make it to 30, and yet here you are nearly 10 years later wondering what you want to do next.
You 40s really need to be about embracing the life you want to live and reinforcing those things you love most. There’s no question you love writing books on your own, thinking deeply about difficult things, and sharing experiences with others who would never do see what you see without you. Your 40s should be about being bolder in the things you excel at, and cutting free the things that drag. All the philosophy you want to live by is already within you, already hashed out in your notes - now if the time to live it fully.
So what do you want to do before your 40? Shed the dead-weight. That’s physically losing weight and being fitter, shedding mental loads by organising yourself with a Digital Garden, cutting free the emotional bonds that drag on you, and setting yourself free spiritually too. Writing a mini essay about the Mini Essay - Physical Baggage, Mini Essay - Mental Baggage, Mini Essay - Emotional Baggage, and Mini Essay - Spiritual Baggage weight you want to shed will help you a lot too. Look at what’s holding you back and weighing you down, and cut it free - that’s the way you’ll dig your way out of this current slump. Do less, expect less, push less… and it will free you to be who you want to be.

content:
For the last few months since I turned 40, I’ve been trying to reassess my life and all the things I’ve done so far with limited success. Much of the challenge has come from knowing just how much there is to sort through and reframe, coupled with having ignored my writing for so long that it feels like there’s a kind of psychic constipation built-up - my recent writing is easing that pressure, but there is a whole lot clogged up that needs to be processed while still more builds up behind it.
With all of that going on, it feels like looking back and sorting everything out should be the priority right now, but it’s not. If I make a concerted effort to write every day (and I do mean every day, being particularly conscious that I’ve missed the last few days) then that pressure will ease and I’ll quickly create writing and art that I’m keen to share and be proud of. Knowing that pressure will ease over the next few months, and that it will stay low as after I start my new role at the MSSP, the question quickly becomes “What do I want to do with my future?”.
So much of the last 20 years has been future focused, but now I’m really struggling to set new goals and push for new things. Part of me wants to say I’m “tired” but that’s not true - it feels more like I want to truly experience things, appreciate them fully, and write about them to share with others too. So maybe the next 10 years before I turn 50 is about appreciating what I do rather than simply rushing to do more. I don’t want to drop my bundle and just do the minimum, but I do want to fully appreciate and savour the things I put my time and energy into. That will inevitably mean doing things at a slower pace than I have in the past, but that’s okay - I’m sucking more out of each experience instead of just going fast.
So what are some of the experiences you want to fully appreciate before you turn 50? There is undoubtably diving experiences you want to tackle, and some of them are in your near future, with a trip to Cocklebiddy in 2026 and Bikini Atoll in 2027 already being organised. Looking at my Bucket List I see things like the Long Solo, walking the Inca Trail, and crossing the Sahara, as well as seeing a rocket launch and an erupting volcano. There are other experiences like doing a biathalon, racing skeleton, and other things from the Bucket List.
All of these feel a little bit flat right now though, and I think it’s to do with that writing “constipation” I’m experiencing. I have so many incredible stories to tell already that I’m wary of doing more incredible things without writing about what I’ve already done. I write this 2 days before I leave for an expedition to Antarctica, but that feeling still stands - so much of the last 20 years has been pushing to tick off bucket list items one after another and to experience consistently incredible things, I now feel like I haven’t put in the effort to share those experiences with others through my writing.
Writing about my experiences also helps me fully process and understand them, and I know there are so many different things that I’ve seen and done that I simply haven’t processed properly because I’ve been pushing on to the next experience. So what do I want to do before I’m 50? I want to catch up on my experiences. I want to write about all the weird and wild things I’ve had the chance to do and see, and to fully appreciate all that I’ve had the chance to do so far. Before I’m 50 I want to turn all those different stray ideas into things that I love, that I can value properly, and that I can share. If the last 20 years has been about chasing experience, then I want to spend the next 10 years experiencing the sense of fulfilment that comes from giving those experiences meaning through writing.
I have no doubt that I’ll still go on wild adventures between now and when I turn 50, but I’d love to cultivate a writing practice that values and cultivates the details of those experiences for myself and others, rather than just doing things and sharing a few snaps through Instagram. I want to turn what I’ve done and what I will continue to do into books at every opportunity I get, and I intend to use the next 10 years to catch up on the previous 20.

content:
Right now you’re looking at two different job opportunities, and both of them offer different elements of what you’re looking for in a career in cyber. It’s also important to remember that you don’t need either of these roles - they’re the first to come back to you, and they’ve both provided you with 2nd interviews today, but that doesn’t mean that either of them is the right fit for you - only that they’re the things that are being offered this week.
On one side we have a junior analyst role with a really renowned MSSP - a company that I’ve seen as the best around since before I started working in this industry, and still see as the best organisation in the business. They have made a solid offer, and the perks of working there are pretty incredible, however the role and the income are both a step backwards from where I’ve been. On the plus side, the job will be incredibly easy compared to what I’ve been doing, it’ll allow me to develop skills and work on my own things (I’ll almost certainly get a book published next year if I accept their role), and the money is still very good (just not as good as I’ve been on, or what I could get elsewhere). The role may be a step backwards, and it’ll be a whole lot less interesting than what I might do elsewhere, but I’d be joining an organisation that is there for the long-haul - if I’m serious about working in cybersecurity in Australia for the next few years, then this would be the place to be. Likewise, they’d be making a significant investment in me - training, support, mentoring, security clearance, and other opportunities that I simply wouldn’t get elsewhere.
On the other side, I have the high probability (but not an offer) to work in a fully remote role on more money than I currently am, and do it as a senior threat intelligence analyst with an emerging organisation that is directly supporting critical infrastructure. If I stop and think about it, my concerns here are bigger - I’d be getting the well-paying remote role that I’ve been seeking, but I’d be doing it by stepping into a role that I’m not 100% sure I’m ready for, which will involve a great deal of extra work and study to keep my head above water before I became confident enough to hold it. I’d be earning good money, but I’d be potentially pidgeon-holing myself into threat intelligence (something that is already quite niche) while pushing to stay on top of everything that’s going on in the world. Yes, I’d be earning good money and I’d be working from home, but I’d also have nowhere to go to when I wanted to work out of the house.
A lot of this comes down to what I was asked in my interview with the threat intel CEO today - where do I want to be in 3-5 years? There are lots of things on the horizon, and I will have a lot of flexibility to wherever I go, so I need to have a sense of why I’m doing this and what I want to be doing when I’m in my mid 40’s. Do I want to push myself with cyber and invest more time and energy into developing it, or do I want to step back slightly and do something much easier for a year? Would the threat intel role really be pushing myself, or would it be an opportunity to learn more about something I’m interested in while being paid good money?
Right now I only have one offer, and that’s for a well-paying (but not exceptional) role at the same level that I’m currently at. The MSSP is well-renowned, and it would be without a doubt a wonderful place to work - I just need to decide if taking a pay cut and a career regression for a year is worth it to join them. And if I get offered the senior threat intel role, I need to ask myself if that’s the direction I really want to take myself at the expense of an opportunity at the MSSP. Right now I don’t know what I should do, and I’m a little scared to ask my gut which direction I should be heading either…
My gut is saying I should go with the MSSP, and that I shouldn’t wait around to hear what other offers come through. I have a coffee catchup with the MSSP’s SOC Manager on Tuesday morning, so I’ll ask myself again before then… but based on what I’m feeling now with a clear head and open heart, it feels like the right role to accept is the one that’s being offered to me.

content:
To determine what you want from work and your career in cybersecurity more generally, you really need to go back to why you got into cyber in the first place. This whole journey started because you were looking for work that was IT-related, because you haven’t never worked in IT have an aptitude for it. Your initial investigations were leading you down the Gaming pathway - that’s why you spoke to Martin about his work as much as you did, and why you bought a couple of cheap courses in modelling/gaming design in Unity. The interest in working with computers came first, and then the specialisation.
Ultimately you decided to pursue cybersecurity because it’s IT-related and you quickly realised you have the right kind of mindset to work in cyber rather than IT. Your background with the military and working intelligence-related fields has helped accelerate your path considerably, and helped guide you into this career too. Your experience in writing has drawn you towards GRC and policy work too, as well as it being a point of difference from others who want to pursue more technical paths.
So what do you want from cyber and your current job? You got involved in cyber to earn good money (resources), doing something interesting that you’re good at (fulfilment), that provides you the flexibility to do the travel and organise the expeditions that are important to you. In your work’s case they offer good money doing work that is adjacent to your interests (threat intelligence) and which draws on your experience (risk management). They also offer the opportunity to develop both certifications (CISSP) and vital experience that can be applied in a range of different roles.
So what do you want from cyber? A flexible and fully remote role doing threat intelligence, risk reporting, and/or GRC - something an IRAP Assessor would have, or someone doing Threat Intelligence remotely.
And what do you want from your current role? My CISSP certification, gaining more experience in Threat Intelligence and cyber, and as much flexibility as I can have to plan my future outside of the organisation - plan my next move while still being paid a lot where I am.

First #mini-essay
While the internet has been overwhelmingly consumed with a “feed” or “stream” style where information and opinions are delivered as an unalterable fact, the early days of the internet were far more collaborative and interwoven.
The earliest web pages behaved much like a digital “garden” rather than a feed or chronological blog - posts and snippets of information being woven together in a dense tapestry that was always evolving and interlinking. While a feed provides the most recent and “important” content at the top, a digital garden provides a wide array of entry points and no two journey’s through it are the same. For the last 20 years the internet has evolved into a broad array of feeds all vying for the attention of visitors, delivering the latest and greatest at all times.
Whereas a digital garden doesn’t strive for perfection or relevance - it simply grows through cultivation and contribution, developing over time into a wealth of knowledge and ideas. Connection is critical in a digital garden, as any snippet of information in it - a mini essay like this, a series of interesting links, brief thoughts on another article - is meaningless in isolation, but feeds an incredible web of possibility when it’s linked to a wide array of other snippets.
In much the same way a brain operates, the notes and snippets are individual synapses - the real power comes from the connections between those synapses, and the way that waves of activity passing through those connections creates new ideas and opportunities which are far bigger than the sum of the parts.
Digital gardens offer a vital alternative to the relentless stream of Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and all the other sources of “content” which deliver knowledge and novelty, but provide little opportunity for the development of wisdom or even genuine engagement. Rather than being hooked into the addictive cycle of checking the “latest” on social media, I’m going to strive to cultivate my own digital garden whenever I can.

A few months ago I made the decision that I’d write a book about my first 500 cave dives, right around the time I realised I’d be hitting my 500th cave dive during Trip - Sulawesi - 2025 Aug. Since then the ideas associated with this book have rolled around my head, but I’ve not sat down to make a solid go at a draft, and if I’m honest this #mini-essay is potentially another stalling tactic, but at least I’m writing about the idea of this book - it’s a start.
There’s absolutely no way I’d write a book about every one of those 500 dives though, and limiting this to simply those very specific 500 dives would be quite limiting too, so I know that the final book needs to be broader than that - it’s where the idea of BC (Before Cave), CC (Cave Course) and AC (After Cave) or PC (Post Cave) comes from. I also have zero interest in naming the training either - I just want to define the points where I was unqualifed, qualifying, and qualified to enter full overhead environments. This isn’t an advert for any particular training or instructor - this is about telling interesting stories about my cave diving experiences and sharing them with people who may never even scuba dive.
That is what the highest priority of this book needs to be - writing something that people who don’t scuba dive (let alone cave dive) will find interesting. Something that is engaging, informative, and funny. And it needs to tell stories that I think are important too. I’m not interested in sharing the stories that other people think I should, I want to tell the stories from my diving that are memorable and made an impact on me.
Subsurface logs all my dives, so I’ll use the number it has as a quick reference. But when I think about the dives that impacted me most, I think about:

content:
For years now I’ve felt this overwhelming connection to the Dune universe, and in many ways that connection has felt as undefinable as the series itself. Some might refer to the “vibe” of Dune being appealing, but for me there’s something more than just enjoying the aesthetic - it’s the whole body understanding that if you stop moving, if you try to stay in one place, to put up defences, to block the flow of energy… then you’ll be destroyed and swept away regardless.
So much of the Dune universe is intricate and mysterious, and yet so much of it makes intuitive sense without being explained. Maybe that’s the appeal - that it’s based on intuition and feeling, but so unbelievably technologically advanced. The technology is seamlessly built-in too, and if it’s not then it’s eventually worn down and destroyed.
All I can think about it the flow of sand and water wearing down anything that doesn’t flow with it. The Holtzman shields are a classic example of pure force being deflected and destroyed, whereas subtlety and finesse will slip through hit the goal without trying. The whole thing feels and seems very Zen, like the art of archery as you do without doing.
There is no wobbling in the Dune universe - those who freeze with indecision or attempt to resist through force are soon destroyed. Like Gandalf, characters in Dune are never early or late - they arrive exactly when they need to. This isn’t clockwork, fate or predestination either - it’s knowing yourself and knowing the universe, and surfing the circumstances in such a way that you and the universe are co-creators. You don’t resist the circumstances you find yourself in, but use them to move with the flow of the universe in a direction you do desire. Be flexible in all things, but especially in your desires, because if they do not bend or break, then you will bend and break in their place.
Dune’s appeal is in the ever moving, ever evolving, intuitive merging with the universe. It’s being like water and sand - finding the lowest and most natural path, blending with the universe as a whole, using the tools you have with subtlety and grace, and working with the wind to get where you both know you should be.
References Dune, 50 years on: how a science fiction novel changed the world - Guardian
References to Carl Jung, Collective Unconscious, Alan Watts and Zen
title: Mini Essay - Dune

content:
For awhile now I’ve been thinking about the emotional baggage I’m still carrying, and the overwhelming desire to shed it. As far as I can tell, it really centers on two different perceptions: a sense of hurt or harm from the things that happened in the past, and the sense that I’ve invested so much previously and feel drained by the lack of return.
On the “hurt” front, I guess a big part of me still feels broken by 2020, and even by things that happened in 2019. There’s no question that the experience of Georgie’s crash and then the final collapse of Mars One really broke me, but I also know that I’ve recovered from worse. It’s also nearly 6 years since all of that happened - another year and all of the cells in my body will have changed, and I’ll literally be a new person. The bigger issue isn’t the loss or the hurt, it’s that it’s not been replaced with something that was bigger or better. You’ve always sought adventure, and then used the valleys between to develop your stories, but after being involved in something like Mars One a lot of what’ s to come is going to feel like valleys. You will continue to be drawn into extraordinary adventures, and you’ll plan and develop your own adventures too, but there is really too much story inside you right now and it’s making it difficult to enjoy the daily joys. You wrote Cosmic Nomad as a way of letting go of Mars One, and you started your Australian cave diving adventure a year before - now is the time to write the book about your cave diving beginnings and let them go too. You’re ready to level up what you’re doing, and it really feels like you have until ADEX to get all of that sorted - to publish and talk about your Book - Cave Diving at ADEX. Everything else you’re doing is amazing, but the real strength for you is in storytelling about an incredible sport that you love. So let go of that hurt by telling the story of how you got to where you are today.
The investment element seems very small now compared to the opportunity you have to release that hurt through a book. When you look honestly at you “investment” it’s really just the things you’ve tried to cover the wound and distract yourself with. You should absolutely work on things like a podcast, about improving your storytelling opportunities, and about converting your ideas into amazing works of art. But you also know that many of them are simple distractions from the thing you know will produce the best results - writing your next book. You have so much invested in the next 5 years and you’ve done your best to develop and entertain a wide range of ideas… But you know that your next steps should be focused on writing books. All the answers you need can be found within yourself, and you simply need to focus in on writing to bring them out onto the page.
You’ve just tried to distract yourself with all the different plans you had for 2026, and yet you’ve now stopped and reflected on what you can do in this moment… And it’s really just about Writing Mini Essays and continuing to develop that Storytelling element that you know is so important. So use the notes you have, but start to condense them as you generate articles, blog posts, and so many other outputs that you can be proud of. Take what you have and turn it into great art - that’s all there is to it.

content:
“Fear is the mind killer” is the most easily recognised line from the “Litany Against Fear” from the Dune universe. Recited by high-born characters in times of high stress or when death threatens, it acts to centre and stabilise the emotions of those who recited it through the application of cold logic.
Accepting fear and allowing it to pass over you is vital to remaining in control when it could take control of your mind. In the universe of Dune, the litany is adopted as a vaccine to a digital virus that feeds on fear. However it’s origin can be traced back to Act II of Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar, in a quote which has been adapted numerous times - most notably paraphrased as “A coward dies a thousand deaths, but the brave die only once”.
Fear is seen as a powerful but ephemeral emotion, and with the tools provided by a logical mind it is possible to accept the emotion without giving in to it and being overwhelmed. Fear, like joy or despair, is a natural emotion felt in response to a threat to our body, mind, or loved ones. Fear can be an excellent motivator, but giving in to fear allows it to eat up our mental faculties and reduce us to a whimpering mass. Far better to face a fear when you feel it, to allow it to pass over you like any other emotion, and realise that once it’s gone only you will be left behind to think, act, and move forward.
The Litany Against Fear is a unique addition to the Dune universe, drawing from and inspiring many other sources but still carving out a distinct fragment of lore within the book series. It is an acknowledgement of death and the fear associated with it, and provides those who recite it as a way to release the debilitating effects of fear by facing it head-on.
References Mini Essay - Dune
Litany Against Fear
“I must not fear. Fear is the mind-killer. Fear is the little-death that brings total obliteration. I will face my fear. I will permit it to pass over me and through me. And when it has gone past, I will turn the inner eye to see its path. Where the fear has gone there will be nothing. Only I will remain.”
Shakespeare - Julius Caesar Act II scene 2 - “Litany against Fear” is derived from this
Cowards die many times before their deaths;
The valiant never taste of death but once.
Of all the wonders that I yet have heard,
It seems to me most strange that men should fear,
Seeing that death, a necessary end,
Will come when it will come.
title: Mini Essay - Fear Is The Mind Killer

It’s your first day in Ushuaia and you’re naturally shattered from not sleeping in the last 2.5 days, but you’re managing well considering that. You definitely got a good feel for this place though, enough that you certainly reached a point earlier where you were tired, hungry and sore, and the magic of being so close to Antarctica (with the matching weather) had worn off and you just wanted to stop.
Based on how you’ve done today, you should be able to check in to the Antarctica Hostel, have a shower, then nap for a couple of hours to recover, then figure out your next steps. You’ll likely meet folks once you check in, and I’m sure there will be something social happening tonight (it’s Friday afterall). Worse case though you can simply squirrel away and write or read tonight until you know you’re ready for sleep. Tomorrow is an open-ended questions, and one that you don’t need to answer just yet (even though you’ like to). You also don’t NEED to do anything tomorrow - it could easily be a day of wandering around Ushuaia and then going through your writing and tasks. You could even tackle the PRC paperwork tomorrow if you felt inclined. You have no obligations though, and it’s important to remember that - you don’t have to do anything at all.
Getting food here is straightforward too, so you could simply sit, write, read, and drink coffee if you wanted. It feels weird not to have any obligations, but knowing there’s plenty you could be doing, which is always dangerous. Ultimately the only thing you need to do today is to check into the Antarctica Hostel, which you’ll do within the hour. I’d love to go through all the amazing things that I have coming up over the next few months, and how that is all setting up even more incredible things further down the line, but right now I just want to do the one thing I need to do today, then shower and sleep.
When I do have the bandwidth to start sorting through things, don’t forget that there’s an A5 notepad slipped into the laptop sleeve of my bag. Sketching things on that may help spread the ideas out enough that I can acknowledge, process, and prioritise them. Go through your bag, reorganise things now that you’re no longer flying, and then start working through your own brain too. Lay out what’s happening over the next few months, figure out what’s important to you and what you need to do for it, and layout what your priorities are and how you’ll put them first.

I’m starting to realise that the issues I’ve had with Australian cave divers over the last 5-6 years has a lot of parallels with the way I struggled dealing with people in mining and in the military. Because right now it feels like the Australian cave diving community is bringing out the worst in me much the same way that the Royal Marines brought out the worst in me, and mining nearly drove me to suicide. I know that it’s the schemas that I use to view the world that are creating these parallels, but that doesn’t mean that they impact me any less - it simply means that I can address them by identifying my own thought patterns.
Like my experience in the military, my deep emotional investment in cave diving amplifies the positive and negative emotions I experience with it. Like the military, I’m also very good at cave diving and often judge others based on their capabilities at what we’re doing together. I’m very forgiving of people developing their skills, but I also need to see genuine acknowledgment of their skill gaps and a clear effort to be better. I expect nothing less of myself, and hold others to the same standard.
Above all though I want to do cool shit, and while I’m happy to share my experiences I don’t actually need to have them with other people around. But I will deeply resent other people if they get in the way or try to hold me back from doing what I love. This can take the form of incompetence, jealousy, being dismissive of my efforts, or just straight out insecurity on their part.
Facebook isn’t the source of this, but it absolutely amplifies all of it. It makes me crave those communities that don’t want me to be part of them, and makes me feel like even more of an outsider than I usually do. Generally I quite like my outsider nature, but Facebook absolutely makes it feel like a negative - like something I should be ashamed of and try to change. Facebook makes me crave acceptance by the “tribe”, and I’ve always hated tribalism - breaking free of that mindset is what made Mars One so appealing. The idea that we as a species could lift above our petty nationalism and small-minded squabbles to do remarkable things has always been the most important thing for me.
Hearing Martin and Chloe say “People are shit” was incredibly challenging, because I know they’re not. I get frustrated and rage against people and communities because so often I see them acting selfishly and at their most basic levels rather than acting in the highest and best interests of those around them. Instead of acting in the best interests of the universe. I see them harm others out of fear for themselves, like drowning swimmers trying to climb on top of each other instead of helping each other swim to the shore. I think people are absolutely remarkable sparks of light, that we are all tremendously powerful, and that we are all capable of doing extraordinary good for those around us. That we don’t need to be so scared all the time.
My frustration with Australian cave divers, with the military, and with mining, all stems from the belief that we are so much better when we help each other do remarkable things, and that we lose nothing by helping. That help may not be appreciated or valued, it may even be taken advantage of because of other people’s insecurities. But no matter what, it’s still helped. Through your action you’ve helped push humanity along just a little bit further, and that’s to be admired. I’m grateful to still be here to help others, and I’ll continue to do it regardless of the outcome. Ultimately this is about creating small works of art and showing love, and I will never regret showing the universe how much I love being here.

content:
There’s no question that writing has played an absolutely vital role in your development since you first discovered Mars One in September 2012. It took awhile for you to figure out how you wanted to do this, but handwritten journals have formed the mainstay for more than a decade. In the last few years though, you’ve noticed your journaling drop right off, with regular gaps ever since 2020 and the COVID nightmare. You were working so hard on Cosmic Nomad that you poured out your heart and mind into that book, leaving no desire or need to then write by hand in a journal. And the reality is you’ve never really picked that up properly since.
The question in this essay is whether you return to handwritten journals, whether your mini essays and daily notes can replace the journal, or if there’s something in-between. You know that typing doesn’t always work - you have your little Bluetooth keyboard for typing on your phone, but there is still an appeal in writing without a screen. Most of what you do is typing, and the most meaningful writing you do is typed into a keyboard like this. But curling up in bed and pouring your heart out into a handwritten note still holds huge appeal - it’s still a vital part of your expression. If you want to photograph your journals and use OCR to transcribe them, then that’s still an option. But you do need to write by hand occasionally, so it’s important to keep some sort of journal around. Does it need to be a moleskin? No. And will you still keep looking for digital alternatives? Of course - the move to digital seems very natural, just as you’ve looked a the Remarkable e-paper devices so you can write a journal without it going on paper.
But the devices can’t replace the pure simplicity of paper just yet. There’ll come a time in your future that they will, and so it’s good that you’re consolidating everything into Obsidian the way you are - eventually everything you write and think about will be available here. So for now, keep your green journal around, but definitely don’t feel bad for not writing in it every day - you’re shifting your writing more fully into the digital realm, and you’re becoming a more consistent writer for it.
Think about things, take notes on things, and write up little essays on things the way you are here. By typing and thinking about the world you live in, you’re clearing your mind the same way you do with a handwritten journal, AND you’re producing an easily referenced digital product that you can index, copy/paste from, and edit without it needing to be some museum piece. By typing this stuff and putting it all into Obsidian, you’re slowly creating the digital garden that you so desperately want to share with people - soon it’ll be ready, but not if you writer everything into a green journal no one (not even you) will really read.

content:
For some time you’ve been aware that the shutdown of Mars One in 2020 has left you very adrift and directionless in the world, and one of the questions that’s come up repeatedly is what you’d do if Mars One suddenly rebooted. Bas floated the idea when the Ridley Scott documentary was first being discussed, but we’ve heard nothing on that for well beyond the 12 month exclusivity contract. But the question remains - what would you do if Mars One rebooted tomorrow?
The most obvious thing is you’d be looking to shed all your gear again. Anything excess or outstanding would be immediately trimmed out - physically, emotionally, mentally, and probably spiritually too. So what would that look like?
Physically I’d be selling the compressor immediately, and everything in the storage unit would be getting a very hard look to see if it’s worth keeping. I’d go through all my clothes and figure out what I really want to keep, what I want to replace, and then ditch anything that doesn’t suit. I’d be stocktaking everything I have in the house and asking really tough questions about why I have it. I’ve already gone through the car, but I’d be asking if I keep it either. Physically I’d also be trying to shed weight and get up to a substantial level of fitness too, because I’d have a substantial motivation to push on when it’d be easier to quit or treat myself. I’d be driving hard every single day towards that goal, and that would be all I’d need to be a whole lot fitter and lighter.
Mentally is probably where the biggest shift would occur, because I’d be slipping back into that highly optimised backpack lifestyle, ready to travel and speak about Mars One all over again. I’d want to read all the book on my bookshelf and then give them away, and I’d be reading everything I could find in my digital library that might help me with preparation for Mars One selection. Cave diving would immediately drop to the background, because as much as I love it there is nothing that compares with a one-way mission to Mars. Interestingly though, I know how vital it’d be to write out all the notes and mini essays I already have planned, because I’d want to cut all my attachments and clear the decks as much as possible so I’d be approaching selection as cleanly as possible. So I’d still be grateful for all the time I have coming up, and I’d be pushing to write as much as possible so that I had my emotions and mental state as clear as possible.
The emotional impact is very hard to predict, and I suspect it would follow the actions I’d take in the physical and mental realm when I got news that Mars One was rebooting. The response from my partner is really hard to predict - I know she’d be supportive in her way, but Ialso know she’d hate the changes that would follow. I’ve know for some time that I shouldn’t (and really can’t afford) live in fear of upsetting her, but I also know that Mars is bigger than her, bigger than our relationship, and bigger than any of the relationships I have. So I know I’d do what I needed to do to be emotionally ready for selection, regardless of the consequences. It sounds brutal, but the opportunity to be part of a Mars mission is bigger than any one person.
The one area where I’m certain the impact of a Mars One reboot would be immediately and undeniably positive is in my spiritual health. This is the one area that has lapsed most in the last 5 years, and my trip to Antarctica is the first time since 2020 that I’ve felt my spirit really ignite. I don’t want the rest of my life to be simply pursuing different experiences and writing about them - I want to feel unbridled joy seeing, doing, and creating extraordinary things. Paddling away from that leopard seal, I knew I’d had one of the most incredible experiences of my life so far, and I know that the life I’m currently living really lacks that. Discovering new underwater caves are one example from the last 5 years, but I can’t think of many others and certainly not the way I’d feel getting an update from Mars One. Every morning I’d wake up hopeful for an email, and while that anticipation was exhausting over time it was still an incredible rush when I did see an official Mars One email arrive with an update.
So what would I do if Mars One rebooted? I’d cut back a lot of the things that have crept into my life over the last 5 years that I don’t like. I’d regain a clear sense of purpose, and I’d be absolutely brutal in my dealing with people because I’d know I was on a mission that was bigger than any of us. And the next question obviously becomes “Why not live my life like that anyway?”. You asked yourself the question of what you’d do if you had 10 years left on Earth, and you took a potential Mars mission and stretched it into a question around mortality.
So why not ask yourself what you’d do if you knew you were going to die in the next 10 years? Because you might. What would you regret if you were paliating in hospital tomorrow? Would you wish you’d done the safe thing? Or would you want to go out doing something that boring people would say “He deserved it”? You’ve always joked about that, but it’s never really been a joke at all - I’d much rather die doing something fucking awesome but stupid than die in an old and broken body. Life is for living, and it’s not the years in your life but the life in your years that counts. So go and do extraordinary things. Make trouble doing the right thing, and die because you deserved it not because you were old or unlucky. Mars One gave you the focus you needed to see life that way, but there’s no reason why you can’t live life to the fullest now that the prospect of being sent to another plant has become more remote. Every day you must remember death, and sleep in a coffin incase you don’t wake up.

content:
If you knew you were going to die in a year, what would you do? Would you stay at work? Fuck no. Would you stay here with Chloe? Maybe, but only if it were to write as much as you possibly could with your final year. If you were going to die before you turned 41, there’s no question you’d travel and write constantly. And you certainly wouldn’t be diving in Mt Gambier - you’d be going straight to Spain to cave dive, maybe France for more of the same.
You’d burn fucking everything too - sharing all that you had and making sure there was as little left behind as you could. You’d leave as neat a pile as possible, with nothing that others have to sort through - all your files and notes and snippets filed away so someone else could use them if they wanted, but not taking up any more space than needed.
You’d want to experience weightlessness and go to space if possible. You’d want to see Antarctica and get close to Leopard Seals if you could, maybe swim with orca and sleep in the snow in Norway. You’d want to experience Skeleton too, and see the Northern lights again. Would you go on a long walk? Maybe - something to disappear and be with your own thoughts for awhile as you contemplate existence. Ayahuasca in the Amazon might be on the agenda, but I think spending time alone will provide the clarity you seek.
Would you try to help people with your last year? You probably would. There’s no one you feel you need to settle things with or try to make right with, but you’d want to make sure that you made life better for those around you even as your life ended. Above all you’d want to write though - to put together books that make people laugh and think. That’s been your greatest sense of achievement so far - writing and publishing Cosmic Nomad. You want to have the incredible experiences and learn the incredible things that it takes to be able to sit down and write a book about it. You have to have lived those experiences, to have walked the talk.
So if I had a year to live, I’d probably write a book about it while travelling. I’d shed all my excess shit, travel on adventures, and write about it every step of the way. That’s what’s most important to you, and that’s what you’d like to spend your days doing - writing books that make people laugh and think.

content:
Much of my challenge recently has been knowing where to begin, or struggling to start even when you think you know where to begin. Right now you know you want to focus on creating your Book - Cave Diving, yet you’re struggling to find the ways to focus on it or to begin. You’re looking for different prompts and courses, but you also know that you simply need to begin.
It’s easy to put this down to “motivation”, but you also know that classic quote from Tchaikovsky about being in the mood for work. If you wait for motivation then you’ll never begin, so you need to keep showing up each day and just starting.
This little “1000 words” script is designed to get you writing each day, which is what you ultimately want to do. It’s about simply beginning and getting 1000 words out so you can move easily onto other writing projects. I’m not sure if 1000 words counts as towards your Mini Essays but some of them could - while 1000 words is probably a bit big for a #mini-essay you’re still capturing ideas and putting them down somewhere they could be useful. So yeah, even if you end up dropping this down to 400 or 500 words (the average length of your Mini Essays) it’d be very easy to put something down each day that helps develop your writing practice while sorting through the random thoughts that run through your brain.
Your challenge with the Book - Cave Diving is that you’re not quite sure how to begin with Book - Cave Diving. Ultimately this is just about having Subsurface open in one window and looking at your early dives, then writing about your memories from each. You don’t need a full skeleton or even a specific direction that the book might take, because you know that the first draft is always trash and requires an 80% re-write anyway. So just get that trash out of the way so you can create the read book you want to publish. Initially going over this stuff helps you form your perspective on it by forcing you to think through things and reflect, so your first take is always going to be garbage - accept that, and just begin at the beginning.
You’re also realising that you don’t need to write so much - you’ve already dropped this word counter down to 500, and there’s serious consideration to drop it to 300 or even 200. You don’t need to write a huge amount to get this all going - your ideas form in snippets, and you should use this to start the process then bounce out to other things. You’re already doing it now - wanting to breakaway from this to write a #mini-essay on the time-dilation & far-future game you want to create through vibe coding. So drop your daily word count to 300, and start getting your Ideas down so you can start to create your Book - Cave Diving and get the various ideas and nonsense you have bouncing around your head out and onto a screen where it can be useful.

content:
Topic: Kids Meals on Planes
I’d never realised it before, but every meal on a plane is basically a kids meal. I’ve just visited my relentlessly obnoxious 3 year old nephew, and on the flight back to Adelaide I’ve been served focaccia topped with chorizo, pesto, bell peppers & goats cheese. Seems fancy as fuck, but looking at the box it was served in I realised it’s just like what you’d pull out of a Happy Meal. And that’s the trick, isn’t it? We’re being served little boxes of snacks to keep us happy as we fly through space in an aluminium tube full of recycled farts.
Trying to tame a toddler who’s kicking off in the back of a car is impossible, but fully grown adults still need a Happy Meal to keep them from kicking off and crashing the fucking plane. Ultimately it’s just a light tranquillizer for a stressful situation - you’re being loaded into something our monkey brains can’t process, you have limited mobility and freedom for an extended period of time which amplifies the stress, and one way of reducing that stress is through endorphin-releasing snacks (like a starchy, carb-loaded focaccia). Even the alcohol comes in those ridiculous little bottles - they’re basically an adult juice box so that the 40 year old toddler in 18C doesn’t try to crack a window. Sit down, be quiet, listen to the lady at the front, eat your happy meal and drink your juice box.
This also reminds me of… How would a caveman process a bunch of shaven apes climbing into a plane?

content:
Where do I want to be in 5 Years time?
Dear Josh in 2031, Firstly I hope you’re still around to read this. Given the way your life has changed through the years, you’ve gone through plenty of period where you didn’t think you’d make it another 5 years. So if you’re reading this, nice work - you made it!
You’ll be 45 when you’re reading this and a about a month and a half away from your 46th birthday. Right now 46 doesn’t feel as significant at 45 does, in much the same way 40 didn’t feel as significant as I think 42 will be. You’ll have been diving for 34 years, with the last 2 of them cave diving. You’ll also have a decade of Cyber Security experience if you’re still doing it, which seems pretty uncertain right now. You’ve just started work with Alpha Echo after a bumpy 6-8 months leaving ElectraNet, going to Sulawesi and Antarctica, breaking up with Chloe, living in a Van, moving in with Simone, and asking a lot of questions about who or what you want to be.
One thing that you’ve figured out is that cyber is just a way to fund your adventures, and what you really are is an Explorer-Storyteller - someone who goes on incredible adventures, learns from them, and brings those lessons back to others through storytelling in books, speaking, comedy, video and anything else you can imagine. The most obvious way for you to push ahead right now is to put your heart and soul into writing books about things you love.
While I hope you’re doing all sorts of speaking, comedy, and even TV about exploration; the greatest hope I have by 2031 is that you’ve published at least three books - your cave diving book “517”, your anthology of Book - 101 Things, and your book Book - Calling ET. Looking at those three books, I’m simultaneously scared of how little and also how much time 5 years might be. You’re the only one who knows if I got all three done, but I also know it’s more than possible to have 5 published books before the end of my 45th year. You’ve talked about writing a book every 2 years, and yet the Book - 101 Things book has so much ready made content that you could write it much quicker if you make the commitment to. So you’ll smash out your cave diving book in 2026, put together your Book - 101 Things through 2027 before you dedicate the next 2-3 years to researching, writing, rewriting and then publishing Book - Calling ET.
Writing the Book - 101 Things will help stir you to reflect on and do more of your bucket list, and likewise I think writing Book - Calling ET will help you work through your relationship with Space Exploration too, and I hope you can find some peace when you think about the time, effort, and passion you had/have for Mars Exploration. I hope that writing these books have helped shape you into the focused and determined Explorer-Storyteller I know you are capable of being, and I hope you have been supported throughout the last 5 years to be the best and most capable version of yourself possible.
Keep being amazing and doing amazing things, and I hope you’re making us both proud with what you’re doing and where you’re going next.
Stay awesome, Josh in 2026

content:
There’s something really unique about my life-long relationship with the BattleTech / MechWarrior videogame series. The tabletop game look interesting too, but I’ve never really gone in for tabletop wargames except to paint them as models. But the videogames have always held a very special place in my heart, and it goes all the way back to my first exposure through MechWarrior 2.
Being able to stop around in such a huge bipedal robot and shoot things has to be a huge part of this. The idea of controlling a building size walking machine fitted with lasers and rockets is certainly awe inspiring, far more than I’d feel driving a tracked vehicle. In fact the tracked and flying vehicles in MechWarrior 5 often feel out of place when I see them in-game - more like a machine and less like a powerful giant.
The view is certainly an important element in this too, as I don’t enjoy the small cramped view of the cockpit and always immediately opt for the wider 3rd person perspective. Being able to see my mech (and it is my mech) looking cool, shooting shit and hearing the epic sound of my weapons while weaving over terrain and between buildings, and generally dominating the battlefield - it feels incredible.
It’s important to note that the lore of MechWarrior endlessly fascinates me as well. Having churned through over a dozen BattleTech audiobooks, hearing the details of that universe is almost as good as playing the games that recreate it. Even now I want to soak up the stories in a way that WH40k never quite recreated. The idea of the clans is particularly interesting to you, along with the stories of the star league and the Lostech caches left behind. None of it is real - it’s all complete fiction set in an alternate universe 1000 years in the future. And yet reading about it makes me want to go out into the universe and discover these incredible caches of information and knowledge that only exist in the minds of lore writers.
The elements of lore that I really connect with are vital here too. I know I don’t give the slightest shit about the palace intrigue of the inner sphere, but the culture and single-mindedness of the clans and the mercenaries is fascinating. They’re not interested in the petty bullshit - they’re bred for war, armed with refined war-fighting machines, and they’re very fucking good at what they do. That’s the appeal for you - the raw do-or-die attitude couched in a very real capability to do your job. Follow the process, think about how to be the best you can be, and take setbacks and success in your stride - it’s just another day.
This also reminds me of…
Being really good at your job and doing it every day because you love it Having a singular focus on what you need to do to survive Being fascinated by the idea of lost knowledge and seeking it out Feeling like a powerful machine being an extension of yourself Looking at changes to humanity and technology 100’s and 1000’s of years into the future. content:
One of my ongoing challenges is keeping track of and managing all the different things that engage my attention. This can mean my Personal, asking Mini Essay - What are your obligations, my Work, and anything else that contacts my senses and hooks my attention. While I can track a wide range of interests and passions, the real challenge for me is task-switching: being invested in one thing, but needing to keep something else in mind at the same time, or being pulled away from my focus to handle some other issue.
Recently this rapid task-switching has started to really erode my mental health, and moving to Obsidian as a Digital Garden means I can keep everything in one place. Currently I still have a few other areas which I need to track, but Obsidian is quickly becoming the default for storing and organising my mental baggage. I also need to remember that I don’t need to sort it all out immediately, but I do need to contain as much here as possible. Sorting out knowledge is an ongoing process, and I really am overdue for a very long sort out which will mature into something extraordinary… but for now I’m happy with getting all my thoughts, ideas and work into one place so I’m not losing anything.
Clearing out my mental baggage is an ongoing process, and one that I really love. But for now, the most important thing is that I’m making an effort to consolidate all my knowledge into one sprawling digital garden which I can prune/cultivate/harvest as my priorities allow. Spend time collecting all your baggage in one place (eg. Obsidian) and you’ll be able to sort/shed it with time.

content:
This expedition feels important for a wide variety of reasons, and not just for what we discovered or did while we were out there. First and foremost this trip feels like the end of a major phase for the Soggy Wombats as there were four of us out there, but it was always intended to be all of us. The fact that the two Matts and Simon didn’t come wasn’t a huge surprise, and I’m certainly not upset with them for not being there, but it does reflect that when a trip was organise 12 months in advance for them to make time to be there, they had other priorities. The fact that Martin said yes, but then pulled out without telling any of us, and that he replaced himself with Farzad says everything about where that relationship has now gone. There’s no need to dwell on it, but it does mean that he won’t be asked to participate in any trips again.
Corey proved himself throughout the entire experience, and Will did exactly what he said he would be able to do, and I value both of them all the more for living up to expectations and being clear about what they would and wouldn’t do. Likewise with James, Nancy and Toby - all three of them proved to be excellent additions to the trip, to be incredibly capable and resilient, and I’m really glad I got to be there alongside each of them. Chloe is an interesting one from this trip, as we managed to get through it without our personal issues blowing over, but there’s no doubt that there’s still lingering resentment there. It’s not a showstopper for her joining future trips that I organise, but it is definitely something to consider before extending an invite.
More importantly though, this trip acted as the end of a phase for me - one where I feel like I need to support and work with others when it comes to cave diving. I originally created the Soggy Wombats as cover for my own activities - to present a united team who made these discoveries and deflect some of the attention from myself. After the shitshow of the last few years where I’ve been consistently punished by the Australian cave diving community for sharing the things I’ve discovered, there is exactly zero incentive to organise things with other people in mind. I know now that I don’t owe the community anything, and what I do share deserves to be acknowledged and celebrated. Being suspended puts me solidly outside of the community, and that’s really forced my hand when it comes to trying to work with others - I really can’t give or plan to support others, because I’m expressly forbidden from it. So this trip has really served as a hard full stop on my concern for supporting the community and for what the Soggy Wombats were. What we evolve into next will be something different - something that Will, Corey and I can shape and use as a brand rather than a team.
In terms of actual caves, it was wonderful to be able to collect meaningful data from three different sites too. Finally getting back to Murra-El-Elevyn - 6N47 to collect meaningful photogrammetry data and run line into Mitch’s Maze has been nearly a year in the making, and from all accounts it was exactly what we needed to do. I’ve given Will everything he needs to turn that cave into an extraordinary 3D model, and to be able to map this new section using 360 imagery alongside the MNemo survey data too. Part of me is disappointed to have bottomed out the two branches of Mitch’s Maze, but I think the photogrammetry processing will reveal a whole range of interesting opportunities for exploration that I haven’t foreseen yet. I am also keeping in mind that there are several lakes in Murra to the north of the Crystal room that have never been dived or properly explored - there is enormous potential for exploration there if someone like me is willing to put in the effort to get there.
Getting into Tommy Graham’s Cave - 6N56 for the first time was an interesting experience too, and one that I’m very glad I took the 360 camera for. The effort to get into Tommy’s makes it prohibitive, but there is no question that I will be going back there - it has so much more to give, and we didn’t even go close to collecting all the photogrammetry data from it that I’d have liked. Losing the X4 in there is frustrating, but that’s just the nature of the beast given what we were trying to achieve, and there are clear lessons from that loss for the future too. I am definitely keen to return to Tommy’s for a dedicated push - not to just visit for the day, but to spend several days there with some strong cave divers in order to push and thoroughly explore it without carrying weaker members of the group.
And finally Cocklebiddy Cave - 6N48 was it’s own experience entirely. I’m glad that I’ve done it, and I’m glad that the people who were there have now done that trip, but I’m equally glad not to be going back. It was never about diving Cocklebiddy for me - it was about supporting a Nullarbor expedition for the Soggy Wombats and a few others to collect data from an epic cave, and I’m glad that we’ve done that. Do I ever need to go back to Cocklebiddy? I don’t think so, and I’d put places like Pannikin Plains - 6N49 well ahead of any return to Cocklebiddy. Am I glad that we collected photogrammetry data from the surface all the way through to Toad Hall? Fuck yes I am, and I have no issue with staying on the surface as support while other people collected that data either - at the end of the day it’s about producing a 3D model that gives people some sense of how truly epic these places are and how hard it is to get people safely in and out again. So I have no issue with the outcome from Cocklebiddy, and I’m glad that I went. I’m equally glad that I didn’t dive, and that the conflict we experienced out there has hammered home to me that I need to plan trips for myself rather than for others - do the things that I’m excited for, and figure out who will add positively to the experience rather than feeling like I need to invite others to make it happen. I am more than capable of travelling completely solo and collecting meaningful data that will help others, so don’t feel like you need to carry others - share the experience through storytelling, video, and writing. Don’t feel like you need to indulge others - this is a pretty selfish sport, and you absolutely do not need to share anything unless you want to.
