Mini Essay - Why Antarctica is Important to you Mini Essay - PRIVATE - What has changed in you since Antarctica Mini Essay - November 23
Today marks two months since the end of Trip - Antarctica - 2025 Nov, and I feel like it’s well overdue for a reflection on what happened and the highlights of visiting the frozen continent.
The most immediate aspect of visiting Antarctica is that it was my “7th continent”. I still don’t feel like I’ve properly visited South America, as I really just flew through Santiago and Buenos Aires on the way to Ushuaia, then wandered around Ushuaia for a few days before boarding the ship to Antarctica… but I have now set foot on all 7 continents. That was never really that big a deal for me though - I never set out to visit all 7 continents (even though it’s one of the Bucket List) and I’ve always been a little disgusted by folks who count the number of countries they’ve visited. Travel is extraordinary and vital to our emotional growth, but visiting or ticking off places for just the sake of it always felt disrespectful to the places you were visiting. I’ve travelled extensively through North America and Europe, done multiple visits to Africa, and been to a variety of places through Asia too. But this most recent trip is the only time I’ve been to South America, and it felt like it was just a trip in transit to Antarctica. Visiting Antarctica is understandably difficult so a 10 day trip is not to be ignored, but I still don’t feel like I’ve really experienced the continent either - that’s something I think will require an overwinter stay. So ticking off my 6th and 7th continents weren’t really highlights from the trip.
Seeing orca as we arrived at Deception Island was one of the most unexpected and genuinely incredible things I’ve ever seen. To have our ship surrounded by three separate pods, with 40-45 animals swimming on every side of the ship, was simply breath-taking. I just remember locking eyes with one of the expedition guides and seeing the seer awe in her face at what we were witnessing, and realising this was as special for the people guiding us as it was for the folks who’d paid to be there. It was here that part of me wished I had a substantial digital camera, but I also know that I simply loved being in a place where I could enjoy the spectacle of the animals rather than trying to capture it. Seeing such stunning animals breaching with their young was extraordinary, and I still don’t really have words for it.
Setting foot on deception Island didn’t really mean much, and if I’m honest it was all a bit uncomfortable - I was more worried about Stacey, Soori, and Jeanette all being unwell, although I wasn’t overly impressed with Deception Island if I’m honest. It also didn’t count as “setting foot on Antarctica” either, as it wasn’t part of the peninsula. Kissing the rock while kayaking with Jeanette meant a lot more though, mostly because of how ridiculous and fun it felt. It was also in the larger context of the extraordinary whale experience we’d had that morning, and the 2nd humpback experience we had a little later on. The time that I really “set foot on Antarctica” was the polar plunge, which was a lot of fun but not really an opportunity to soak up the experience of “touching” the continent… even if I was barefoot.
As fun as it was, the polar plunge was really overshadowed by kayaking all week to see a leopard seal. I still get emotional thinking about what an incredible experience that was, and how utterly life-changing it was to see such an awe-inspiring animal up close and in a genuinely peaceful state. I’d gone to Antarctica with the hope of seeing a leopard seal, but had never been brave enough to truly admit that was my reason for being there. My 5 star review of “Keith looks back in Anger” came out the day I cancelled the show, but I never felt bad about it because I knew the show had done exactly what it needed to do… and I kind of dismiss all the other things that happened during this trip when I think about how important it was to kayak next to that leopard seal. How life-changing it was to spend a week on the water silently hoping for an encounter, and then being able to experience a half ton apex predator sleeping on an iceberg with just one other kayak on the water. I felt like spending time around that leopard seal was a way of honouring the 24 year old kid who was leaving the Royal Marines and didn’t know what he wanted to do with his life, and who saw a photo on a doctor’s wall of a kayak and a leopard seal in Antarctica and said “I’m going to do that one day”. I’m not the same person who sat in that doctor’s office 15 years ago, but I’m very grateful to him that he saw something extraordinary on the wall and decided to create the opportunities to experience it himself.

content:
The last few years have all been about work and study, and now that you’ve left work and have several months to yourself, you’re not sure what to do with yourself. Not because there’s nothing to do, but because there’s dozen of different potential projects that you could spend your time and energy on, and you’re not sure which will help you achieve your long term goals. Primarily because you’re not sure what you want to want!
The first thing that comes to mind is the development of your websites, both personal and the Soggy Wombats. But you also know that they primarily showcase what you’ve created and done, and you don’t really know what you want to be showcasing or working towards right now. There’s no doubt that you want to be writing books though, and you know that writing (like you are now) is important for you to establish where you’re going, what you’re doing, and why you’re doing it.
You have things like 2025, 2025 Goals, Tasks, and Stray - Ideas all crowding your mind, and that’s without looking further afield to your Bucket List. The real question becomes “What do you want to do in 2026, and what can you do to support that over the next 3 months?”.
So figure out 2026.
You’re going to visit Thailand in early January, which you’ve already started the conversation on. Why are you going to Thailand? Because you want to explore caves, there are plenty to discover there, and you want to take people on overseas expeditions. That’s going to mean getting a ChOptima (which you’re already organising) and doing a crossover (which you have multiple options for, but need to figure out your preference).
You’re going to need to find some sort of cyber work in order to earn money for Bikini Atoll. Having CISSP helps a lot, but the bigger decision you need to ask is what kind of cyber work can you do that will use your skills in a way that is not draining. Because ultimately cyber work is not what you want to be doing with your life - it should be an easy and well-paying job that leaves plenty of bandwidth so you can write books and go on cave diving expeditions. That’s what you really want to be doing, and in some ways you’re doing what Harry did with medicine - studying and working in something well paying and respected even though your real interest is exploration.
So ask yourself what kind of cyber work will allow you to disconnect emotionally while still paying really well and being flexible? There are dozens of different roles out there, and one factor may be how much money you want/need to earn to pay for Trip - Bikini Atoll - 2028 June. You have plenty of money right now, but you’ll need to pay for the CCR, crossover, a trip to get hours, a trip for MOD2, and then to pay for the Bikini Trip itself. You don’t need much, but you do need to work in 2026 to do the training and pay the Bikini balance before 2027.
The other factor with work is that all the exceptional roles require NV1, and that is starting to become a barrier for you. Doing your IRAP assessor course is a fast way to organise that, although you’re not sure if you want to spend a significant chunk of time studying for Cyber - Training & Certifications when you’re currently so burned out. There’s no doubt that you’ll do both the CISA and IRAP Assessor courses in 2026 though… he writes hesitating. If IRAP is just a pathway to NV1, why not apply for easy and straight-forward jobs that will sponsor an NV1? Or are you interested in it because it’s remote? Remote auditing?
Something tells me I’ll end up accepting a full-time role that is less dysfunctional. I’ll do that for a year, earn CISA/CRISC & IRAP, and then see where things stand for 2027. The important thing is that I have plenty of flexibility to write what I need to write and go on the cave diving expeditions that I so keenly want to experience. The last 3 years have been very full-on, and I’m not sure I want to keep doing what I’m doing, but I also don’t want to tear up everything I have. Writing is something I simply need to allocate a little time to each and every day. If I need to get up at silly o’clock and write something before I start my day in a regular job, then do it!
You also know you’re very capable of multi-tasking when it comes to work, so you can pretend to be doing one job while preparing for the next. That may be a bonus for taking on something much lighter or fully remote - do what you need to do to stay in the bosses good books, show up without over-achieving, and then make sure you’re putting your mind and heart into writing books.
Maybe cybersecurity is the thing that gets you enough money to afford a CCR and a trip to Bikini Atoll, but you don’t owe it anything. The real question you need to ask is what DO you owe your heart and mind to? If it’s writing, then you should be making damn sure that you’re putting an enormous amount of effort into developing a platform to share what you write, and then be turning up every single day to write something that you’re proud of. This isn’t about legacy, it’s about developing and sharing things that you care about and that other people can appreciate.
So do only what you need to with work - find something that pays well and you can be emotionally disengaged from. You don’t need to be passionate or try to leave a legacy. You’re doing what you’re good at for money to be able to live. The bigger question you need to answer is how you want to live.

content:
There’s no denying that the last few months have been pretty turbulent, and I have a whole series of fairly significant life changes heading my way in the next month too. My perspective on life has massively shifted since turning 40 in August, leaving ElectraNet in September, and especially since Trip - Antarctica - 2025 Nov so it’s natural to look ahead and wonder where I’m trying to go next.
While everyone seems to put a lot of focus on turning 40, having drinks with Cairo last night reminded me that I’m still a massive Htchhikers Guide to the Galaxy nerd so I’ve always been more curious about what my life would look like at age 42. I’ll hit that milestone in August 2027, so I’m really curious about what my life is going to look like 4 months after that in 2028.
Between now and then I’ll be finally embracing my desire to live in the VW Transporter; I’ll have the experience and certifications to do any kind of Cyber Security work I want (realistically I’m already at that point, but even more so with my plans for 2026), and I’ll have achieved a lifelong dream of diving at Bikini Atoll as part of Trip - Bikini Atoll - 2028 June. So the real question is what I’d like to do after all of that? And what do I want to do to prepare for the life I want to live at age 42?
Working in Antarctica is the most obvious option right now. After the experience of Trip - Antarctica - 2025 Nov I know that I absolutely the incrediblely stark and beautiful nature of the place, but I also know I don’t want to go back as a tourist or really as a tour guide. I’d love to do that in the Arctic, but there’s a huge part of me that desperately wants to truly live and work in that environment for an extended period of time. I’m keenly aware that it’d disconnect me from #diving for an extended period, but it’d also disconnect me from much of my current life too, and that has a lot of appeal. It’s not that I want to disappear from the world, but I’d like to turn the noise down and be pulled in fewer directions at once. In the same way I love organising a pet/housesit so I can work on a book, I love the idea of extended disconnection from the outside world so I can work on the things that I truly care about.
The idea of studying for a masters in Slovenia is also present, but the more I reflect on it the more I realise that I’ve been down this path before - my physical degree is still at a university in the Netherlands because I was deadset about enrolling in a masters there, then realised that a return to uni would be interesting but wouldn’t actually move me forward very much. Anything that I find interesting, I could (and likely should) write a book about instead. There are so many books I’d like to write, and the ideas clog up the longer they go untapped, so studying for something that doesn’t have a clear outcome (like studying for a CISA certification as a pathway to becoming an IRAP Assessor) doesn’ make a whole lot of sense, but I know I get wrapped up in the enthusiasm of how cool it’d be to live in another country and study something I’m passionate about. Do you need to do that within a university framework? No, but that doesn’t mean you need to reject the idea outright - just be very wary of allowing the fantasy override the practicalities of investing in the idea.
The are many other things on your Bucket List which I want to put energy into, but they don’t leap to mind right now without looking at them. One thing that I might also look at doing is a Long Solo - getting on a bike, kayak, or even on foot to cover a significant distance. Much like the idea of Study - Masters though, there kind of needs to be a reason to get to the end of it. Is it about Writing Books? There are far too many other things you want to write about more than what it’s like being on the move for months. The one thing that you know you can do endlessly is write, so having the achievement of a Long Solo would be nice, there are plenty of other things in my past to be proud of already, and I’d rather write about them first.
So what do I want to be doing in 2028 after turning 42? I want to be a travelling author. I might be in Antarctica, I might be on a boat travelling the world, I might be living in a wood cabin by a lake in a pine forest… But whatever it is I’m doing, I want to be working on writing Books. Everything else is a way of experiencing the world so I can create stories in my Writing. So keep doing the things you’re doing and working towards what you’ve made a priority, but remember that in two years you want to be doing things that directly support writing more books, rather than hindering or distracting me from the goal of writing 10 books in your life.

content:
As you sit in the airport at Buenos Aires after such a hefty few days of flying, it’s starting to really dawn on me that I’m about to flying to Ushuaia - the gateway to Antarctica. And in just a few days, I’ll be getting onboard an expedition ship Going to the Antarctic Peninsula!
There’s a big part of me that is simply not processing that fact - that in a few days I’ll be in Antarctica. I’m not sure if it’s the numbness you’ve experienced a lot of these last few years, but it’s not clear if my lack of excitement is because I haven’t come to terms with the reality of the trip yet, or if I’m downplaying it all in an attempt to protect my psyche from potential disappointment.
What is clear is that I’m not overly excited, and I wonder if that’s just always been my way? Thinking back I’ve often done the same thing before big trips - busy getting things ready, other bullshit things popping up that demand attention, and just general tiredness from juggling too many priorities at once. Likely a combination of all these things which are slowing you down from unbridled enthusiasm. But I think this trip will cut through much of that - you’re off on a lifelong dream to see the white continent, and you’re doing all you can to see leopard seals while kayaking. That is going to be fucking WILD.
Even as you type that though, you’re trying to downplay it and be fine with it not happening. It was genuinely tough to write :That is going to be fucking WILD" because there’s part of you that is adding doubt to protect yourself from it not happening. But you don’t need protecting - you need to throw yourself out there and be wrong instead! Say “I’m going to Antarctica to kayak with leopard seals because it’s something I’ve always dreamed of.” and don’t try to protect your ego by adding caveats. Do you have control over what the leopard seals do? No! Will you be disappointed if you don’t see any? Probably! But will it ruin the entire trip? FUCK NO! Because this is all about putting yourself out there, making bold claims, and then owning it when things don’t work out as hoped or planned.
You had someone at your last job who could never commit to any thing or any measurable statement - it was always qualified with a whole lot of bullshit and hand-waving so he couldn’t be pinned to any specific statement later. I fear that my lack of enthusiasm for life might be stemming from a cynicism and insecurity about the things I do - that I’ve spent too long taking people’s comments personally that I’ve been Self-censoring and adding caveats to everything. YOU DO NOT NEED TO BE RIGHT ABOUT ANYTHING! Be wrong! Be wrong on a regular basis, and be okay with it, because being wrong makes life more interesting - it makes for a better story, and it makes you stronger too!
So why is Antarctica so important to you? Because this trip is an opportunity to be raw and open and honest about how much this shit excites you! Fuck, you’re about to fly to the southern-most tip of South America (a continent you’ve never been to before!) and then get on a fucking boat to the bottom of the world! You’re going to rock and roll through the Drake Passage, you’re going to see an absolute shitton of penguins and seals, and you’re going to see leopard seals fucking them all up!
This is an important, expensive, and exciting trip - stop trying to protect yourself from disappointment and start living life as fully as you can as you experience things you love!

content:
Writing a book about cave diving isn’t just the “right thing to do”, it’s also something I genuinely love the idea of doing. Writing is a huge part of my life and how I process things over time, and Diving is equally important to me having been part of my life for nearly 30 of my 40 years now. Cave diving is something that I’m fiercely passionate about and incredibly invested in, so it makes sense that I’d be drawn to the idea of combining these interests into writing a book about cave diving, especially if I put it in the context of my first 500 cave dives.
Beyond the most obvious elements though, I know that writing a book about cave diving is important to both the sport and myself. I’m a good and engaging writer, and I know deep down that writing is where I excel - the artform that I know I’m strongest at, where I can make the greatest impact. Likewise, I am an exceptional cave diver with a natural instinct for finding new tunnel where others couldn’t. Discovering and sharing new tunnel with people, being able to show non-divers why we do the dives we do, and embracing that raw sense of exploration all help me be a better version of myself.
There’s also no doubt that a lot has happened in the last 6 years too, as much above water as below. Right now I have a lot of strong feelings about the Australian cave diving community and the way I’ve been treated by specific parts of it over the last couple of years. There’s no question I’m angry and hurt about some of it, but that’s not my motivation for writing this book - if it were, I’d have thrown the idea out months ago. But I know this is a worthwhile project to pursue, specifically because I’m worried that my anger over the vindictive and petty politics will spill out into a book that might encourage others to engage with cave diving. I genuinely love this sport, and the last thing I’d want would be to write something that put people off it because of the old-boy politics that goes on.
I have numerous things that I could write, and probably plenty of other things that in some ways I should write before a book on cave diving… but I know this is the right thing to do. If I were to switch my daily Mini Essays over to writing about various dives I’ve done, I have no doubt I’d be able to create this book in a matter of months. Better yet, I’d love to turn my daily Mini Essays into a project to write up the 101 Things that I’ve completed, and then allocate a separate hour each day to writing about my 500 cave dives.
Part of me worries that I’ll need more time to write these things than I’m currently willing to give, or that I won’t write them properly because I’m trying to make them fit into the #mini-essay format. But those are both poor excuses for procrastination - ultimately this is just about showing up and writing the next thing on the list. The Book - 101 Things will be incredibly straight forward because you just need to write the next entry on the 101 Things - Complete List list. Likewise with your cave diving book, you just need to write about the next dive. That may mean putting together a list of your cave diving experiences so you can simply pick the next entry and start writing about it, but creating that list should be fairly straight-forward (especially if you add “Make a list of cave dives” to your Tasks).
So why am I writing a book about cave diving? Because I have some incredible experiences to share and stories to tell - I saw that first hand talking to Mitch and Keith at the bottom of Murra El Elevyn when I was causally dropping stories while sorting out gear that was blowing the minds of them both. I’m writing this book because people are interested in what I do, the cave diving stories are particularly great, and I love sharing experiences with people who are interested.
As I write this book, just remember that “interesting” is the key. My goal with Cosmic Nomad was to make it as funny as possible, but that’s not the aim this time around. In the wise words of Ivor Dembina, “You don’t always have to be funny, but you do have to be interesting.”

content:
Related:
One of the challenges I routinely face is trying to prioritise writing as a regular practice. or as any kind of practice, regular or not. I know that I love writing, and even as I type this I can feel that sense of creation that I truly crave whenever I sit down and start typing out my thoughts on a keyboard - a particularly visceral experience where each click of the keyboard is another step towards an artistic expression that’s yearning to be shared.
Over and over again however, I find myself either distracted or making other things a priority over sitting down to write something I really want to write. There is SO much in my Mini Essays document which is just begging to be written about, and that’s not even taking into account all the writing I want to do towards a cave diving book, all the writing I’d like to do about the cave diving sites I love, or all the writing you have queued up around the #101-Things and your #bucket-list.
There is an extraordinary amount of writing that you genuinely want to do, but time and time again you find yourself trying to finish other tasks before you’ll write. Today is a classic example - you made writing a mini essay your highest priority for today, and you’re only just sitting here typing it out at 9pm after a full day of doing other shit. Was that other shit important? Absolutely! You spent a significant chunk of today fixing your Digital Garden so that you can better share the notes and ideas that you have. But was it the highest priority for today? Certainly not.
I think part of the challenge is not feeling inspired to write about certain things when you sit down. But you also know that inspiration is bullshit - you simply need to write, and the inspiration comes from turning your creative outlet into a habit and an obsession. You have an extraordinarily long list of potential mini essay topics to write about already, so there’s no reason why you can’t glance at any one of them and start typing. In fact, the entire point of the mini-essays is to start writing when you’re NOT inspired! They’re there to lower the barrier to entry on writing - something that doesn’t mean much, but you can use to process ideas in a quick and easy way without being too invested on whether the writing is good or not. Assume the writing is bad, but simply get writing and turn it into a habit.
The idea of making writing a priority/habit/obsession is all about turning up to work on it every day. My journal is good for processing things on a personal level, and it’s nice to slow down and write things out by hand. But what I write there is never going to be published (burning my journals still feels important) and something certainly changes when you know that your writing may have an audience (however small). Journaling the things that shouldn’t be said aloud seems vital to my mental health, but not as important as writing out my ideas and making them available for others to read too.
So how do I make writing a priority and avoid being distracted? Easy - you make writing something that you must do each day. Journaling doesn’t count: you need to make sure that you write something each day that could be read by other humans. It may have taken you until 9pm tonight to sit down and write this, but you’ve done it, and 20 mins later you’re struggling to wrap this up into a conclusion because you want to keep typing.
Make writing for publication a priority for each day, even if it’s just a mini essay (most of them will probably be mini essays), and before you go to bed each night you need to set a plan on what to write the next day. You can even build it into your Template - Mini Essay - add “tomorrow’s mini essay” to the template so that you can put down some sort of plan for the next day before you close out today.

content:
Throughout most of my 20’s I was certain I wouldn’t be alive to turn 30. It’s not like I can pinpoint exactly where that idea came from, but there’s no question it was a recurring belief that shaped the way I thought and planned my life. If I try to trace it back, I suspect I’ll wind up back at April 19th, 2008. I made a choice that night to live, and it was certainly a close-call, but I’ve used that night as a reference for most of my life since - no matter what awful shit I’ve been through since then, I know that I will never allow myself to be trapped in that mindset ever again, where suicide felt like the only way out.
But I know those thoughts didn’t suddenly disappear that night just because I made a decision to live. Looking back on it more than 17 years later, I think that sense of despair evolved from feeling helplessly trapped and suicidal, and it became a sense that I’d die in the next few years doing something ridiculous. Not because I actually wanted to die, or that I was seeking out an end, but simply because I was throwing my full force at things and activities that made death by misadventure likely.
Breaking out of that depressive-suicidal cycle, I think I started thinking “I got through my darkest valley, so now it doesn’t matter what happens”. In many ways that’s exactly that healthy mindset I needed and still want to cultivate. Where it went too far was signing up for dangerous, awful things because I didn’t think staying alive mattered at all. I remember thinking that the French Foreign Legion or the British Royal Marines were the only places I might feel a sense of belonging, because shooting and blowing things up were “all I was good for”. Because I was still hurting, and I thought at least I could die through circumstances I created rather than directly ending it myself. I didn’t think I’d make it to 30 because I believed I’d die in a firefight or trying to defuse an IED - not because I wanted to serve the greater good, but because that’s all I thought I was good for, and maybe I’d die doing something that might matter.
Seeing what I saw in the marines, it was pretty clear that shit regularly happens to good people and it doesn’t mean anything in the grand scheme of things. Realising that is why I left - because awful, meaningless things would happen to people I cared about, and I didn’t want to be the person I needed to be to survive and protect others in an environment where people often died through meaningless violence.
Leaving the military didn’t fix the sense that I had nothing to offer though, and if I’m honest it made it even worse. I didn’t slip back into seeking death through suicide - I’d never allow myself to be mentally trapped in that space again. But I did still see death before 30 as an “inevitable relief”, and I think that only started to change with Mars One.
Suddenly Mars One gave me the opportunity for a “death” that would be worthwhile and 10 years away - after that “inevitable” end point of 30. I had a reason to get out of bed every day, because I was working towards something extraordinary. Something that would help people, which gave me a sense of meaning, and would still provide the sense of finality that I seemed to need. Leaving for Mars would be a relief, because I could let go of the complications and pain of life on Earth, and serve humanity by being as far away from it as possible.
Losing Mars One hurt me profoundly, and it continues to taunt me as that thing I put every once of my being into for 10 years which eventually just dissolved. Mars One gave me a reason to look forward to a life beyond 30, and now that I’m 40 I wonder what meaning I get from the life I live today? In some ways my life doesn’t matter at all - I’m just one human of billions that’s wandering around this planet doing things and trying to find meaning from it. But I’m still here, and I still have the opportunity to live, breathe, and help others every day.
There are so many things that I would never have experienced or learned about myself if I’d made a different choice on that night in April 2008 - rediscovering my passion for science and exploration through Mars One for starters. And there are so many extraordinary things I’ve been lucky enough to do in the last 10 years since I turned 30 - I’ve written two books, toured globally as a comedian, met astronauts, discovered caves, owned a cave diving hostel, and been celebrated as a world-class explorer. In less than two weeks I’ll be on my next extraordinary adventure in Antarctica!
I’m incredibly lucky to be here, and I can’t even begin to imagine what kind of incredible experiences I’ll have over the next 10 years if I’m still alive at 50. I don’t want to die, but I’m going to make damn sure that when I do go I’ll do it with my stories told and no doubt in anyone’s mind that I made the most of the time I had.

content:
Now that you’ve been suspended by the CDAA, you have an amazing opportunity to look ahead and ask what kind of future you want to have in cave diving. You knew the suspension was coming, and you’ve been more than emotionally ready to tackle it - part of you has even relished it finally coming to pass. So the question now is how you want to develop as an exploration cave diver outside of Mt Gambier and the CDAA.
First and foremost you’re heading to Sulawesi to dive and chat to Robin Cuesta, which presents exciting opportunities for both your podcast and to discuss the importance of water security. A major point of interest for your cave exploration is to give it a purpose and scientific legitimacy - you want to explore not just for the sake of exploring, but to also bring back valuable data and to help the people who are responsible for the land you’re diving under.
Your future also involves diving outside of Mt Gambier, and mostly outside of Australia for that matter too. There’s no doubt you want to visit incredible places and to help others see them too - your real interest is in making adventures easier for everyone so they can support the exploration too. At the heart of this however is your own desire to explore, experience and share cave diving with others - to tap into that passion for an “underground Google Maps” that you dreamed of so many years ago. That means having a list of places you want to explore AND to collect publishable data from. It’s not enough to just see these places and take a select few - you really want to share these places with anyone who’s interested, to feed that passion for adventure, and to do good science so we can understand these places better.
So ask yourself - where do you want to cave dive, and how can you collect great data to support the production of incredible maps and models for the places you visit? Even the most touristy caves don’t have 3D models, so don’t just go for the most difficult or remote places you can think of - dives like Mjonar Janos and Gozo are absolutely worth the journey. And don’t worry about how you’ll fit this around work - you have the resources to do these things, so plan them out and make them happen. Whatever you figure out with work, you’ll be able to support yourself and see the places you want to see.
First priority? Figure out how to get Lewy to the Eastern Mediterranean, and make sure you record that journey. Taking Australia’s pre-eminent underwater cave geologist on his dream trip would be an extraordinary thing to do, and there’s only so many years available to do it.

content:
Ask yourself “What is your evil secret plan?”. Ultimately this is a question about how you’re going to use the system to do the things that YOU want to do and live the life you want to live. We’re not talking about blindly trying to “Live your dreams” - we’re talking about gaming the system so it looks like you’re playing along with everyone else, but you’re hacking the game so you do exactly what you want regardless of what others may expect or even demand of you. So you’re not playing by any rules, but you are faking compliance while you put all the pieces into place to subvert expectations.
For you, it’s clear you want to explore the universe and share those experiences with others through videos and books - it’s where your interest in Jacques Cousteau comes from. Under the current paradigm you need an income to live, to travel, and to share the adventures you go on - I’m not interested in trying to subvert Capitalism, but it doesn’t mean I’m not a Communist at heart. So you need to earn money, but that’s just a tool for doing what you really want to do.
My evil secret plan is to subvert the muggle world and live like a folk legend. You want folks to say “Yeah, I met Josh Richards - he was doing some ridiculous shit and then he disappeared again”.
My evil secret plan is to never let the muggles know what I’ll do next - to have layers they’ll never touch, to have connections and stories from every corner of human experience, and to leave the people I meet wondering how the fuck I’ve done all this shit in the time I’ve had, knowing they’ll never understand.
My evil secret plan is earn enough money to turn up in all sorts of weird places whenever it suits, to carry out random acts of kindness, and to disappear again. I don’t want stability or infrastructure or predictability - I want to adapt to unexpected chaos and to keep moving forward as the universe throws new and unusual things at me.
My evil secret plan is that there is no plan - I’m just tacking my way through the flow of the universe. If I feel the wind changing, then I’ll work with it. If the drops to nothing, I’ll wait. But when it picks up again, I’ll use it - to go with it, to tack into it, or to cut across it. It doesn’t matter - what does matter is that you explore the universe and you share it with others who won’t go to the places or situations that you will.
References “To see the world, things dangerous to come to, to see behind walls, to draw closer, to find each other and to feel. That is the purpose of life.”
“Life” motto from “The Secret Life of Walter Mitty”

Details Identification Feature type: Cave Cave and exploration data Cave rating: Advanced Highest cave rating: Advanced Goes to water: Yes Diving data Water type: Fresh Tidal: No References Portions of the following information were taken from www.cavediving.com.
The entrance to Minotauro (the Minotaur, from Greek mythology) is directly across from Club Robinson Tulum, and immediately to the right of the new Pemex station. Be forewarned: The road back is rugged and there is not a lot of parking space at its end.
Minotauro is an excellent example of why it is a good idea to employ a professional guide — at least until you gain a much greater familiarity with area dive sites. Without a guide, you could waste an entire dive simply trying to find the right cave entrance (it is nowhere near as obvious as it may seem).
A good first dive is simply to take the main upstream line all the way to its end (it loops back on itself, forming an enjoyable circuit dive). If your gas consumption is good, you may even be able to take an offshoot tunnel to another cenote, such as Cenote Escalera or Cenote Estrella.

Details Identification Feature type: Cave Source: Wondermondo.com Cave and exploration data Exploration potential: Medium Tourism potential: Low Additional Notes “Initially it was considered that the cave passages at the bottom of Minyé are not too significant. This was not true.
Thus far there have been investigated 5,421 m long passages, but this may be just a small part of the system.
Powerful subterranean rivers require large passages – and caves under Minyé certainly are giants in this respect. The largest room in this cave is Tuké chamber – one of the largest cave chambers in the world. It is 240 m long, 200 m wide, and 180 m high. The floor area of this chamber is 48,000 m², volume is 6,240,000 m³.
Cave system contains exciting cave organisms, many of them endemic.” “Caves in Nakanai belong to the technically most difficult caves in the world. Everything here is challenging – coming to this far-away (when looking from Europe or the United States) place, ascending the wild, jungle-covered mountains along the slot canyons of torrential rivers in nearly constant rain. Imagine building your camp in the wet jungle, in constant rain. Jeez, think about the bad odor from feet, better have separate tents… Then one should descend half a kilometer deep, through the jungle – can you imagine hanging in half a kilometer-long rope?
And only then it begins… Pristine, incredibly beautiful and opulent dripstone formations, giant passages, and the constant roar of rivers struggling through the cave and falling over countless waterfalls. Only the most experienced explorers should dare to dive into this powerful stream to pass the numerous siphons.”

Details Identification Feature type: Cave Reference: 6J-3 System name: Drovers Cave National Park Additional Notes Mindat.org: https://www.mindat.org/loc-25591.html When you get a collection of bats roosting in a cave, you clearly end up with a pile of bat guano underneath. This sometimes reacts with the chemicals in the rock of the cave, and over time produces minerals, sometimes including rare new species. Often bland and powdery, these species are highly sought after by collectors of rare mineral species. In Australia, mineral species are available from some caves on the Nullarbor in Western Australia, a couple of caves in Victoria, and Moorba Cave which is a little inland from Jurien Bay, Western Australia, in the Drovers Cave National Park. Jurien Bay is 220 kilometres north of Perth.
This limestone region contains a number of shallow caves. Moorba Cave is shallow but a torch is still needed and is open to the public. A four-wheel-drive vehicle is essential. The guano was caused by the bat species Macroderma gigas (Ghost Bat). The soluble components in the cave are brushite, ardealite, gypsum, and collophane, with insoluble quartz. Taranakite is minor. Newberyite was recently discovered in the cave.
This heathland region contains more species of flora per square kilometre than the Amazon rainforest.
References Journal: https://library.dbca.wa.gov.au/static/FullTextFiles/064008.pdf Images

The unique feature of this fresh water cave is that it starts in the Mediterranean Sea. In the beautiful village of Benitachell, to the right of the car park near the beach, there is a little basin protected from the waves, that one can use to get into the water and avoid the swell and sand from a traditional shore entry. From here one needs to swim some 100m along the cliff face to find an opening in the wall (clearly visible from the surface); inside one gets a beautiful view of the cliff rising some 100m up and one then needs to find water conduit pipes and hoses that lead into the cave.
The first 200m of the cave are large (some 5m diameter tunnels) and not very clean; a lot of human debris and junk has been left in the cave and it is considerably damaged in some places. The cave only drops below 30m after 600m of penetration.

content: Details Identification Feature type: Cave Cave and exploration data Cave rating: Advanced Highest cave rating: Advanced Goes to water: Yes Diving data Water type: Fresh Tidal: No References Portions of the following information were taken from Florida Geological Survey Bulletin 66. Morgan Spring is located approximately 3.2 miles northwest of Ellaville on the northern Withlacoochee River. From the intersection of US 90 and CR 141 just north of Ellaville, travel east on CR 141 approximately 1.8 miles to the bridge over the Withlacoochee River. Morgan Spring is located on the east bank approximately 2.5 miles north of the SR 141 bridge. Description - Morgan Spring has a man-made dam about 9.0 ft long which impounds the spring and creates the spring pool. There is a large wooden deck around the spring pool. The vent is located roughly in the center of the pool. The spring pool is oval shaped and measures 81.0 ft long and 66.0 ft wide. The depth is 19.2 ft; however, Hornsby and Ceryak (1998) reported a maximum depth of 80 ft. During the September 2002 visit, the water was dark with poor visibility. The spring pool was completely covered with duckweed, and no boil was visible on the spring surface. The spring run flows northwest about 400 ft into the Withlacoochee River. The run has large limestone boulders and contains slow-moving water that is covered with duckweed. The surroundings are densely forested. High ground surrounding the spring varies from 3 ft to the east to 25 ft to the northeast above the pool. A house is situated 150 ft southwest of the spring, and Morgan Spring is surrounded by private land. Discharge on June 10, 1998 measured 17.59 ft3/s. An aquatic cave system is present at this spring and has been explored by divers.
title: Morgan Spring

Details Identification Feature type: Cave Reference: L0034b Source: Forestry SA Cave and exploration data Cave rating: Cave Vertical access: Yes Exploration potential: Low Tourism potential: High Disabled access potential: Medium Goes to water: Yes Diving data Water type: Fresh Tidal: No Access and warnings Forestry
Amenities hasShowers: No hasToilets: No References LSECR: Page 84 Morgans Cave is a horizontally-developed feature containing more than 200 metres of passage and several very interesting features. Its entrance is a one metre diameter, nearly perfectly circular (and almost certainly artificially-enlarged) “chimney” tube in a small doline, which drops vertically for about 6 metres to the top of a cone of dirt and domestic rubbish. The main (popular) route is via a low duck-under to the north-west, towards an adjacent forest track, where the passage slopes down a little and immediately opens up into a wide, high gallery which is unfortunately badly marked with graffiti of all types (including red spray-paint). Further along this section, one encounters some water-table pools and stepping stones, and evidence of phreatic solution becomes apparent in the beautifully sculptured shapes and tube-like passages which are to be found in many areas. Some old decoration remains, but most has been damaged, removed or destroyed over the years. Due to the presence of masses of ugly tree roots, the south-eastern side is not so popular, but if cavers can put up with the effort of battling through the heftier ones (climbing a few small boulders and watching out for snakes in the rubbish near the entrance!), a final crawl along a narrow section at the apparent ’end’ leads to a unique, 5 metre deep hidden lake which is viewed from a picturesque wall window (sometimes called “The Portal”). This lake was dived by the author in April 1983, but it is quite narrow and silty and does not lead to any extensions, rising to the surface again as seen by dry cavers. The cave is rated as being suitable for use as an “adventure” cave by the National Parks and Wildlife Service, whose Tantanoola Caves staff often use to encourage responsible public education about such features. Morrison Spring is approximately 4.9 miles southeast of Ponce de Leon. From I-10 just south of Ponce
de Leon, travel 3.7 miles south on SR 81. Turn east (left) on SR 181 and travel 1.7 miles. Turn
south (right) on SR 181 A. Travel 0.5 miles then turn east (left) into the park.
Description - Morrison Spring occupies a large, bowl-shaped depression and forms a circular
spring pool with a diameter of 300 ft. The vent is near the center of the pool at a depth of 46 ft.
The bottom is sand except near the vent where limestone is exposed. The water is light blue and
slightly turbid with a prominent boil on the pool surface. However, cave divers report that the
water is crystal clear in the cavern and cave system. There is abundant aquatic vegetation and
very little algae. The spring run is 150 ft wide and slow-moving. It flows approximately 0.7 miles
southeastward into the murky Choctawhatchee River. When the river is in flood stage, river water
reportedly backs up into the spring pool. On the south side of the spring run, approximately 300 ft
downstream from the pool, high ground meets the run’s shore and rises steeply to 15 ft above the
water. The spring and its run are within the western lowland floodplain of the Choctawhatchee River,
in a dense gum and cypress forest. A house and picnic pavilion are east of the spring pool, and a
cleared swath leads from the pavilion down to the water’s edge. Rosenau et al. (1977) report that
there are 3 cavities at the bottom of the spring pool. One of those cavities reaches an eventual
depth of 300 ft.
Utilization - The spring is a private park operated primarily for swimming and scuba diving.
title: Morrison Springs

Amenities hasShowers: No hasToilets: No hasPhone: Yes family: Good parking: Ok Additional Notes CAVE/KARST FEATURE NUMBERS: 5L69/70 MOUNT BURR CAVE (Pub Paddock Cave; Mt. Burr Bat Cave). This extensively-developed cave system has long been known, although its relatively isolated location in a swampy area of forest many kilometres from the nearest town has protected it from excessive visitation. Access is best made via SL69, which is a group of low openings at the base of a rockface around the perimeter of a swamp basin, 51.70 is more difficult, being some 50 metres up a nearby rise and consisting of a 2m diameter chimney-type tube or shaft about 4 metres deep. It basically consists of some 300 metres of irregular passage about 50m wide and between 1.5 and 4.5m high, containing quite a lot of decoration, a few weird “sculpted” shapes and some guano (ie, bat poo!). The feature was mentioned by the Reverend Julian Edmund Woods in his “Geological Observations in South Australia” (1862), where he described it as being accessible only via a “…very small aperture, through which a man can barely creep” Father Woods went on to say that after moving through the orifice, “a very large chamber is discovered, with the roof not more than sixteen, or, in places, at most twenty, feet from the ground, but very irregular. There are few or no stalactites, but the water drops through in quantities quite large enough to make them in a very short time, and, therefore, we may conclude that the caves have not been very long in existence. “…the whole extent of the caves has not been ascertained, but they have been followed for an immense distance, without diminishing in width or in height” Father woods also went on to discuss the fine tree roots, thick mud deposits and fossil bones which he observed. CEGSA first became aware of the feature through the overseer of the District Council of Beachport, Mr. Bob Somerville, sometime prior to January 1964 the date of the Trip Report by Bob Sexton. In October 1964, Elery Hamilton-Smith reported that the cave had a good population of bats, and that “this cave hast yielded a large number of recoveries of Naracoorte bats including some of the first ones banded”. The feature really doesn’t appear to extend for what even local cavers would call an “immense distance”!

content:
INTERVIEWER: That’s the character who makes a brief appearance in Something Wicked This Way Comes, right? And you’ve often spoken of a real-life Mr. Electrico, though no scholar has ever been able to confirm his existence. The story has taken on a kind of mythic stature—the director of the Center for Ray Bradbury Studies calls the search for Mr. Electrico the “Holy Grail” of Bradbury scholarship.
BRADBURY: Yes, but he was a real man. That was his real name. Circuses and carnivals were always passing through Illinois during my childhood and I was in love with their mystery. One autumn weekend in 1932, when I was twelve years old, the Dill Brothers Combined Shows came to town. One of the performers was Mr. Electrico. He sat in an electric chair. A stagehand pulled a switch and he was charged with fifty thousand volts of pure electricity. Lightning flashed in his eyes and his hair stood on end.
The next day, I had to go the funeral of one of my favorite uncles. Driving back from the graveyard with my family, I looked down the hill toward the shoreline of Lake Michigan and I saw the tents and the flags of the carnival and I said to my father, Stop the car. He said, What do you mean? And I said, I have to get out. My father was furious with me. He expected me to stay with the family to mourn, but I got out of the car anyway and I ran down the hill toward the carnival.
It didn’t occur to me at the time, but I was running away from death, wasn’t I? I was running toward life. And there was Mr. Electrico sitting on the platform out in front of the carnival and I didn’t know what to say. I was scared of making a fool of myself. I had a magic trick in my pocket, one of those little ball-and-vase tricks—a little container that had a ball in it that you make disappear and reappear—and I got that out and asked, Can you show me how to do this? It was the right thing to do. It made a contact. He knew he was talking to a young magician. He took it, showed me how to do it, gave it back to me, then he looked at my face and said, Would you like to meet those people in that tent over there? Those strange people? And I said, Yes sir, I would. So he led me over there and he hit the tent with his cane and said, Clean up your language! Clean up your language! He took me in, and the first person I met was the illustrated man. Isn’t that wonderful? The Illustrated Man! He called himself the tattooed man, but I changed his name later for my book. I also met the strong man, the fat lady, the trapeze people, the dwarf, and the skeleton. They all became characters.
Mr. Electrico was a beautiful man, see, because he knew that he had a little weird kid there who was twelve years old and wanted lots of things. We walked along the shore of Lake Michigan and he treated me like a grown-up. I talked my big philosophies and he talked his little ones. Then we went out and sat on the dunes near the lake and all of a sudden he leaned over and said, I’m glad you’re back in my life. I said, What do you mean? I don’t know you. He said, You were my best friend outside of Paris in 1918. You were wounded in the Ardennes and you died in my arms there. I’m glad you’re back in the world. You have a different face, a different name, but the soul shining out of your face is the same as my friend. Welcome back.
Now why did he say that? Explain that to me, why? Maybe he had a dead son, maybe he had no sons, maybe he was lonely, maybe he was an ironical jokester. Who knows? It could be that he saw the intensity with which I live. Every once in a while at a book signing I see young boys and girls who are so full of fire that it shines out of their face and you pay more attention to that. Maybe that’s what attracted him.
When I left the carnival that day I stood by the carousel and I watched the horses running around and around to the music of “Beautiful Ohio,” and I cried. Tears streamed down my cheeks. I knew something important had happened to me that day because of Mr. Electrico. I felt changed. He gave me importance, immortality, a mystical gift. My life was turned around completely. It makes me cold all over to think about it, but I went home and within days I started to write. I’ve never stopped.
Seventy-seven years ago, and I’ve remembered it perfectly. I went back and saw him that night. He sat in the chair with his sword, they pulled the switch, and his hair stood up. He reached out with his sword and touched everyone in the front row, boys and girls, men and women, with the electricity that sizzled from the sword. When he came to me, he touched me on the brow, and on the nose, and on the chin, and he said to me, in a whisper, “Live forever.” And I decided to.
References

Mud Spring has also been known as Sulfur Spring and Mud River Spring. The spring is at the
head of Mud River, about 400 ft S. of State Hwy 50, 1.3 mi E. of Bayport, and 3,000 ft W. of the
intersection of State Hwys 50 and 595.
Description - The head pool of Mud River is about 400 ft in diameter with a 200-ft wide run
flowing from the east side. The spring is near the southwest side of the pool about 15 ft E. of a
dock. The spring basin is elongate in a north-south direction and slopes irregularly down on the
north, east, and south sides. The west side is essentially vertical to a depth of 185 ft
(Sinclair, 1977, Table 2). Divers report a horizontal westward 3 mi per hour current at a
depth of 50 ft. The bottom is obscured by a brown flaky material, probably algal, that gives the
river and spring the name “Mud.” Tidally affected, Mud Spring discharge has been measured at
128 ft3/s on January 18, 1961; and at 101 ft3/s and 83.1 ft3/s on a changing tide on
December ll, 1975. The chloride content, based on a specific conductance of 23,000 micromhos/cm,
was 8,000 mg/L at a depth of 58 ft, and the temperature was 20.5°C. (69°F.) on December 16, 1960.
Mud Spring is a fishing and boat launching site.

Maps CaveDB - site - 40aeb711-ea4dacca.kml — Source References LSECR: Page 192 The CEGSA number 5L97 was originally allocated to a large oval sinkhole with dimensions of about 30 x 25 metres and some 5m deep, which has a flat floor containing a lot of cutting grasses and other swamp plants (unfortunately including the stinging nettle Urtica incisa). In his CEGSA Trip Report dated 28 June 1965, Fred W. Aslin mentioned that “water is accessible in the north-western end and shows promise of going to some considerable depth”, and this suspicion was confirmed when cave divers followed a flooded passage into a low silty chamber which pinched off 17 metres below the surface. Although divers had visited the then-unnamed cave in the mid-1960s, the general cave diving fraternity, keen to find exciting “new” sites, only began to hear of the feature in the early 1980s. when it was called “Elaines”. (This name seems to have been brought into being through a mis- take, when someone confused the sinkhole with another feature nearby, 5L84/85 (Alleyns Cave), because the pronunciation for Alleyn - according to Mr. Alleyn, who used to live nearby - sounds like Al-Lain.) Because 5184/85 was identified as Alleyns Cave on fire-control maps, and to avoid further confusion and possible delays in the event of an emergency, 5L97 was renamed “Mud Hole” by the CDAA in the mid 1980s after discussion with the Woods and Forests Dep- artment. In 1990, Adelaide divers Grant Pearce and Chris Murphy dug out a mass of loose rubble fill at the south-eastern end of the doline and reached the water table, subsequently discovering the much larger waterfilled Nettle-Bed Cave, which was given a completely different number (SL290) to prevent it from being confused with Mud Hole. The water is constantly shaded and subsequently usually very clear, and cave-adapted crustacea have been observed here. Nevertheless, it is far from an exciting dive and really only entices divers who are getting desper- ate! Forestry SA: L0097, Thin Roof: N, Fence: N. Dimensions: ?. Features: popular diving site www.cavediving.net.au: https://www.cavediving.net.au/images/articles/maps/5L-97.gif https://www.cavediving.net.au/index.php/siteinfo/?site=37: Small water-filled cave on the edge of a large shallow doline. https://www.trimixdivers.com/trimix5/?p=4935: Mud hole is in the same (ex) pine forest as Pines and Iddlebiddy Cave, and lies in the same doline as Nettle bed. The water in mud hole is crystal clear… until you get in. The bottom is covered in thick, black, sticky mud, hence the name. It?s practically impossible to get in the water without stirring it up. The method we used was, one foot on the step, one foot in the mud. Completely inflate dry suit and wing, and jump out face first as far as possible, slapping on the water, but not touching the mud, except for that first step. If you can do this successfully, and put your fins on in the deeper water, you’ll have an enjoyable dive. If you silt up too bad, get out and go back tomorrow. On descent, you’ll be traveling down a fairly steep, narrow tunnel, to a smallish room, with a slot in the floor. Through this vertical slot is the main chamber, with a depth of about 16meters. Until recently, everyone thought this was the end of the dive, but in the far corner of this chamber, is a VERY tight restriction, which a diver with side mounted 7’s can JUST squeeze through. This leads down another 5 meters into another, smaller chamber. Quite a pretty little dive, if you don’t silt up. Two divers maximum, as more will cause more silt, and its really too small for more anyway.
On the way back out, you will see the (hopefully small amount) silt you caused on entry rolling down the tunnel, making it quite dark on exit. If you do silt out badly on entry, and continue the dive (you’ll be out of the silt quite quickly on descent), you’ll be coming out of the dive, including the restriction, in an almost total blackout.

About Also known as Cocklebiddy 3 Mile Cave, the entrance is a small overhanging doline 20m in diameter. A 20m pitch leads to a loose talus and silt slope which becomes a boulder floored passage after the doline. The passage continues to a small lake at 89m. There are wetas near the entrance of the cave. There was a thylacine carcase found on early trips to the cave. Uphill of the lake leads to further boulder floored chambers with bats. There are 300m of low maze passages beyond the lake, which contains gypsum flowers and needles. The cave breathes in maze section. Beyond the lake underwater, the cave extends into a series of passages and boulder floored chambers with an average depth of 10m. There is a section of silt floor and parts of the cave passages which have a colouration similar to “coffee and cream”. There are three cave passages which have small air chambers.
Access The cave is close to a vehicle track. It is possible to camp near the cave. A typical trip into the cave would take up to 5 hours.
Rigging A 20m ladder or SRT is required. Rigging off trees near the entrance is the best option for anchors.
Cave Diving There are fixed lines in the side passages, these are shown on the map N47-CEG34002, parties will need to use their own reel to reach these fixed lines. It is possible use tripods to lower gear from the high side of the doline to reduce transporting of gear down the steep talus slope. Rigging to a vehicle is the best option for anchoring the tripod from this point.
Land use The cave is on Nuytsland Nature Reserve, and specific permission is required to visit the cave.
Potential Leads Interfaces around the “large rock” in the main chamber
Breakdown piles often mask bypass tubes. Check behind and above the boulder for blind domes or tube lips; inspect for faint percolation staining or clean, eddy-scoured floor patches indicating through-draft water movement.
“Gary’s Back Passage” and the entrance-to-main-tunnel shortcut Both are named as Advanced segments—good flags that they’re tighter/less travelled. These are prime spots to find side tubes that were skipped when the main line was established. Slow, close wall-scans often reveal inset phreatic notches.
Joint-controlled leads aligned with regional structure Nullarbor caves commonly exploit joint sets; historical mapping notes exist for Murrawijinie (SA) showing joint frequency plots—useful analogs for what to look for in plan view at Murra-el-Elevyn: straight runs, right-angle turns, bead-string chambers.
Ceiling domes & cupolas in the half-filled network
In mixed air/water sections, inspect cupolas for high-level feeders. Dry-tooling to a visible rim may reveal a tubes’ continuation once submerged a few metres farther on.

Details Identification Feature type: Sinkhole Cave and exploration data Vertical access: No Tourism potential: Medium Goes to water: No Additional Notes History of The Musufur Sinkhole in Qatar The Musufur Sinkhole in Qatar occurs with a geological layer called the Upper Dammam Unit. It was formed with the water created a dissolution layer of gypsum, that led to an overlaying stratum of lime-stone to collapse eventually, like any other Karst caves in the Middle East. A layer of Dolomite fell apart with the size of the chamber underneath. It continues to evolve and will in the future as well. Pieces of rock from the dolomite and limestone layers fall and huge sections of the roof could collapse one fine day.
What Can One See In The Sinkhole Musfur? Sinkhole Musfur is one of the deepest accessible caves in Qatar. Even though the bottom is about 100m deep, most scientist believe a larger cave system extended even further. People will have to adjust their eyes in the dark as the cave is quite small, however a larger chamber opening up will be seen. One can also see:
Layering of different kinds of rock and sediments Graffiti on the rocks Hundreds of nesting birds Traces of small mammals
Things To Do In Musfur Sinkhole One of the many things to do in Qatar is to scramble down into the cave. One can wear normal shoes while walking around the cave, but will expect a lot of sand in their shoes. One of the many activities people can enjoy is rock- climbing or bouldering, one of the adventure activities in Qatar. There are a few boulder issues that will keep you occupied for a while. Visitors have on various occasions used the cool environment of the sinkhole to meditate or do Yoga.
Things To Know About The Sinkhole The sinkhole has a chain- link fence around it but is open to visitors via a small gate. There aren’t any steps in the hole, but the ground is steady for a descent. Once the climb down starts, the temperature starts to drop, suggested a much-needed break from the heat of the desert. When it comes to getting away from the treaded heat, the sinkhole is your best spot. There are certain things that people should know about the Sinkhole, which include:
No body of water to swim in at the bottom of the sinkhole It’s a sinkhole and not a cave, so don’t go around looking for bats hanging 3.Descending is a lot tougher than climbing up Heaven For Photographers In case your claustrophobic, don’t look down References Regency Holidays: https://www.regencyholidays.com/blog/biggest-sinkhole-in-qatar/ Images

Details Identification Feature type: Cave Source: Wikicave.org Cave and exploration data Vertical access: No Tourism potential: Medium Disabled access potential: Low Goes to water: Yes Additional Notes Nereo Cave is an underwater sea-cave situated on the north-west of Sardinia in the Coral riviera of Alghero, Italy. The name was given by the discovers in honour of the mythological figure Nereus, who is often billed as the Old Man of the Sea, father of the Nereids. The site is under the high limestone cliffs of Capo Caccia, 100 metres north of the famous Neptune’s Grotto. The cave is considered the biggest marine cave in the Mediterranean Sea. With the many entrances, arches and tunnels, it is possible to make dives from 0 to 35 m, through long and large tunnels, air chambers and different ways. The walls are covered with red coral and yellow leptosamnia.
With the other cape of Punta Giglio and the Porto Conte Bay, the cave is part of a Marine reserve set up in 2003. Its flora and fauna are typically Mediterranean including groupers, lobsters, congers and moray eels, and thriving crustacean life.

About Nettlebed Cave is home to a range of interesting features for cave divers to explore. The wall-scratchings which can seen once inside “The Gallery” are probable evidence of megafauna, while entrenched seashells provide insight into the cave’s Ice Age inhabitants.
Beyond The Gallery, the cave drops deeper and breaks into additional rooms containing many large, dark silt-covered boulders, black walls and white-clay floored passages.
The cave finishes in a chamber at 28m, but with an actual penetration distance from the surface of 80m.
Nettlebed Cave is only available for diving on Saturdays and Sundays. A maximum of four divers per day, with one dive each per day, is permitted.
Book through Foresttry SA here
References Images LSECR: Page 568 Nettle-Bed Cave was named by cave diver Grant Pearce, after he and his diving partner, Chris Murphy, discovered it on 27 January 1990 after labouring to remove dozens of limestone boulders which choked the south-eastern end of the popular diving doline known as 5L97 (Mud Hole). Grant and Chris’ efforts revealed the presence of a body-sized lake which dropped to an unknown depth under the wall, and their early dives found them exploring two large, virgin submerged chambers which extended for a distance of almost 80 metres from the entrance. The upper sections of the main entry passage were found to harbor unusual wall scratchings to a depth of around 7 metres underwater, and these have subsequently been tentatively identified as being prehistoric megafaunal markings (and perhaps including human petroglyphs) which require urgent protection and further detailed archaeological investigation. Further mapping and research dives were still taking place at this site at the time of this writing.
Forestry SA: L0290, Thin Roof: N, Fence: N. Dimensions: ?. Features: popular diving site
www.cavediving.net.au: https://www.cavediving.net.au/images/articles/maps/5L-290.gif
https://www.trimixdivers.com/trimix5/?p=4937: Nettle-Bed Cave (South Australia) was discovered and named by Grant Pearce and Chris Murphy in January 1990. It lies at the opposite end of the doline which contains Mud Hole, in what was until recently a large pine forest.
Early dives required divers to work their ways through the muddy entrance restriction and heaps of limestone rubble to emerge into a wider, higher entrance passage (The Gallery). This has a steep rubbly floor and numerous wall scratchings which were initially suspected as being human in origin, although later studies by specialists reached the conclusion that they were probably caused by now-extinct megafaunal animals. Some old sea-shells were also found in this area of the cave, indicating that Nettle-Bed might well have been used as a habitation site sometime before the last Ice Age ended thousands of years ago.
From The Gallery the cave drops deeper and breaks into a large room which contains many large boulders before dropping again into a low, white clay-floored passage which leads into a smaller final chamber. The cave is not deep by local sinkhole standards – just 28 metres or so in the final room, and with a penetration distance from the surface of some 80 metres – but the restrictive entrance, the delicate wall features and scratchings and the need for divers to possess excellent buoyancy control and near-perfect finning techniques resulted in the feature being rated as a “Penetration” site. The cave has also been listed as a potential site of significance under the Aboriginal Heritage Act (1988).

North Macedonia offers some intriguing caving opportunities, particularly for dry cave exploration, with limited—but potentially promising—cave diving potential. The country lies within the Dinaric karst region, which spans much of the western Balkans and is known for extensive limestone formations, karst plateaus, sinkholes, and underground rivers. Here’s a breakdown of what you can expect:
Dry Caving Opportunities North Macedonia is home to hundreds of known caves, many of which remain poorly explored. Some of the most significant include:
Slatinski Izvor Cave (also known as Slatina Cave): One of the longest and most beautiful caves in North Macedonia. Located near Demir Hisar, it features galleries, speleothems, and a river system. While dry sections are well-documented, parts of the cave remain unexplored and could offer sump diving potential. Vrelo Cave, Matka Canyon: This is perhaps the most famous cave in the country and where cave diving becomes especially relevant. Potential for Further Exploration Given the widespread karst landscape, it’s likely that many spring sources and sumps in the country remain unmapped or uninvestigated. Particularly promising are:
Karst springs in the Mavrovo and Pelagonia regions, which could hide resurgence caves. Sinkholes and poljes in the western and southern mountain ranges may conceal deep vertical systems or hydrological connections between dry and submerged cave systems. Regulatory and Access Notes Caving and diving are largely unregulated at the hobbyist level, but protected areas like Matka Canyon may require permits for organized expeditions. Collaboration with local speleological societies such as the Macedonian Speleological Federation is advisable for gaining access and understanding the current state of cave mapping.

Brief History & Ethos of the Digital Garden Avoiding “personal blog” and more like free-form work-in-progress wikis A collection of evolving ideas not organised by publication Half-finished thoughts that grow and evolve with time “Less perfect” - like the early days of the web
WikiGardeners https://wiki.c2.com/?WikiGardener and WikiGnomes - https://wiki.c2.com/?WikiGnome Mike Caulfield coining the term “Digital Gardening” “Campfires” as conversational spaces to exchange still-forming ideas Joel Hooks “My blog is a digital garden” Amy Hoy’s “How the Blog Broke the Web Is GitHub you digital garden? A space to share ideas, work, files, ect in a semi-structured manner?
Tiago Forte - Building a second brain - https://www.buildingasecondbrain.com/ Learn in Public (Digital Gardens without Code) - https://www.swyx.io/learn-in-public/
Web movement to break free of Squarespace and Wordpress
Six Patterns of Digital Gardens
Topography over Timelines - Context through links, publication date is irrelevant thematic piles , nested folders , tags and filtering functionality, advanced search bars or central indexes “The Piles” with links to tags is cool Continuous Growth - constantly growing, evolving, and changing Editing is one of the strengths of the web - there is no “final version” Test ideas, get feedback, evolve. Gardens make their imperfection known to readers Learning in Public - Don’t hide the rough edge Blogging evolved in premium mediocre culture (personal brands & SEO-optimised content) Digital Gardening is both public and intimate, weird and welcoming Gardening sits between chaos stream (DMs, Group Chats, Tweet threads) and cultivated artefacts (published articles/books) Include dates I planted and last tended a post Gwern.net includes: topic tags, start & end date, stage tag (draft/progress/finished), certainty (impossible/unlikely/certain), 1-10 importance tag Digital Gardening “Terms of Service” Playful, Personal, Experimental Question the established norms of a “personal website” - make space for weirded, wilder experiments Gardens avoid cookie-cutter presentation - complete with quirks, contradictions, complexity Intercropping & Content Diversity Blend AV, images, diagrams, animations, tweets, code snippets Independent Ownership Gardening is about claiming a small patch of the web for yourself Do not live on Facebook, LinkedIn, Twitter, Instagram, Medium - most rail against personal knowledge development If any of them go down, your writing goes with it Avoid walled gardens Think about how you’ll grow your own space over the next few decades, not just the next few months. This reminds me of… Losing so much work because I published everything on Patreon and then deleted my account without properly exporting everything.

About Situated to the east of Madura Pass, approximately 1400km from Perth, you’ll find a fascinating cave on the Roe Plain. Here, the limestone surface is in close proximity to the water table. This underwater cave is a complex network of intersecting fissures, with a generally small breakdown passage. It features distinct bedding planes at depths of 3, 5, and 7 meters, which house stunning horizontal elliptical phreatic passages as well as low flat passages, all interconnected. The deepest point is a 7m bedding plane, and so far, 410m of underwater passage has been explored (as of February 2004).
The water in the cave, with a temperature of a cool 16C, is saline at 18,000ppm salt, just slightly less than sea water’s 19,000ppm. It has a unique blue hue, reminiscent of Tommy Grahams Cave located to the west. This cave is particularly interesting to speleological biologists due to its rich biodiversity. It is home to the highest number of troglobitic animal species found in a single cave on the Nullarbor, including two different types of troglobitic spiders, a troglobitic cockroach, an isopod, and an amphipod, which is a small aquatic crustacean.

About Overview Located in the vast expanse of the Nullarbor desert, over 2500 km from Melbourne, Australia, lies a hidden gem known as the Olwolgin Cave. This underwater cave system, named after a nearby bluff on the Roe Plain escarpment, is a fascinating destination for adventurous divers and explorers.
Getting there The journey to Olwolgin Cave is an adventure in itself. It begins with meticulous packing for a road trip to the middle of nowhere. The route takes you through major multilane highways, rolling hills, and farmed greenery, before the landscape gives way to the single-lane highway snaking along the southern coastline of the continent.
After two days of travel, you arrive on the Nullarbor proper, where the Southern Ocean crashes against high limestone cliffs. The entrance to Olwolgin Cave is just a hundred meters from the campsite.
Unique Features Olwolgin Cave is unique in its structure, combining sculpted fissures and main conduits. The cave has two separate parts, Upstream on the left and Downstream on the right. It hosts numerous interesting features, including rocks covered in black bacteria, hanging roots, and green tannic water. Many of the passages are very tight and silty, requiring side mount configuration to pass.
The water in the cave has very high salinity, similar to Nurina Cave. The haloclines produce some amazing visual distortions. Unlike the clear-blue water and huge tunnels of the deep caves above the cliff line, Olwolgin features dark-green water. It a has approximately 2,700m of surveyed passage Upstream and 7,200m of passage Downstream.
Ecosystem Despite its rugged exterior, Olwolgin Cave is a fragile ecosystem. The cave’s beauty and fragility make it a site of great interest for divers and researchers alike. However, the cave’s delicate environment also necessitates careful exploration to preserve its natural features.
Conclusion Olwolgin Cave is a testament to the hidden wonders that lie beneath the surface of our planet. Its unique features and fragile ecosystem make it a fascinating destination for divers and nature enthusiasts. As we continue to explore these subterranean marvels, we gain a deeper appreciation for the intricate and delicate balance of our natural world.

LSECR: Page 36 Popularly known as “One Tree” after a lone pine tree which stands near the northern edge of the feature in an otherwise bare paddock, this large open “cenote”-style waterfilled sinkhole is about 36 metres in diameter with 8m high sheer walls all around, except on the southern side where a rough cutting makes access to the present-day water level relatively easy. The walls slope in towards the centre of the sinkhole for a few metres underwater and then gradually bell out, creating a flooded cavern which has a much larger diameter than the entrance lake. The top of the silt-covered collapse mound is reached at a depth of around 32 metres, where some old farming machinery (including two harrowers which are commonly called “The Harvesters”) can be found. The bottom then drops away under the walls to a flatter floor, where many large boulders and an almost-buried, upside-down car are the only items to break the otherwise featureless view. There are also some “swimthroughs” between the boulders, and some graffiti can be found on the walls near the deepest area on the northern and north-western sides. Native trout (Galaxias maculatus) and introduced redfin perch, along with various crustaceans (especially the common yabbie, Cherax destructor), are also frequently observed by divers. The first reference to this sinkhole in CEGSA’s Records was made by Elery Hamilton-Smith in December 1954, when he reported it as a “very deep lake, of bright blue colour”. Bob Sexton reported in April 1962 that the name ‘Wurwurlooloo’ was shown on older Lands Department maps and, according to Norman B. Tindale, this means “Teatree Swamp or Place”. Even older Lands Department maps referring to the cave as “Wurwurkooloo” have been found recently, and because it is widely known by cave divers (its main users) as “One Tree”, this name is nowadays preferred. The first known logged scuba dives in this sinkhole occurred in November 1962, when local divers Philip (“Mick”) Potter and Jock Huxtable descended to about 45 metres, and in the early 1980s, some preliminary environmental studies and mapping attempts by the author and others provided a lot of useful information about this mysterious place. Nitrate contamination was also low (around 13 mg/l) when samples were analysed by Mount Gambier’s Engineering and Water Supply Department around that period.
